articles.title: Serbia’s populist president Aleksandar Vučić resigns to run for prime minister
articles.summary:
Vučić not allowed to seek third presidential term and PM election will test his grip on rule after widespread protests

Serbia’s populist president, Aleksandar Vučić, has resigned to pursue…

blocks.text: Serbia’s populist president, Aleksandar Vučić, has resigned to pursue an attempt to become the prime minister in an upcoming early parliamentary election that will test his firm rule in the Balkan country after nearly two years of protests.

Vučić’s second presidential term would otherwise end in May next year. He is banned by the Serbian constitution from seeking a third term and said he was resigning to lead his rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) in the 25 October ballot.

The governing populists face a major challenge at the ballot from a youth-backed movement that led the protests triggered by a train station canopy collapse in November 2024 that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad.

University students demanded accountability for the tragedy. Their struggle for justice and against corruption has grown into a strong movement that will attempt to oust Vučić’s government after 14 years in power. Vučić has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years.
“I am resigning the duty of the president of the republic,” Vučić said, reading the text of his resignation.

The ballot in October will be held against a backdrop of high political tensions as Vučić’s populists seek to remain in office despite widespread discontent. His decision to run for prime minister is seen both as an attempt to retain a top position, and to boost his party’s chances against the student movement.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Vučić light flares outside the presidency of Serbia in Belgrade after his resignation. Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/Reuters

blocks.text: In recent weeks Vučić has toured the country with live coverage on pro-government media. He has opened new roads, offered assistance money and cheaper medicines, and visited voters in their homes. More recently, he was filmed driving in his brother’s car to some of the events.

The prime minister in Serbia is formally more powerful than the president. But Vučić still took a dominant role during his two five-year terms, sometimes presiding over government sessions and routinely announcing all important decisions and plans.

Serbia’s independent Bureau for Social Research has filed a complaint alleging that Vučić has abused a public institution as president to promote his party, which he has dismissed. There has been no response from the anti-corruption authorities that are under government control.

After Vučić’s resignation, the acting president will be a close ally and former prime minister, Ana Brnabić, who is the outgoing speaker of Serbia’s 250-member parliament. After a new parliament is elected in the 25 October ballot, the new speaker will take over from Brnabić, appoint the prime minister and schedule a presidential vote.

Vučić and his party have been accused of rampant corruption, organised crime links and a clampdown on democratic freedoms, including the critical media. The SNS have gradually taken control of all state institutions since coming to power in 2012, while denying abuse of office and repeatedly pledging to fight graft.

The student-backed election list includes little-known experts, professors, teachers, athletes and other individuals from all walks of life. Groups of students have been touring the country on bicycles as part of their campaign urging the rule of law and an end to corruption.

Analysts say the student group and Vučić are polling closely, heralding a tight race and a referendum-like atmosphere. Also running are Vučić’s allies, the Socialist party, a pro-EU opposition alliance and several smaller groups.

Authorities have pushed hard against protesters with police violence and detentions, as Vučić, without offering evidence, accused his opponents and critical media of an intention to “destroy the state” under unspecified foreign influence.
He told Serbia’s state RTS Television earlier on Sunday that foreign powers and unidentified people in the country planned to stir unrest on election night.
Serbia’s efforts to join the EU have stalled under Vučić because of democratic backsliding and a refusal to join sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Andy Burnham to fight next election with plan for NHS-style care service
articles.summary: PM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service that would be funded by ‘everybody’
articles.byline: Pippa Crerar, Alexandra Topping and Kiran Stacey

blocks.text: Andy Burnham will fight the next election with a pledge to finally fix the broken social care system, acknowledging that he is willing to expend political capital by asking taxpayers to cover the cost.

As Labour’s party conference began in Liverpool, he pledged to “rip the plaster off” to radically transform care, setting out a vision for a universal service that would be free at the point of use for everybody in England.

The prime minister said the new NHS-style service would be funded by “everybody” but did not give further details of how his long-term plan would be paid for, indicating that a tax rise may be on the cards.

He said Labour would put the proposals into its next general election manifesto so that voters could give their endorsement, in the hope of reducing the risk that political attacks over “death taxes” would sink the policy.

Burnham acknowledged there were risks in a nationwide reform, likely to be costly and complicated to implement, although he rejected suggestions it could cost £18bn a year. “It’s not that high,” he told the BBC.

“Somebody needs to grasp the nettle. I will be the one to do that,” he said. “I realise it might require me to spend some political capital, that it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me].”

But he said he would take his time to work out how it could be fairly funded. “The challenge in the public finances is real. So it has to be done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse. But I will bring forward proposals.”

Labour’s annual gathering is intended to be an upbeat affair, with the prime minister wanting to restore hope that some of the country’s most intractable political problems can be solved despite severe economic headwinds.
With political courage a theme of the conference, he said in an interview with the Guardian at the weekend: “There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.”

Burnham acknowledged the public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but he said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems.

A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government with limited room for manoeuvre.
On Sunday, Burnham said he did not want to focus on a “narrative of doom” about the UK’s economy but that he would show in his leader’s speech that he was prepared to take tough decisions.

He acknowledged there was “real concern” in the financial markets about the state of the British economy, pointing to the “febrile” state of the global backdrop. He said he was willing to cut government spending to balance the books, and he believed money could be saved by taking a more “productive” long-term approach to issues such as rough sleeping and youth unemployment.

Amid concerns that the government could be hemmed in at the budget by the parlous state of the public finances, he said the chancellor, John Healey, would be “highly prudent” in running the economy. “I won’t do what the previous Tory government did and take risks with the economy that are actually still hurting us right now,” he said.
Burnham suggested to the Guardian that a significant fiscal buffer would be necessary, with speculation that the Treasury could now consider £15bn acceptable.

“I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things,” he said. “But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances.”

Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said the “heavy lifting” on making the case for rejoining the EU needed to be done by the government now, after Burnham signalled that the move could be in the next manifesto.
“The pitch rolling must be done now, explaining to the country the dis-benefits of being outside the European Union and the benefits of being part of this family,” Khan said.
However, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, appeared to criticise Khan – and Burnham – telling Politico that the speculation “frankly cause[s] a lot of uncertainty for business”.

Meanwhile, plans for a third runway at Heathrow are once again up in the air after Burnham refused to say whether he backed the “contested” project, which is delayed by up to four years, saying it was “principally” a matter for London.

articles.title: Five arrested on terrorism charges after explosives found near RAF base used by US
articles.summary:
Counter-terrorism police investigate whether Iran is behind suspected bomb plot after member of public calls 999 over suspicious vehicles

Counter-terrorism police are investigating whether…
articles.byline: Jamie Grierson, Vikram Dodd and Helena Horton

blocks.text: Counter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives on three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military.

The Guardian understands that after five men were arrested on terrorism charges, investigators were examining materials found in the vans, with an initial view being they were consistent with improvised explosive devices.

Images circulating on Sunday showed shirtless men being handcuffed in a dark country lane in the early hours of Sunday after police were called to reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, which hosts US air force missions against Iran.
The suspected plot appears to have been foiled by chance when a member of the public spotted unusual behaviour late at night in the countryside from a group of men and called 999.

blocks.caption: Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air base

blocks.text: The major incident saw the residents of 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford rapidly evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre and led to a 400m cordon being placed around the white vans as robots from the army’s bomb squad examined them.
Tests were ongoing to see if the suspected explosive devices were viable, with bomb robots deployed in the Gloucestershire countryside as investigations continued.

blocks.caption: Armed police man a roadblock while posted outside RAF Fairford base in Fairford, south-west England on 27 September 2026. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: After their initial arrest over explosives offences, the five men detained early on Sunday were further arrested later in the day on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act. The pictures of the men with their shirts off could point to a precautionary measure against the risk of suicide vests or concealed weapons.

At least one van carried the logo of a fuel company and a phone number missing a digit. A real fuel company of the same name firmly rejected any connection to the incident and said: “We are extremely concerned that our company’s name has been used without our knowledge or permission.” It said it was cooperating with the authorities.

In a statement counter-terrorism police said: “At around 12.45am today (Sunday 27 September), police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase.

blocks.caption: Police moved on the three vans after a 999 call from a local resident who spotted them as she drove home. Photograph: BBC news

blocks.text: “Armed officers responded and five men were arrested in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. They were further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act.”

The arrests come as the war between the US and Iran limps on. In July Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.

Counter-terror police and the security services are searching for the motive. The circumstances of the arrest near the base and prior warnings from Tehran, leave an Iranian motive high in the investigators’ and government’s thinking. But sources warn nothing is being ruled out including a jihadist or other motive, and the UK threat level remains at severe, the second highest, meaning an attack is highly likely.
Whether there was any foreign involvement forms part of the investigation, and Iran’s ministry of intelligence and security has orchestrated attacks overseas before.

Any proven link with Iran would be a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the UK and Tehran. While several recent incidents in the UK have been linked to the Middle-Eastern country, including the antisemitic arson attack on four Hatzola ambulances in Golders Green, the alleged plot at RAF Fairford appears to be significantly more serious.

And it raises urgent questions for the UK security services after it appeared the authorities had been unaware of the alleged plot, with police only moving on the three vans after a 999 call from a local resident who spotted them as she drove home.

blocks.caption: RAF Fairford is a military base that hosts US Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict.  Photograph: Getty Images

blocks.text: The US president, Donald Trump, claimed to have had the suspects under view for a “long time” and alleged the men “were looking to do big damage” – although the Guardian understands the operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance.
“It was fantastic. Working with Britain, it was an amazing job,” Trump said.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was being updated on the matter from Liverpool, where the Labour party conference is taking place. He cancelled plans to take part in a journalists versus politicians football match in order to take calls about the incident.
He said it was “deeply concerning” and the government will “always take every step necessary” to protect people.

blocks.caption: A B‑1B Lancer bomber parked at the RAF Fairford airbase, which hosts US air force (USAF) personnel, in Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain, 27 September 2026.  Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters

blocks.text: Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs.

In March this year, after then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, granted permission for “defensive” US action against Iranian missile sites from UK bases, four American bombers landed at RAF Fairford and the US started using British bases for “specific defensive operations”.

There have been protests in recent months over the UK government’s decision to allow the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the strait of Hormuz.

At the time of Iran’s warning in July, a government spokesperson said: “Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it’s on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself.”
Evacuated residents of Whelford spoke of “heightened tensions” in recent weeks around the base with more frequent, visible police patrols.

Outside Cirencester leisure centre, Jason, a resident of Whelford who declined to give his surname, said: “There have been heightened tensions recently around the base, we are aware it is used by the USAF … It always feels pretty safe. Some residents have seen increased police patrols.”

blocks.caption: Residents of the Cotswolds village of Whelford were evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre. Photograph: Getty Images

blocks.text: It was unclear when people would be able to go back to their normal lives; those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night.

The Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles (2.4km) north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds.

blocks.caption: Fairford Youth Football club. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters

blocks.text: Richard Ocone, the assistant chief constable with Gloucestershire constabulary, said: “We appreciate the disruption this will have caused and would like to reassure them we are working as quickly as we can to get them back in their properties.”

articles.title: Tragically Hip, Feist and more inducted into Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame
articles.summary: The memory of the late Gord Downie was in sharp focus as the Kingston alt-rock band the Tragically Hip were among four musical acts inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame at a…

image.caption: From left: Paul Langlois, Rob Baker and Gord Sinclair of the Tragically Hip speak after being inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame on stage in Toronto Saturday. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment

The memory of the late Gord Downie was in sharp focus as the Kingston alt-rock band the Tragically Hip were among four musical acts inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame at a star-studded gala held at Toronto's Massey Hall on Saturday night.
Roch Voisine and members of Loverboy also inducted in Toronto ceremony Saturday
As members of the Tragically Hip took the stage to accept the honour, the band paid tribute to their bandmate, who died in 2017 after he was diagnosed with a rare and incurable form of brain cancer.
Guitarist Rob Baker shared a message he said was from Downie, "who couldn't be here."

"I stood before the songwriters' cabal, bearing gifts of drugs and alcohol. That's not enough, and that's not all. Wait over there until your number's called. I stood before the songwriters' cabal, all wide-eyed and enthralled, just to be included at all," said Baker, who stood on stage alongside his bandmates Gord Sinclair and Paul Langlois.
The Hip entered the 2026 class along with Toronto indie music pioneer Feist, the songwriting duo behind rock band Loverboy (Mike Reno and Paul Dean) and French-Canadian artist Roch Voisine.

items: Tragically Hip band members reflect on Gord Downie and farewell tour 10 years after final show
Celebratory crowd gathers in Kingston, Ont., to watch Tragically Hip's final concert

blocks.text: The inductees' beloved songs provided the soundtrack for the evening that had the crowd tapping their feet, clapping their hands and dancing in their seats as performers, including Finneas, Our Lady Peace, Wilco's Jeff Tweedy and others who took the stage for the genre-spanning tributes that covered arena rock to indie pop to love ballads.

As the tribute to the Hip closed out the night's ceremonies, a purple feathered hat hung on a microphone stand on stage, a nod to Downie's eclectic fashion. Allison Russell, who was among the artists performing the Hip's music, blew a kiss to the mic stand as she began Wheat Kings, then ended the song by saying, "We will always love you, Gord."

items: Angine de Poitrine were the big winners at this year's Polaris Music Prize gala
Canadian Country Music Awards take over SaskTel Centre in Saskatoon

blocks.text: Baker said in his speech that the band had been thrilled "to have such a great frontman."

"I remember taking (bassist) Gord Sinclair down to see him at a place in Kingston, saying, 'You've got to see this guy, we're going to stand on his coattails and ride them,"' said Baker in his speech, which also noted the Hip's practice of sharing songwriting credit among all the band members.
Finneas performs, inducts Feist

Earlier in the evening, the Los Angeles songwriter and producer Finneas inducted Leslie Feist. The brother of Billie Eilish told a charming story about a chance meeting with the Toronto singer-songwriter at an airport in 2018 before calling her an "incredibly important, inspiring figure in my life." Finneas performed her 2007 song My Moon My Man.

As she accepted her accolade on stage, Feist told the crowd, "talking is harder than singing for me" before launching into a speech that detailed how the 50-year-old musician used songs to process the ebbs and flows of her life.

"If all of the messy and meaningful and honest work can eventually lead anyone to a moment like this, then that's how I figured out how to stand here and genuinely from my heart say thank you," said Feist, who received video messages from notable figures such as Sam Smith, Joe Jonas, Olivia Rodrigo and director Jacob Tierney, whose hit TV show Heated Rivalry featured two Feist songs.

Among the evening's many captivating performances was Tweedy, who host George Stroumboulopoulos introduced as one of the best living songwriters. The Wilco frontman sang a heartfelt cover of Feist's mournful song The Park.
Lots of love for Loverboy

Earlier, Canadian songstress Amanda Marshall opened the show with a booming rendition of Loverboy's 1980 hit Turn Me Loose that had the audience up from their seats immediately, while Toronto folk singer Charlotte Cornfield followed with a smooth and soulful performance of Feist's How Come You Never Go There.

Later, the Ottawa-based musician Talk, wearing a fitted baby blue jumpsuit with fringed sleeves, rocked the venue with a high-energy cover of Loverboy's classic hit Working for the Weekend, earning him a standing ovation.

The night also included notes of Canadian pride. Jim Vallance, inducted into the Hall of Fame alongside songwriting partner Bryan Adams in 2022, began his tribute to Loverboy by saying he was "so proud to be Canadian" and pointed out that the nation punched above its weight in producing great musicians.

Dean, Loverboy's guitarist, accepted the honour on behalf of himself and lead singer Reno, who could not attend. Dean also thanked the other members of the band, including former bassist Scott Smith, who died in 2000 following a boating accident.
Voisine performs emotional duet
Other highlights included Olympic hockey gold medallists Laura Stacey and Marie Philip-Poulin, who inducted Voisine and noted the 63-year-old's time playing hockey before he took up music.

Voisine said in his speech he started writing songs only for himself. But while studying at the University of Ottawa, he'd practice his songs in his residence's stairwell and later learned fellow students would study along with his music.

Following his bilingual speech, in which he thanked his family and songwriting collaborators, Voisine performed an emotional, choir-backed duet of his ballad I'll Always Be There with French Canadian artist Isabelle Boulay.
Beloved Canadian alt-rock band Our Lady Peace closed out the show with a high-octane cover of the Hip's Locked in the Trunk of a Car.
Lead singer Raine Maida shared how watching a performance by the Tragically Hip when he was 18 inspired him to chase art over entertainment.
Before beginning the song, he told the crowd to get on their feet.
"And light your phones up for Mr. Gord Downie."

articles.title: Republican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’
articles.summary:
Thom Tillis says Trump’s decision to back Paxton over John Cornyn has put the Senate seat at risk for Republicans

US senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticized

blocks.text: US senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticized Donald Trump, his fellow Republican, for the president’s support of Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn in the Texas Senate Republican primary.

“He made a colossal mistake,” Tillis, a frequent Trump critic from North Carolina, said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union in reference to the president’s support of Paxton who defeated Cornyn in the May primary.
“John Cornyn’s a great member of the US Senate. Paxton has his challenges,” the retiring Tillis added. “We would not be spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in Texas if Cornyn had won.”
Tillis pointed to the president’s involvement in the contest and described Trump’s decision to back Paxton instead of Cornyn as an “unforced error” that has put the Senate seat at risk for the GOP.

Trump endorsed Paxton just days before the Texas attorney general defeated Cornyn, a four-term senator, and advanced to face Democratic candidate James Talarico, a in the general election on 3 November.

The race had wide implications for Trump’s strength heading into November’s midterm federal elections. Paxton will now face Talarico, a Democratic pastor and state legislator whose message of peace and populism has attracted much attention. If he wins, Talarico would become the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win statewide office in Texas.
When he chose to support Paxton over Cornyn, Trump highlighted the Texas attorney general’s record as a steadfast supporter of the president’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.
Cornyn had previously said during the 2024 presidential campaign that Republicans should move on from Trump.
In a social media post shortly before the election day, Trump said Cornyn had been “VERY disloyal” to him and implored voters in Texas to “REMEMBER!”

Paxton, meanwhile, is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud, but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement.
In July 2025, his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery.

Tillis is one of a handful of Republicans to repeatedly break with Trump and publicly criticize the president’s decisions. In April, he spoke out in defense of the Nato military alliance after Trump said he was “absolutely” considering withdrawing the US from it.

“Any president that contemplates attempting to withdraw from Nato is not only fulfilling [Russian leader] Vladimir Putin and [Chinese premier] Xi Jinping’s greatest dreams but would be undermining America’s own national security interests,” Tillis said at the time.

He also called for then secretary of homeland security Kristi Noem’s resignation after immigration agents killed two US citizens in Minneapolis in January, calling her leadership “a disaster” during the last Senate hearing before her firing.

Tillis was one of a small number of Republicans on Thursday to vote in favor of a Democrat-led war powers resolution that aimed to end the US war with Iran. Despite gaining some Republican support, the proposal failed to pass in the Senate by a 49-50 vote.

articles.title: ‘Don’t squander it’: Can Labour hang onto the Burnham bounce?
articles.summary: Conference delegates grateful ousting Starmer has paid off, but relief tempered by fiscal headwinds ahead

blocks.text: Even Andy Burnham’s closest allies accept that deposing Keir Starmer to install their man as leader was a huge political gamble. But if the mood at the Labour party conference in Liverpool is anything to go by, it is one that – so far – has paid off.

The contrast with last year, when Starmer retained his grip on the party and Burnham slunk away from Liverpool early, could not be more stark. Their relief at their turn of fortune is tempered only by the fiscal headwinds ahead.

Cabinet ministers recount how at their political meeting two weeks ago, they were shown a series of charts showing the metrics behind the Burnham bounce. One in particular stood out to those in the room.

It was a graph showing whether the public felt the government was heading in the right direction. Until the end of June, it had been on a downward trajectory as public frustration mounted over Starmer’s leadership.

But once Burnham took over at the start of July, the line suddenly rebounded and, while still in negative territory, has been moving definitively upwards since. “We’ve got a second hearing with the public,” one cabinet minister said. “We can’t squander it.”

This time last year, just 14 months after coming to power, several were privately despairing about Labour’s electoral prospects. But with an energetic new prime minister and after a difficult summer for Nigel Farage, they now believe that a second term is winnable.

It is perhaps unsurprising, then, that speculation about a snap election escalated in the run-up to the conference, to the extent that Burnham felt compelled to “knock that dead” and confirm a 2029 date instead.

Some of the prime minister’s closest advisers wanted him to rule out an early election from the off, pressing him to be explicit. “The polling isn’t good enough. We could end up being the biggest party but we could lose our majority,” one said. Another said: “Elections have to be about a choice, not a referendum on an alternative plan.”
after newsletter promotion

But others inside No 10 felt he should go to the country while the polling was good, Farage was on the back foot, and before Burnham’s big plans for change ran headfirst into fiscal reality. “Right now the public is willing to give us the benefit of the doubt – that won’t last for ever,” one said.

For his part, Burnham claims he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite the severe economic headwinds, by delivering tangible – albeit smaller – improvements in the short term while setting out a longer-term vision to transform things such as social care and youth unemployment at the same time.

“There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them,” he told the Guardian at the weekend. “I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change.”

The slogan of his first conference as leader has been “hope again” – but with the bleak global economic landscape there is less hope around than there was when he walked into Downing Street two months ago.

The first crucial test for Burnham will be next month’s budget, at which he said the government would be “highly prudent” with the public finances, amid concerns that Labour needs to reassure the markets.

But if the budget is about intent, next summer’s spending review is about proof, and as such, that could prove to be a make-or-break moment for this prime minister. It’s easy to make the promises, but much harder to deliver on them.

With obstacles ahead, the relief felt by Labour MPs and ministers in Liverpool is heavily caveated. One cabinet minister quoted Alastair Campbell’s election mantra as a warning to colleagues who might be getting ahead of themselves: “Lots done, lots to do, lots to lose.”

articles.summary: The Chinese Embassy on Sunday once again hit out at Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., accusing him of attacking China at a forum on Saturday.

blocks.text: Published September 28, 2026 2:01am
The Chinese Embassy on Sunday once again hit out at Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., accusing him of attacking China at a forum on Saturday.
In a statement, the embassy called Teodoro "extremely anti-China" and said he has been "smearing" China in an "attempt to gain political capital and serve his personal gains."
"What he said concerning China disregards the facts, distorts right and wrong, and seeks to disrupt and undermine China-Philippines relations," it said.

At the forum, Teodoro discussed various illegal activities allegedly involving Chinese nationals, including the case of dismissed Bamban, Tarlac mayor Alice Guo and the proliferation of substandard steel plants.
He said that he is investigating "nefarious" foreign activities in the country and that Beijing continues to exert pressure on Philippine interests.
Teodoro also warned that China was attempting to create a “Sinocentric” world.

While he said he did not want to foster a culture of sinophobia in the Philippines, the defense chief argued that any such sentiment would be a consequence of the actions of the Chinese Communist Party.

"He aims to drive a wedge between the peoples of the two countries and stoke confrontation between China and the Philippines and their peoples. But such attempts are doomed to fail," the Chinese Embassy said.

The Chinese Embassy made the statement on the same day it hit back at the US Embassy after the latter sided with the Philippines over Beijing's reported interference in a recent rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin Shoal.
Guo, substandard steel

Alice Guo, the former Bamban mayor, is serving a life sentence for qualified human trafficking in connection with POGO activities in the town. Also known as Chinese national Guo Hua Ping, she has also been accused of spying for China, an allegation she has denied.

The factories recently raided by authorities for substandard steel products, meanwhile, are believed to have been used as a possible point of entry for Chinese nationals who want to illegally enter and stay in the Philippines, according to the military.
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. said that the problem is "bigger than most people know," citing the danger of using substandard steel as building material.

China, meanwhile, has targeted Teodoro in its attacks, barring him and his family from entering China, including Hong Kong and Macau, and saying he distorts the facts on the West Philippine Sea encounters as well as the arrests of the Chinese steel workers. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: UK to open new refugee resettlement routes for Afghan women and Palestinians
articles.summary: Exclusive: Move by Shabana Mahmood comes after closure of Afghan scheme last year but experts say numbers too small to deter Channel crossings

blocks.text: Shabana Mahmood will announce a new legal route for refugees that prioritises Afghan women and girls and Palestinians, unfreezing a scheme that will put the most vulnerable refugees on a faster path to permanent status.

The change marks a shift in Mahmood’s approach to asylum seekers after the abrupt closure of the Afghan resettlement scheme last year and changes that will keep refugee status under constant review for two decades.

The home secretary is to say the changes will show there is fairness in the immigration system to support the most vulnerable refugees and that a balanced system will “unlock the inherent generosity of this country”.
However, immigration experts and refugee charities have said the numbers who will be eligible are too small to deter asylum seekers crossing the Channel in small boats.
The reopening of the scheme is likely to attract criticism from the right, especially as women and girls and people with disabilities are the most likely to be dependent on the welfare state.

Reform UK and the Conservatives are also likely to raise questions about security checks – which the Home Office says will be carried out – after the Sunday Times revealed that a former Hamas bodyguard had been granted asylum in the UK and was recently arrested on suspicion of being part of a terrorist plot.
Mahmood will tell the Labour conference on Sunday that she will reopen the UK resettlement scheme, which was in effect suspended for two years, though never formally closed.

blocks.caption: Shabana Mahmood is to say the changes will help ‘unlock the inherent generosity of this country’. Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA

blocks.text: The home secretary will say that a tougher migration system, combined with a new scheme for the most vulnerable, will be the best way to ensure there is still broad consensus for helping refugees.

“Fairness is what unites us in this country. A fair society is what unlocks the very best of us. Because when people think this country is fair, they are more open and generous to others. When this country feels unfair, people turn inwards. They grow less willing to tolerate difference,” she will say.

“I know the British people have not given up on their belief that we should be compassionate, live up to our international obligations, and save the lives of those fleeing war and persecution. But I also know this process must be capped and controlled, and communities must be ready and able to welcome those who come here.
“This is what we can do and who we can be as we restore control to our borders, bear down on the small boat crossings, and unlock the inherent generosity of this country.”

The Home Office expects about one in four arrivals to be Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, though numbers will initially be very small and capped each year. Under the scheme, potential refugees will undergo security and criminality checks.

Those who arrive via the scheme will have a far more generous route to permanent settlement – granted indefinite leave to remain, which will give them a five-year path, in contrast to the constant review of status for those who arrive via irregular routes such as small boat crossings.

The home secretary will also formally open another scheme announced earlier this year allowing community sponsors from next month to apply to bring refugees to build a new life in the UK. A sponsored work route for refugees is expected to follow in the spring.
Home Office sources said the plan would be to begin with numbers in the hundreds and grow to the low thousands as levels of illegal migration fall. A cap would be set each year, sources said.
Refugees will be identified by the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) and the International Refugee Assistance Project (Irap).

The scheme had stopped taking any new referrals in December 2024. By that point, it was being used by only a tiny number. It will be reopened immediately, Mahmood will announce, with priority given to people with disabilities and for women and girls deemed to be vulnerable.
Family units will be able to come together under the scheme, though not extended families because of a crackdown on family reunification introduced earlier by the government.
after newsletter promotion

Government statistics show that almost 300 “legacy cases” arrived under the existing UK resettlement scheme over the first half of this year. Officials said they were people who had been referred under the scheme before it was suspended and who had taken time to arrive in the UK.

blocks.caption: People embark in a dinghy from the northern coast of France in an attempt to cross the Channel to the UK. Photograph: Jean-François Badias/AP

blocks.text: Mahmood will also confirm two of three other settlement schemes that have previously been announced. Starting in October, charities and nonprofits will be able to apply to become sponsors, allowing communities and universities to host refugees. The first batch of arrivals on that scheme are expected to arrive by autumn next year.

Applications for sponsors for a work sponsorship route, under which companies will host refugees, will open in spring 2027. Sponsors must provide accommodation, integration support and help finding work, with the aim of reducing pressure on local authorities.

Numbers across all of the schemes are likely to be tightly limited, meaning the vast majority of refugees in the UK who arrive via irregular routes will still be subject to new and harsh restrictions on their status.

Mahmood has previously announced that refugees will have their status reviewed every 30 months for up to 20 years, with the possibility of returning them to their home countries should those be deemed safe.

Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the reopened route bore similarities to a scheme that was closed by Labour last year, and that its impact would depend on the numbers allowed to enter the UK.
“It has been framed primarily as a matter of principle – in other words, the UK should be doing its bit, and not as a strategy to reduce unauthorised arrivals.

“That is just as well, because there is no reason to believe that resettlement would have a large impact on unauthorised arrivals,” she said. Allowing in the “most vulnerable” in the resettlement part of the scheme would be a “trade-off” because of rising costs to the state, Sumption said.
“On one hand, there is widespread political support for the idea of prioritising more vulnerable refugees who would not have been able to make it over on a small boat.

“On the other hand, previous data suggests that these more vulnerable refugees, for understandable reasons, struggle more to support themselves in the UK, and fare considerably worse in the labour market, for example, than people who arrive through the asylum system,” she said.

Responding to the announcement, Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “The government deserves credit for creating new safe and legal routes that will help refugees reach the UK without risking their lives. Safe and legal routes are essential to undermining people-smugglers’ business model, but they only work if they operate at scale. That means thousands of places, not hundreds.”

articles.title: Yemen: Houthis report deadly Saudi strikes on Taiz market
articles.summary: The Houthi-run health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," vowing to retaliate. The Houthis' account of the attack cannot be independently verified.

image.caption: Children were among those reportedly killed in two Saudi airstrikesImage: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday accused the Saudi Arabian Air Force of having struck a shopping area around the central market of Taiz. The Iran-aligned Houthis said at least seven people had been killed and dozens injured.
What do we know so far?

The group's Al-Masirah TV channel showed footage of large plumes of smoke and a destroyed warehouse stacked with food in cardboard boxes. Al-Masirah TV also reported that children were among those wounded, citing the Houthis' health ministry.

Taiz is currently under the control of Yemeni government forces, but it has long been besieged by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in the country's civil war. Taiz is located in southwestern Yemen.
The escalation in fighting comes after a fragile truce between Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels broke down months ago and new regional tensions sparked by the Iran war.
The Houthi health ministry accused the Saudi Air Force of committing an "abominable crime," saying it was directly and deliberately targeting civilian sites in Taiz.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit the market, adding that blood was "unjustly and aggressively spilled" in a statement posted online.
The group has vowed to retaliate.
The claims made by the Houthis cannot be independently verified.
In response to the Houthi report, troops loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen confirmed that their air force had struck a Houthi depot and vehicles in the area.
France sends troops as Houthi attacks threaten Saudi oil
Saudi-backed coalition ramps up attacks after new Houthi offensive
The civil war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government. They went on to take control of vast swaths of the country's north.

Saudi Arabia joined forces against the Houthis the following year, leading an international coalition against them. But so far, Yemen's government forces have not been able to effectively repel the latest Houthi offensive.

Fighting has spiked in September as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them seize Yemen's entire Red Sea coast. The rebels have also launched a blockade on Saudi energy exports to coincide with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Renewed clashes are is under way in several parts of the country, with at least 125,000 people displaced by it.
The Yemeni government has meanwhile called for a general mobilization, urging Yemenis to join the army and security forces.
Yemen is one of the poorest in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.

articles.title: Avalanche in Nepal leaves 2 dead, several missing
articles.summary: An avalanche has struck the Himlung Himal base camp in Nepal after days of severe weather. Two guides are confirmed dead and at least 14 people remain missing in the remote region.

image.caption: The Himalayas in Nepal are home to many peaks popular with tourist climbers from around the globe [FILE: April 17, 2026]Image: Elisa Schu/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two people have died when an avalanche struck the base camp of a mountain in Nepal with at least 14 others still missing.
The avalanche hit the 7,126-meter (23,380-foot) Himlung Himal after several days of heavy rain and snowfall across the region.
The dead and missing are all mountain guides and staff of Nepalese expedition companies who had been preparing the base camp for paying customers to climb the mountain.

"There were a total of 14 kitchen staff members and two climbing guides from different companies who were missing," the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association said. "The two climbing guides have been found, but sadly, both were found deceased."
Unclear how many are missing

There was conflicting information as to how many people were in the affected area near the border with Tibet at the time of disaster. Local police said there were at least 22 people at the base camp when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.

Bibhuti Chand Thakur, head of trekking company Himalayan Holidays Nepal, told news agency DPA that search and rescue operations were under way. "The chance of survival remains high because of fresh snow," he said, adding that he did not yet have a definitive number of missing or survivors, as the area is remote and cut off from communication.

blocks.caption: While Mount Everest (pictured) is Nepal's most famous peak, peaks like Himlung Himal are also popular with climbers [FILE: May 21, 2024]Image: Narendra Shahi Thakuri/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Authorities had warned of severe weather across Nepal over the weekend. Rain has affected much of the country since Thursday, with snowfall reported in the higher northern regions. The conditions have disrupted roads and trekking routes and led authorities to suspend climbing and trekking activities on several mountains.
The Himalayan nation is home to eight of the world's 14 mountains higher than 8,000 meters, and trekking and mountaineering tourism is vital to the country's economy.
The latest avalanche comes as Nepal continues to recover from devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing.

articles.title: Late-night drive and a 999 call: chance encounter that led to terrorism arrests at RAF base
articles.summary:
Local people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnight

In the early hours of Sunday morning, a resident of the village of Whelford was…

blocks.text: In the early hours of Sunday morning, a resident of the village of Whelford was driving home when she saw three white vans parked on a country road.
She was immediately suspicious, she said – all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclava’d” men.
She called 999 – and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later.

The resident, who asked not to be named, told the Press Association: “It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they were planning. A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting an unusual bit of activity at 1am when the airbase is on high alert. I think it’s absolutely astonishing.”
If there had been no 999 call, it appears the authorities would have been unaware of the vans, and the potential threat they posed to nearby RAF Fairford.
People living in the area have been used to disturbance from protesters and a heavy police presence ever since the decision to allow the US air force to use it as a base for attacks on Iran.

blocks.caption: Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air base

blocks.text: But in recent weeks, they have noticed dramatically increased security measures, with the gates of the base newly barricaded.
“In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy vehicles across all gates,” another resident said.
She described them as “very big tractors and things like that” parked behind gates into the base, adding: “So obviously they’re taking security seriously.”
The resident said “great big concrete walls” had also been placed behind some gates, including on Dunfield Loop and Whelford Road.

If local people had questioned the necessity of those steps, they may have been persuaded this weekend. In the early hours of Sunday morning, others in Whelford noticed became aware of suspicious activity as the local WhatsApp group lit up with messages.

One resident of Whelford, named Jason, who declined to give his surname, said they were first aware something was happening overnight at about 1.30am, when people on the chat group started discussing the vans.

Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said that the 999 call had only come after an attempt to contact the airbase itself. “Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn’t answer the phone,” he said. “It just rang out, so she dialled 999.”

A photograph published by the Daily Mail showed police arresting five shirtless men at night. Police later confirmed that five men had been taken into custody on suspicion of explosives and terror-related offences.
Residents were then woken at 6am by police banging on their doors and telling them to leave immediately. People from 85 households were taken to a nearby leisure centre.

Tudsbery added: “[The police] were then banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown.There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate.”

blocks.caption: US air force military personnel tend to Jdam precision-guided munition and a Rockwell B-1 Lancer heavy bomber on the tarmac at RAF Fairford in April. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA

blocks.text: Thirty emergency vehicles were seen in the village, with the army, a bomb squad and counter-terrorism police all investigating at the scene. Explosives experts were seen examining the three vans.

The RAF base has come to prominence since March, and the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran. From the perimeter of the RAF base it has been possible to see heavy bombs being loaded on to American aircraft.

Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs.
Jason, 50, was evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre at 6am on Sunday with his family and 11-week-old puppy, Poppy, and friends who were visiting from London.
“We went to bed,” he said. “It was early the next morning when the doorbell rang. It was the police, asking residents to evacuate as there had been a major incident.”

Jason, who works in consulting, said earlier on Sunday there were about 40 to 50 people in the leisure centre, ranging from toddlers to elderly villagers, as well as a number of dogs. He said they had been given no more details than those that had been released publicly by police.

blocks.caption: A Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is stopped at a roadblock in Fairford. Photograph: Getty Images

blocks.text: The Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds.
It was unclear when people would be able to go back to their normal lives; those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night.

By Sunday afternoon, the cordon around the village had expanded so no one could get anywhere near it. Access to the village of Whelford remained closed. With RAF Fairford located along one side of the road, a single police vehicle acted as a blockade against further passage into the village.
Tudsbery said he hoped he could get home soon: he had left his cat, Misty, behind.

articles.title: Woman charged with stealing from patients and staff at hospitals across Ontario
articles.summary: The 34-year-old is under investigation for incidents that began in February 2024 up until as recently as last month.

blocks.text: Police in Ontario, Canada, have charged a woman with 65 offences including fraud and theft for allegedly stealing from patients and staff at several healthcare centres in the province.
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) identified the suspect as Nassim Eronn, 34, from Burlington, a city 56km (34 miles) south of Toronto.
"The investigation was initiated following multiple reports of theft and fraud involving patients and staff members within healthcare facilities," police said in a statement to BBC News.
They say the incidents under investigation began in February 2024 and continued until as recently as last month. The suspect worked at health centres across the province.

The suspect faces charges including 34 counts of fraud under $5,000 (£3,800), 13 counts of theft under $5,000 and seven counts of disobeying a court order, according to police. Other charges include breach of trust and impersonation.
OPP began investigating the woman in May after a report of theft when she worked at Orillia Soldiers' Memorial Hospital, about 130km north of Toronto.
"This investigation was prompted by several complaints of theft and fraud from patients and staff within the hospital," police said at the time.
The investigation was expanded to cover more hospitals where further incidents were uncovered.
"Multiple search warrants were executed where significant amounts of property were seized," police said.

articles.title: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war
articles.summary:
Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’

The Trump…

blocks.text: The Trump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”.

Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz.

“They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.”

Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said.
Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”.
Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace.
Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”.
Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel.

“Our conditions are clear, ​and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”
Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country is prepared to resume fighting with the US but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal.
“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war.
“At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”

The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for ​talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not ​accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will ​defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
On CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region.

Waltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China premier Xi Jinping during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz.
“I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.”
Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”.

“They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.”

Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating.

“The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”

articles.title: Tensions run high in Northern Ireland after contentious march given go-ahead
articles.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm in Northern Ireland on Sunday after a contentious parade was given the go-ahead by the High Court in Belfast in a late-night sitting.

image.caption: People block Garvaghy Road, a Catholic enclave in the largely Protestant town of Portadown, Northern Ireland, on the day members of the Protestant Orange Order are expected to march through the area as they take part in the annual Drumcree parade, on Sunday. (Cathal McNaughton/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm in Northern Ireland on Sunday after a contentious parade was given the go-ahead by the High Court in Belfast in a late-night sitting.
First time in decades Orange Order parade has been allowed to go down Garvaghy Road

Thousands of protesters, many wearing balaclavas, gathered to block the marchers from the Orange Order, a group hugely supportive of Northern Ireland being part of the U.K., from proceeding down a street in the town of Portadown, where many favour unification with the Republic of Ireland.

It's the first time in nearly 30 years that the Orange Order parade has been allowed to go down the Garvaghy Road, which had been a notorious flashpoint between the communities in the years before the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 largely ended the bloodshed in Northern Ireland. During the so-called Troubles, some 3,600 people were killed while some 50,000 were wounded.

Ending the Troubles meant balancing competing identities in Northern Ireland, which remained in the United Kingdom when the rest of Ireland won independence. Irish nationalists in the north — most of them Catholic — seek union with the Republic of Ireland, while largely Protestant unionists want to stay part of the U.K.
Burnham appealed for "calm on all sides" over the parade, saying there have been "big gains made in Northern Ireland, and we don’t want to see things go backwards."

Jon Boutcher, the head of the Police Service of Northern Ireland, called for "those with influence to encourage people to comply with the law," referring to a large protest blocking the Garvaghy Road. He said there has been no signs of violence or disorder.
"Police are engaging and working with all parties and will continue to do so. It is incumbent on us all to come together at times like this to do all we can to preserve a peaceful Northern Ireland."
Politicians representing the two sides were opposed in their viewpoints on whether the march should go ahead.

items: Trump's call for united Ireland draws swift rejection from pro-British unionists
Thousands rally in Northern Ireland to condemn anti-immigration rioting

blocks.text: Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, who represents Sinn Fein, the party historically linked to the Irish Republican Army, said the decision to give the march the go-ahead "brings into question how this whole peace process works."

"The progress of the last 28 years have been brought into question by the actions of the Orange Order and those within political unionism that want to drag us backwards," she said while attending the counter-protest on the Garvaghy Road.
Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democrat Unionist Party, the largest pro-U.K. party in Northern Ireland, called out Sinn Fein leaders for inflaming the situation.
"The rule of law cannot apply only when Sinn Fein likes the outcome," he said. "Our institutions are founded on respect for the police, the courts and the rule of law."
The march was given the final go-ahead at a court hearing concluded at 2:15 a.m. local time on Sunday.
The Orange Order is named after William of Orange, a Protestant prince of Holland who defeated the Catholic King James to take over the British throne in the 17th century.

articles.title: Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
articles.summary: The initiative would have prevented the nation from imposing sanctions unless approved by the UN.

blocks.text: Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality.
More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed.
The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment.
Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties.

Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia.
"People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility".
While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference".
He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace".
Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe.

This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv.
Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees.
Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s.
Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

articles.title: Nor’easter storm batters US east coast with heavy winds and power outages
articles.summary:
At least one person killed and nearly 150,000 households lost electricity from North Carolina to New England

A strong, deadly storm known as a

blocks.text: A strong, deadly storm known as a nor’easter battered the US’s east coast over the weekend, bringing power outages, flooding, damaging winds and hazardous ocean conditions.

Trees and power lines were knocked down across the region, at least one person was killed and hundreds of thousands were left without electricity as officials cautioned that conditions could deteriorate further.

There was significant coastal flooding, rough surf, powerful winds, rain and dangerous rip currents from North Carolina through New England. Boston and the New York City tri-state area were among the regions affected.

blocks.caption: Waves crash over homes on Rebecca Road during a nor’easter on 26 September in Scituate, Massachusetts. Photograph: Scott Eisen/Getty Images

blocks.text: Power outages by Sunday were already widespread, with nearly 150,000 households losing electricity so far, according to the website Poweroutage.US.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) advised travelers to check with their airlines for updated flight information. FlightAware reported more than 3,000 US delays and nearly 430 cancellations.
As a result of the storm, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared a state of emergency covering the Bronx, Kings, Nassau, New York, Queens, Richmond, Suffolk and Westchester counties.

A fallen tree in the east New York City borough of Brooklyn resulted in a death on Saturday during the nor’easter. A 56-year-old New York City housing authority employee was killed when a tree came down on him in a parking lot.
Police said he was pronounced dead at Brookdale University hospital. Authorities had not immediately determined whether wind caused the tree to fall.

In Queens, high winds caused widespread disruption after a tree fell at about 5.40pm in the Glendale area, with downed power lines forcing authorities to close the roadway. As a precaution, the New York City fire department evacuated a nearby building. No injuries were reported in that incident.

blocks.caption: Crews work to clear fallen trees from the property of Burnet Hill’s Haunted Ridge after a nor’easter storm in Livingston, New Jersey, on Saturday. Photograph: Kyle Mazza/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Along the Jersey Shore, residents spent Saturday removing debris and cleaning up between periods of high tide after the nor’easter forced flood water into streets and homes near the New Jersey coast. Eight counties in New Jersey remain under a state of emergency issued before the coastal storm arrived.

The storm struck the mid-Atlantic and New England over the weekend and was forecast to continue into the early part of this week. As the week continues, flooding was expected to rise and recede along with the tides.

The National Weather Service (NWS) expected coastal flooding to bring significant flooding from the Jersey Shore south to the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina, with more moderate flooding forecast along the Massachusetts coast.

articles.title: Stronger maritime security eyed
articles.summary: At the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Saturday, the Philippines demanded stronger maritime security for Filipinos, who make up 25 percent of the world’s…

blocks.text: September 28, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — At the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Saturday, the Philippines demanded stronger maritime security for Filipinos, who make up 25 percent of the world’s seafarers.

Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said seafarers form an indispensable lifeline of global commerce, with nearly 90 percent of world trade moving by sea, supported by close to two million seafarers, adding that more than 25 percent of those seafarers are Filipinos.

“They are essential workers, yet increasingly vulnerable to conflict and attacks at sea,” Lazaro said, noting a recent incident in the Strait of Hormuz which claimed the lives of two Filipino seafarers and injured many others.
The two Filipino seafarers died following an attack in the Strait of Hormuz while aboard the M/V SIDR on Aug. 31.

“Their tragedy reminds us: Maritime security is human security. As an archipelagic and maritime nation, the Philippines cannot separate the safety of ships and seafarers from supply chains and global commerce,” Lazaro said.

She stressed that millions of migrant workers are entitled to full human rights and fundamental freedoms, regardless of status, and deserve steadfast protection from trafficking and exploitation along perilous migration routes.

“Open and secure seas, free from interference and coercion, are vital to our security, our economy and our people,” she said, emphasizing that international law, along with the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), must remain firmly as the constitution of the oceans.
Lazaro noted that 2027 marks the 45th anniversary of UNCLOS and the Manila Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of International Disputes.

articles.title: Proposed Luzon-Visayas bridge gets P500 million ADB feasibility funding
articles.summary: Renewed proposals to build a 20-kilometer bridge connecting Luzon via Matnog in Sorsogon to Allen in northern Samar in the Visayas received a major boost, with the approval of a P500-million fund…

blocks.text: September 28, 2026 | 12:00am
“We are very pleased that the ADB has decided to come on board the Sorsogon-Samar Transport Crossing (SSTC) project at this early stage,” Eastern Samar Rep. Marcelino Libanan said.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Renewed proposals to build a 20-kilometer bridge connecting Luzon via Matnog in Sorsogon to Allen in northern Samar in the Visayas received a major boost, with the approval of a P500-million fund from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) for a feasibility study for the project.
“We never doubted the readiness of international development partners to support the project, considering its exceptionally high economic rate of return,” Libanan, House minority leader, said.

The ADB funding of P500 million is aimed at helping bankroll the rigorous feasibility study for the proposed 20-kilometer SSTC over the San Bernardino Strait, in the Philippines’ eastern portion of the Pacific Ocean.
Libanan leads the group of Eastern Visayas lawmakers pushing for a fixed link between Matnog and Allen to provide a permanent road connection between Luzon and the Visayas.
The bridge is expected to reduce travel time between Matnog and Allen to 20 minutes, compared with roughly two and a half hours using the existing roll-on/roll-off ferry system.

The ferry service is also vulnerable to port bottlenecks and disruptions during bad weather mostly during the second half of the year, making a fixed crossing potentially important for more reliable transport and connectivity between Luzon and the Visayas.
The ADB feasibility study funding commitment was disclosed during House plenary deliberations on the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH)’s 2027 budget last week.

Surigao del Sur Rep. Romeo Momo Sr. relayed the information from DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon while responding to questions from Libanan about the SSTC feasibility study during the Sept. 24 plenary debates.
Momo said the ADB’s P500-million commitment would augment the P130 million initially appropriated by Congress for the feasibility study.
The ADB itself is expected to bid out the study in November, with completion targeted within 12 months.
The proposed SSTC is considered a technically complex and large-scale infrastructure project that would require extensive marine, bathymetric, geological and geotechnical investigations.
The feasibility study would also examine oceanographic conditions, seismic risks, navigation, environmental and social impacts, and the effects of typhoons and other extreme weather events.
