articles.title: PH, US mark 80 years of partnership with new booklet
articles.summary: The Philippines and the United States have marked 80 years of partnership in business, diplomacy and people-to-people ties with the launch of a new edition of a booklet highlighting the countries'…

blocks.text: The Philippines and the United States have marked 80 years of partnership in business, diplomacy and people-to-people ties with the launch of a new edition of a booklet highlighting the countries' longstanding relationship.

The second edition of the booklet, “The Philippines Matters for America, America Matters for the Philippines,” commemorates eight decades of diplomatic relations between the two countries, which were established on July 4, 1946.
The first edition of the booklet was published in 2022.

A project led by the US East-West Center, an education and research organization, the booklet supposedly highlights the alliance, trade, investment, educational exchanges, partnerships and supply chains between the two countries.

During his speech, US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton underscored the strong relationship between the Philippines and the US and expressed confidence in its continued growth in the years ahead.
Among the areas of Philippine-US partnership highlighted by Lipton were the Luzon Economic Corridor, Pax Silica, artificial intelligence and nuclear energy.
“Our countries share an incredible, incredible history together. We're here to take our relationship to the next level,” Lipton said on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Department of Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Maria Andrelita Austria described the launch of the booklet as a “very strategic and timely” initiative as it coincides with the anniversary of diplomatic relations between the Philippines and the US.

“On July 4, 1946, the Philippines and the United States formally opened a new chapter in our shared history. It was a moment that started not only the recognition of Philippine independence, but also the beginning of a strong diplomatic partnership between two sovereign nations bound by history, democratic values and enduring people-to-people ties,” Austria said.

“Eighty years later, the relationship remains one of the Philippines' most important and deeply valued partnerships. Let me take this opportunity to highlight the top impacts and figures which underscore the depth and breadth of our alliance,” she added.
The booklet noted that bilateral trade between the two countries reached $41.7 billion in 2025, representing a 13% increase from 2024.
The United States is also the Philippines' top single-country trading partner for agricultural products, supplying 15% of its agricultural imports and buying 18% of its agricultural exports in 2025.
The booklet further indicated that US foreign direct investment (FDI) in the Philippines totaled $6 billion, while Philippine FDI in the US amounted to $532 million.
It also showed the number of jobs generated and supported through investments by the two countries, as well as the foreign assistance and health cooperation provided by the US to the Philippines.
Based on the booklet, exports to the Philippines supported 65,400 US jobs in 2024, the majority of which were in California, Texas and Washington.
Since 1949, US assistance to the Philippines has focused on economic development, peace and security, and health.

As of June 2025, the US had provided health assistance funding for global health security, tuberculosis, maternal and child health, neglected tropical diseases, integrated supply chains, nutrition and HIV/AIDS.
The booklet also highlighted Filipino medical workers, noting that they make up 5% of the nursing workforce and 3% of the healthcare workforce in the US.
The Philippines is also the top country of origin for immigrant healthcare professionals in the US, with Filipino immigrants comprising 12% of all foreign-born US healthcare workers.

The booklet also presented figures on income generated by Filipino visitors to the US, as well as the Filipino population, Filipino Americans in elected office and cultural connections between the two countries.
It said Filipinos make up 18% of the Asian American population in the United States, with an estimated 4.6 million people.
California, Hawaii, Texas, Washington and Nevada have the largest Filipino American populations.
Filipino Americans in Hawaii also have a strong political presence, with around 15% of state representatives and 24% of state senators being of Filipino descent.
From 2024 to 2025, there were 4,573 students from the Philippines studying in higher education institutions in the US.
Meanwhile, 326 American students studied in the Philippines from 2023 to 2024.
In terms of travel and tourism, the booklet showed that 1.1 million Americans visited the Philippines, while 315,000 Filipinos visited the US in 2025.
The US also earned $2 billion from Filipino tourist spending in 2024. Most Filipino visitors traveled to California, Florida and New York.
The year 2026 also marks the 75th anniversary of the Mutual Defense Treaty between the Philippines and the US, as well as the 250th anniversary of US independence.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: UK: 5 arrested after 'major incident' near Fairford air base
articles.summary: Scores of homes were evacuated in the UK town of Whelford, near an air base used by the US military, with bomb disposal teams checking "suspicious vehicles" at the scene. Police said five men had…

image.caption: The US Air Force has used the British base for attacks against IranImage: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: British authorities evacuated buildings and deployed military bomb disposal teams over a "major incident" in the town of Whelford on Sunday morning.
The town is located near the Fairford air base, which is used by the US military. Around 30 emergency vehicles were seen in the area, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines.
Counter-terrorism police were leading the investigation. On Sunday afternoon, London's Metropolitan police said five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a "terrorist act."

blocks.caption: UK police blocked roads leading to the Fairford air baseImage: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: Previously, the authorities said that several men were "arrested on suspicion of offences the ​Explosives Act."
"A cordon is currently in place but we'd like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained," British police said.
Bomb disposal units examining three 'suspicious vehicles'
Separately, local police said they had received a call earlier on Sunday about "three suspicious vehicles" heading to the base.
"Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area," assistant chief constable Richard Ocone told reporters.
He added that a cordon of 400 meters, or approximately 1/4 of a mile, has been put in place around the vehicles "while the army's explosive ordinance disposal unit examine them."
"As a precaution, around 85 households have been advised to evacuate while these examinations take place," Ocone said.
He added that some of the evacuees were taken to a nearby leisure center.
The Gloucestershire police representative also asked the public "not to speculate" but follow official channels instead.
Officials stay tight-lipped

A spokesperson for ​the US Air Force refused to discuss specific steps when contacted by the Reuters news agency, saying only that both US and British forces "remain vigilant and will take ⁠appropriate ​actions to ensure the safety and security of our ​US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families."

blocks.caption: This Fairford base gates was blocked by construction machinery Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: The background for the incident was not immediately clear.

The UK has allowed the US to use Fairford for its war against Iran, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards warning UK officials against the move this summer. The evacuations also come at a time of heightened tensions in Northern Ireland, and less than two months after Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone at the Leipzig airport, which its authorities attributed to Russia.

articles.title: Two giant pandas set off to Atlanta zoo from China after Xi-Trump summit
articles.summary:
Pandas departed Chengdu for their new homes in Georgia as part of agreement between Chinese and US governments

Two giant pandas departed Chengdu in south-western

blocks.text: Two giant pandas departed Chengdu in south-western China early on Sunday for their new homes in Atlanta, Georgia, as part of an agreement between the Chinese and US governments.

While in Washington DC for a three-day summit with Donald Trump, Chinese president Xi Jinping announced that the pandas would arrive in Atlanta in the coming days. The loan of the pandas to the Atlanta zoo was one of the few concrete outcomes to come out of Xi’s state visit with the US president, which saw expressions of goodwill between the leaders, but no fixes to any of the longstanding differences between the two countries.
Atlanta said farewell to its last pandas in 2024, leaving the zoo without the bears. The new agreement was announced back in April, but without any dates.

Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the two adult pandas that will be on loan to Zoo Atlanta for 10 years as part of the agreement. Both pandas were born in 2020 and were kept at the Chengdu research base of giant panda breeding. Ping Ping, the male, has dark black circles around his eyes, while Fu Shuang, the female, has a forehead that protrudes a bit, according to the Xinhua News Agency.
China has long used the pandas as part of its diplomacy globally, deploying the bears in loan programs as expressions of goodwill and letting loan agreements lapse when tensions arise.
Xi had said the loan program was an example of “friendship between the Chinese and Americans”.

articles.title: ‘I wanted to help another family’: four surrogates on how they feel about the surrogacy discourse
articles.summary:
The Guardian spoke with surrogates across the US about what they think of the controversy surrounding the practice

Surrogacy has been thrust into the national spotlight in recent weeks, with…

blocks.text: Surrogacy has been thrust into the national spotlight in recent weeks, with both the announcement of Lena Dunham using a surrogate to start a family and the ongoing legal battle surrounding McKenna West, a gestational surrogate who fled to Texas to avoid having an abortion that was requested by the child’s biological parents.

With a renewed public interest on commercial, or compensated, surrogacy, the Guardian spoke with surrogates across the US who shared their experiences and how they feel about surrogacy being part of a global, public conversation.

Liggia Spicer, a 34-year-old woman based in upstate New York, first considered getting involved with surrogacy work after hearing about a mutual friend who was looking into using a surrogate after battling cancer and undergoing a hysterectomy.
“I probably did about two years of research before I turned to my husband and was like: ‘OK I think I want to do this,’” she said.

Spicer ended up working with an agency, ConceiveAbilities, where she was matched with a couple after what she described as a “vigorous” screening process that included a background check, financial check, psychological screen and a review of previous labor and delivery history. Most surrogacy programs require that a woman has given birth previously before becoming a surrogate.

ConceiveAbilities provided her with an attorney to assist with the creation of a surrogacy contract, an agreement that comes to pass before an embryo transfer and details the rights of the surrogate and the intended parents. It also addresses insurance, payment of medical bills, liability for medical complications and the intended parents’ presence during doctor’s visits and at delivery.

Notably, West’s case has brought up questions of how much bodily autonomy carriers are afforded in surrogacy. West violated her surrogacy contract by refusing to get an abortion after the fetus she was carrying was discovered to have a congenital heart defect. She later fled to Texas, where abortion is banned, and gave birth to the child. West has sought conservatorship over the child as well, which would give her a say in the child’s medical treatment. The US supreme court has declined to intervene in the case.

blocks.caption: McKenna West, left, arrivers with her legal team for a court hearing in Dallas, Texas, on 25 August 2026. Photograph: LM Otero/AP

blocks.text: “As surrogates, we do things that we may not do in our own pregnancies, but at the end of the day, it’s not our child,” Spicer said. “As long as what we’re being asked is safe to do.”

Kristy Miller, a 38-year-old, two-time surrogate based in Indianapolis, also worked with ConceiveAbilities. She spoke of the requests that a surrogate can make when being matched with intended parents.

“I remember feeling very strongly that I wanted there to be a trusting relationship [with the intended parents],” she said. “I didn’t want to feel micromanaged. I didn’t want someone to be kind of dictating what I ate every day, or how I took care of myself.”
Critics of surrogacy also argue that the process treats women’s bodies as a commodity.

Under Vogue’s Instagram post announcing Dunham’s essay about her surrogate journey, one commenter wrote: “Let’s not normalize buying humans.” Another said: “The concept of rich people renting poor people’s wombs will never not be strange.”

Dunham has spoken publicly about her fertility issues for years and writes about them at length in her 2026 book, Famesick. Her struggles have included an Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnosis, nearly two decades of advanced endometriosis and a total hysterectomy at 31 years old.
Spicer said: “It’s important that everyone should decide what happens to their body, and I wanted to get pregnant to help another family.
“That’s my decision,” she added. She now works as a surrogate engagement coordinator at ConceiveAbilities.

Christine S, a 38-year-old former gestational surrogate in New York state, carried and gave birth to a child for a same-sex male couple in 2025 with New York Surrogacy Center. Christine, who declined to share her last name for privacy reasons, said she understands concerns about reproductive exploitation, but believes that opponents of commercial surrogacy haven’t been informed enough on the intricacies of the process in the US.

“I think it’s just [that] they don’t understand enough about it,” she said. “Because there are situations where there are women that are held against their will to breed, right? Like that is a legit concern. But I volunteered. I didn’t do this against my will.

“And the journey of working with someone to be a surrogate, not only is it costly, but I also feel like [intended parents are] offering somebody an opportunity too. I had a job for a temporary amount of time, and it was a high-risk job, but it was also a high reward.”

Christine received $45,000 for carrying the child, in addition to coverage for her medical and legal fees. Spicer was paid $67,000, which was broken down and paid out over the course of the pregnancy.

Kimber Alston, a 36-year-old gestational surrogate based in Texas, is pregnant with her fifth surrogate child, and in the middle of her ninth pregnancy overall. Her first experience as a surrogate was in 2018 for a same-sex male couple in Italy. Since then, she has embarked on surrogate journeys both independently and with agencies, and given birth to children who live in Paris and Mexico, among other cities around the world.
She said she has formed close bonds with the intended parents she’s worked with, and frequently receives pictures and videos of the children she carried.

“What keeps me going is being able to help people have something that they couldn’t have otherwise,” she said. Alston, who also now works for a surrogacy agency she previously used, said that interacting with intended parents reminds her why has chosen to be a surrogate multiple times.

“I watch these couples every day come in and tell their stories; I’m in these match calls and watching them cry and not be able to have a child of their own,” she said. “I’m like: ‘If I could do it just one more time, I might as well just do it.’”
Multiple surrogates said the biggest misconception they see is the notion that surrogates get attached to the baby they are carrying, and may refuse to give the child up after delivery.

“I have never known a surrogate who felt like ‘mom’ to the baby [they were] carrying,” said Miller. “I think it’s hard for people to wrap their head around that unless they are truly considering [surrogacy].”
Spicer emphasized the need for levity throughout the experience.

“Honestly, I tell a lot of girls who want to be surrogates: ‘You have to have a sense of humor. You have to just take things on the chin and laugh it off,’” she said. “You could tell them until you’re blue in the face: ‘I’m not attached to this baby,’ and they still just don’t understand.”

articles.title: Marcos expresses gratitude for greetings on his 69th birthday
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Sunday thanked those who greeted him on his 69th birthday on September 13, 2026.

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 8:47pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Sunday thanked those who greeted him on his 69th birthday on September 13, 2026.

“Maraming salamat sa lahat ng bumati sa aking kaarawan noong nakaraang linggo. Hindi na rin ako halos nagkaroon ng oras mag-celebrate kasama ng buong pamilya dahil dire-diretso na ang schedule mula Ilocos hanggang sa India,” Marcos said in a Facebook video.
(Thank you very much to everyone who sent their birthday wishes last week. I barely had time to celebrate with my entire family because of my packed schedule from Ilocos all the way to India.)
Marcos spent his birthday in New Delhi, India, where he was invited to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit as an outreach participant and in his capacity as 2026 ASEAN chair.
Salo-salo sa Palasyo
Similar to last year’s celebration, Marcos hosted a “Salo-Salo sa Palasyo,” opening Malacañang to the public for a special program and festivities.
More than 98 local government units from across the country attended the gathering, according to Marcos.
“Bawat frontline service agency ng gobyerno kasama, kaya parang isang malaking selebrasyon na rin ang naganap,” he said.
(Every frontline government service agency was represented, turning it into one big celebration.)
As part of the celebration, relief aid was also distributed to attendees, Marcos said.
Outreach
In his message, Marcos highlighted the expanded Zero-Balance Billing initiative launched in line with his birthday celebration.

While the Zero-Balance Billing program typically covers only ward patients, Marcos said a special exception was made at around 132 hospitals nationwide, allowing all patients to have their medical bills covered.
“Normally, mga ward patients lang ang kasama dito, pero noong araw na ‘yon nilahat na natin. Basta nasa ospital ka, anumang kwarto, bayad na ang bill ninyo,” Marcos said.
(Normally, this program only applies to ward patients, but on that day, we covered everyone. As long as you were in the hospital, regardless of the room type, your bill was paid.)
“Humigit-kumulang 132 hospitals ang kabilang dito mula sa Luzon, Visayas at Mindanao. ‘Yung iba sa kanila ay umabot na sa milyon ang hospital bill—bayad na ‘yan,” he added.
(Around 132 hospitals took part in the initiative across Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao. Some patients had hospital bills reaching millions of pesos, and those bills have already been paid.)
Aside from hospital assistance, Marcos said outreach initiatives were also conducted in communities and schools, providing medical checkups, free medicines and other forms of aid.
According to Marcos, the initiatives benefited around 175,565 individuals across roughly 282 participating sites. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Ten climbers missing after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp
articles.summary: The Nepali team was preparing to take overseas climbers up the Himlung Himal peak.

blocks.text: At least 10 Nepali climbers who were preparing to lead an expedition are missing after an avalanche hit a base camp in the Himalayas on Sunday.
The climb's organisers said the local guides were at a staging point close to the Himlung Himal peak in Manang district when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.
Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126 metre (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet.
Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams unable to reach the site.
Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told AFP news agency: "Eight members of our expedition team and two more from another company have been reported missing."
The Nepali team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain.
Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry.
Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches.
The latest death of Nepali climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja.
Extreme weather further south in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said.
It comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August.

More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements.

articles.title: Bagunas rues Alas’ lack of support in Asian Games; PNVF apologizes
articles.summary: Bryan Bagunas reveals Alas Pilipinas players have not received their allowances since July, forcing some to miss practices during their Asian Games buildup due to financial constraints

blocks.text: SOAR. Bryan Bagunas in action for Alas Pilipinas Men in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Bryan Bagunas reveals Alas Pilipinas players have not received their allowances since July, forcing some to miss practices during their Asian Games buildup due to financial constraints

MANILA, Philippines – Alas Pilipinas Men team captain Bryan Bagunas rued the lack of financial support in the lead-up to and during the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, revealing that some players were forced to borrow money just to attend training.
xBagunas voiced his frustration after the Philippines’ 25-16, 27-25, 25-22 tournament-opening loss to South Korea on Sunday, September 27.
The star outside spiker said the players have not received their allowances since July, forcing some to miss practices during their Asian Games buildup due to financial constraints.

“Regarding our allowance, even some of the players borrowed money from our teammates or other people just so they could get to training and travel back home. It was really tough for us to practice every day. Sometimes, we’re only seven or eight in training. It was really difficult,” said Bagunas in Filipino.
“I understand because most of the players are student-athletes. We just helped each other out so we could have complete attendance in practice.”
Although the Philippine Sports Commission provided allowances to the athletes, Bagunas said Alas Men players still have to pay for expenses out of their own pockets.
For instance, Bagunas and his teammates sometimes have to buy their own meals because the serving hours at their hotel often clashed with their training sessions.
“It is really disheartening because we’re representing the country. We do not feel the support that we deserve,” said Bagunas.

All Bagunas could do is encourage his teammates as Alas Men focuses on the task at hand, with matches against China and Chinese Taipei in Group D coming up on Monday, September 28, and Tuesday, September 29, respectively.
The Philippines needs a top-two finish in the group to advance to the quarterfinals.
“I just motivate them to keep fighting. Hopefully, we’ll get better support in the future,” Bagunas said.

The Philippine National Volleyball Federation apologized on Sunday following Bagunas’ remarks and explained its side, saying it continues to deal with “substantial financial liabilities and outstanding obligations” that the new administration headed by president Frank Lao inherited.

“We acknowledge the concerns raised by Mr. Bagunas in his recent interview. We recognize the sacrifices our athletes have made, including having to shoulder their own expenses and, in some instances, borrow money. This is a situation that no National Athlete should ever have to endure,” the PNVF said in a statement.
The PNVF also said that Lao gave Alas Men allowances and has advanced funds to address concerns raised by the teams competing in the quadrennial showpiece.

“Our national athletes deserve a federation that works just as hard for them as they battle for our country. Our athletes deserve better. Philippine volleyball deserves better. And we will work tirelessly to deliver better,” the PNVF said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Pope Leo urges healing of ‘deep wounds’ before meeting child sexual abuse survivors in France
articles.summary:
Catholic church must reckon with its ‘painful errors’, pontiff tells crowd in Lourdes during four-day tour

The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful…

blocks.text: The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a meeting with survivors of child sexual abuse as he continues his four-day visit to France.

Addressing a crowd in a large field near the Catholic shrine of Lourdes on Sunday, Pope Leo XIV called on the church to reckon with its past, without directly referencing sexual abuse scandals in France that affected at least 330,000 children over seven decades.

“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and ⁠painful errors that have occurred within [the church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told the estimated crowd of 150,000 people.

Leo is due to privately meet seven survivors of child sexual abuse by French clergy on Sunday after leading an open-air morning mass at Lourdes, one of the most popular Catholic sites for pilgrims and reputed as a place of healing.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo celebrates a mass in Lourdes. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters

blocks.text: Meeting French bishops earlier on Sunday, Leo said they had acted with determination against “the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context against minors”. He urged them “to continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance”, according to a transcript of his remarks released by the Vatican.

Arriving at Lourdes in a white popemobile on Saturday night, Leo would have been reminded of the church’s dark and painful legacy, as he passed boarded-up mosaics by a Jesuit priest who is accused of abusing more than two dozen women over three decades.

Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic church’s best-known mosaic artists, is on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them from the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. The bishop of Lourdes ordered the works covered up, reasoning that survivors of abuse seeking succour at the site should not be forced to see them.

blocks.caption: Leo’s visit to France is the first by a pope in 18 years.  Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rupnik is not known to have commented publicly on the allegations, Reuters reported.

Among the survivors who will meet the pope is a former pupil of the nearby Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram, whose former students have recounted their experiences of violence, rape and sexual assault in what is thought to be the biggest child sexual abuse scandal at a school in French history.

In an interview published last year, the pope spoke of the “crisis” of clerical sexual abuse in the church. He also said “victims must be treated with great respect and with an understanding that those who have suffered very deep wounds because of abuse, sometimes carry those wounds for their entire life”, according to a transcript on Vatican News, the Holy See’s official news site.

The first visit to France by the head of the Catholic church in 18 years follows an announcement last week by the country’s Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation that about 2,000 people who reported sexual abuse by clergy or other church representatives were seeking reparations.
after newsletter promotion

France’s Catholic bishops conference agreed to provide compensation after a landmark report in 2021 estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over seven decades by predatory priests or other Catholic figures. The two-and-a-half-year independent inquiry found that vast numbers of children were subjected to sexual violence by priests and clergy and that the crimes were covered up in a “systemic way” by a deliberate “veil of silence” in the church.

On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors published an open letter voicing fears that his visit would change nothing, criticising that the seven he was due to meet in Lourdes were “carefully selected” by the church, rather than survivors’ groups.

blocks.caption: Carmelite nuns attend mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV in Lourdes, France. Photograph: Valentine Chapuis/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “You will merely ask us for forgiveness. This is not enough. One does not ask for forgiveness for a crime; one is responsible for a crime,” they wrote in the letter published in the newspaper Libération.

The pope arrived to celebrate mass on Sunday morning to a rapturous reception from the faithful, who waved flags and cheered, as they thronged the streets of Lourdes to catch a glimpse of him. The Holy See’s live stream showed Leo making stately progress in his popemobile, stopping frequently to greet and bless babies that were passed to him.

The south-western town near the Spanish border is one of the most important Catholic sites in the world, attracting 3 million pilgrims a year. The Associated Press reported that the pope’s visit had caused accommodation prices to soar, with the price of some one-night hotel stays reaching more than €2,000 (£1,700).

articles.summary: DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel says the Philippines takes part in a 'call for all parties to desist from unilateral actions that erode the conditions of peace and undermine the visibility of a…

blocks.text: WALK OUT. Delegates walk out as Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 24, 2026.
Jeenah Moon/Reuters

DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel says the Philippines takes part in a 'call for all parties to desist from unilateral actions that erode the conditions of peace and undermine the visibility of a future Palestine state'

items: The walkout was in response to Israel's actions in Gaza and the West Bank, as international scrutiny of these policies has intensified.
The Philippines continues to advocate for a two-state solution as a means to achieve lasting peace in the region.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines joined dozens of delegations that walked out of the United Nations General Assembly hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech on Thursday, September 24, in New York, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said.

“Yes, the Philippines joined the walk out, in global solidarity for peace in the Middle East and the call for all parties to desist from unilateral actions that erode the conditions of peace and undermine the visibility of a future Palestine state,” DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel told Rappler on Sunday, September 27.
Reports showed that several delegates left the UN hall as Netanyahu took the podium — in protest over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Netanyahu continued his address to a largely emptied chamber, where he defended Israel’s military operations and rejected accusations that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza. He also took aim at New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Western European leaders, Qatar, and Turkey, accusing them of backing or spreading what he described as false and hostile claims against Israel.

The walkout came as international scrutiny of Israel’s policies in the Palestinian territories intensified. A September 24 UN report highlighted settler violence, settlement expansion, displacement, and movement restrictions that continued to undermine prospects for a viable Palestinian state.

One focus has been Israel’s E1 settlement plan in the occupied West Bank. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that advancing the E1 plan would deal a “deathblow” to the prospect of a contiguous and viable Palestinian state.
The DFA said the Philippines remains concerned about Israel’s actions in both Gaza and the West Bank.

“These actions are detrimental to finding a just, lasting and comprehensive solution to the Middle East conflict,” Ratonel said. “The Philippines has always supported the two-state solution as the viable path to peace in the region.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Only 3% of US sickle cell patients receive red blood cell exchange for disease, researchers find
articles.summary:
Various factors block sufferers of disease from receiving treatment that is effective and has widespread availability

Sickle cell patients are missing out on an effective treatment despite…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: Sickle cell patients are missing out on an effective treatment despite widespread US hospital access to the technology, new research has found.

That treatment is called a red blood cell exchange, a procedure that discards a patient’s damaged red blood cells while simultaneously mixing the patient’s remaining plasma, platelets and white blood cells with red blood cells from a donor before returning them to the body.

But a new nationally representative survey of 100 US-based healthcare providers who actively manage at least one patient with sickle cell disease shows fewer than 3% of patients have been recorded receiving a red blood cell exchange even though 91% of surveyed providers report access to it.

The survey found that providers encountered barriers in administering the treatment, which most commonly included challenges coordinating between different medical departments, a limited supply of donated blood and a general lack of familiarity with the procedure. Only 5% of health providers surveyed had no barriers in delivering this type of treatment, the research found.
Among sickle cell patients, the survey found that a major concern was if red blood cell exchange therapy was covered by their health insurance.

Sickle cell disease, which is also called sickle cell anemia, is an inherited disorder that affects hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells, according to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute. Normal red blood cells are disc-shaped, making them flexible and easy to pass through the blood vessels; someone with sickle cell disease has crescent- or “sickle”-shaped blood cells, meaning they are less flexible and can block blood flow to the rest of the body.

The disease, which affects more than 100,000 people across the United States and 8 million people worldwide, primarily affects people of color. Of those diagnosed with the disease, 90% are non-Hispanic Black or African American while an estimated 3%-9% are Hispanic or Latino.

Dr Aaron Haubner of the University of Kentucky College of Pharmacy, lead author of the research, emphasized the various issues surrounding patient access to these “new therapies” for sickle cell, calling them “exciting” but “out of reach for most patients”.

“Patients with sickle cell disease benefit from coordinated access to hematologists, transfusion and apheresis specialists, nurse educators, care coordinators, and other support services,” he said. “In many communities – outside of dedicated centers of excellence – these resources simply aren’t available.”
He believes the best way to expand access to transfusion care is to grow the number of comprehensive sickle cell disease centers nationally.
“These centers are designed to bring together the expertise and services needed to support long-term disease management and preventive care,” Haubner said.

blocks.caption: A technician at the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute conducts sickle cell disease research. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Dr Edward Donnell Ivy, chief medical officer at the Sickle Cell Disease Association of America, also pointed out an obstacle that patients themselves have control over: asking about different treatments.

“[Other] barriers include patients not being aware to ask about certain therapies, but it is also important for patients to have doctors that are knowledgable about how to treat sickle cell disease, about the risk factors too,” Ivy said. “There’s a gap between the number of providers who understand how to treat sickle cell disease.”

Ivy noted the financial impact of the disease as a significant barrier, disclosing that roughly 80% of sickle cell patients are on Medicaid and face socioeconomic vulnerabilities. He also noted that geography plays a part in care.

“A lot of sickle cell patients live in rural areas and so only have access to rural hospitals. If you look at the distribution of sickle cell disease, it primarily affects African Americans who tend to be in states in the south that can be more rural, and so have less access to some of these equipment,” he said. “And these rural hospitals may be less likely to have access to these therapies”.

He continued: “We need to make sure healthcare providers are aware of the National Alliance of Sickle Cell Center guidelines, and creating a network of providers than can discuss treatment strategies.”

Dr Shannon Kelly, medical director of the apheresis program at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland, said that her hospital often receives referrals of patients from other centers because they cannot provide the same level of care that certain patients need.

“We get referrals to my hospital from other large institutions, where even they don’t have a dedicated apheresis program [involving a centrifuge machine that processes blood from the patient’s body] that provides automated red blood cell exchange. The issue is more that this therapy is not at enough institutions and hospitals,” Kelly said.

“We see patients who do travel from some distance to receive their transfusions with us. It’s a hardship on them because already they have a chronic disease that can be debilitating and then they have to travel a long distance.

“Ideally this would be a therapy that could be offered at more sites, but if you don’t have a decent number of sickle cell patients in your area it’s very difficult to maintain the competencies of this therapy. It would be very hard for some rural centers to maintain a program like this.”

articles.title: ‘Speed kills’ vs. ‘just do it:’ Survey illustrates Albertans’ hopes, fears over highway speed
articles.summary: Two thirds of Albertans who filled out a survey on highway speed limits last year said they supported increasing the speed limit on rural divided highways to 120 km/h, but the results show older…

image.caption: Signs advertise the new 120 km/h speed limit on a section of Highway 2, south of Leduc, Alta. (Madeleine Cummings/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

Two thirds of Albertans who filled out a survey on highway speed limits last year said they supported increasing the speed limit on rural divided highways to 120 km/h, but the results show older drivers were less likely than younger ones to support the idea.
Younger respondents most likely to support raising speed limits on divided highways

Edmonton resident Don Davidson obtained a slide deck summarizing the results prepared by the government's public opinion research unit and more than 1,400-pages of open-ended responses from the survey, using an access to information request. He shared the documents with CBC News.

“I wanted to see the results of the survey because I just couldn't believe that the vast majority of the people in Alberta would want the highway speed increased,” the retired engineer told CBC in an interview last week.
“Most people are concerned about safety, as am I, and I wanted to read the comments and see what motivated them — and reading them, I can’t justify how they could increase the speed.”
Nearly 60,000 people participated in the province’s online survey from Nov. 7 — Dec. 12, 2025.

Because public engagement surveys don’t randomly select respondents, their results are less accurate and representative of the population but they allow the government to hear from a wide range of people.

“Generally speaking, those who are dissatisfied with the status quo are much more likely to sound off on what the problem is rather than to take time out of their day and talk about how they really like things the way they are,” said Stewart Prest, a lecturer in political science at the University of British Columbia.

While not the most scientific way of gauging public sentiment, the survey results offer some insights into why many Albertans want to drive faster on highways and where opposition to the idea is coming from.
Older drivers less keen on speed increase
The slide deck summarizing results shows that support for raising the speed limit decreased with respondent age.

About 87 per cent of people under 35 either strongly or somewhat agreed with the idea of hiking speed limits on divided highways but that share dropped to 76 per cent for the 35-54 age group and 50 per cent of drivers 55 or older.

items: Collisions down on section of Alberta’s Highway 2 that has 120 km/h speed limit

blocks.text: The report also showed more skepticism from more experienced drivers. Eight per cent of drivers with 2-5 years of experience said they were strongly opposed to the idea — compared to nearly a third of drivers with more than 10 years of experience.
“What it comes down to is people don’t know what they don’t know and it’s particularly true of less experienced drivers,” said La Velle Goodwin, the founder of Driving Hero Academy.

Goodwin, whose academy teaches advanced defensive driving skills, said there could be various reasons for the age disparity but she expects older drivers’ experience on highways is informing their opinions.
Why drivers want to go faster
Thirty-six respondents used the phrase “just do it” when answering an open-ended question at the end of the survey about increasing the speed limit.
Higher speed limit supporters most commonly brought up saving time during driving trips in their responses.
More than half of respondents said they agreed that time savings from speed limit increases would translate into broader economic benefit to the province.
Supporters also noted many drivers already surpass the 110 km/h limit.
“Most of us do this already, because it is safe to do so,” one driver wrote.

Goodwin said while increasing the speed limit from 30 to 50 km/h can lead to significant time savings, there are diminishing returns at higher speeds and she doesn’t think the risks of having a higher speed limit outweigh the benefits.
‘Ticket left lane campers!’
The survey also asked drivers for open-ended responses on what else would help improve their experience on provincial highways.
Drivers most frequently called for stricter rules and education on keeping slower vehicles in the right lane.
“Ticket left lane campers!” one respondent wrote.

items: Speed limit on section of Alberta's Highway 2 boosted to 120 km/h in pilot project

blocks.text: The second most popular theme among the suggestions focused on road maintenance and infrastructure improvements.
“Here’s a thought, fix the roads and eliminate potholes, deep cracks, paint the lines and light areas that historically have higher collisions,” one respondent wrote.
Drivers also asked for lane additions, more electronic signs, better winter maintenance, removal of at-grade crossings, more wildlife corridors and extended ramps.
‘Speed kills’
Many respondents, answering the final open-ended question in the survey, shared concerns about safety and increased accident severity.
Hundreds used the slogan “speed kills.”
“My father lost his life on a double highway,” one respondent wrote. “Blood is on your hands if you make highways less safe.”

Another respondent, who said they have been a member of the Sheriff Highway Patrol since 2006, said increasing speed limits will do nothing except increase collisions, “putting further strain on our already overtaxed health system.”
Another respondent, who said they were a retired rural first responder, wrote, “increased speed results in a higher degree of injuries/deaths.”
Pilot zone expanded
RCMP and the provincial government have said that fewer collisions have occurred on the pilot section of Highway 2, compared to the same time period last year.
Earlier this month, Transportation and Economic Corridors Minister Devin Dreeshen told media the 120 km/h pilot has been “a great success” and is now expanded to cover up to 44 kilometres.

“We’re looking at additional expansion of that but we’re going to be data driven on how we expand this project, to see if we can expand 120 on all rural divided highways,” he said during a news conference on Sept. 10.
Mark Perry, a retired transportation engineer in Edmonton, said most Alberta highways aren’t designed for a higher driving speed.
He said there were improvements made to the pilot section of Highway 2 before the experiment began and the public should know the costs associated with further upgrades.
“That's the part that the province has not been telling us,” he said.
He said he estimates it would cost more than $1 billion to convert all of the at-grade intersections to interchanges along Highway 2 between Edmonton and Calgary.

CBC News asked the transportation ministry about Perry’s estimate and a press secretary sent a previous statement saying the initial pilot data is encouraging and the government continues to remind drivers that speed limits are intended for ideal conditions.

articles.title: Albertans divided on immigration, while half still undecided on 9 non-separation questions: poll
articles.summary: Albertans are divided over immigration but attitudes are “softening,” while nearly half still don’t know which way they’ll vote on the nine non-separation questions in the Oct. 19 referendum, a new…

image.caption: Ballot mockups are pictured during a Sept. 3, 2026, referendum technical briefing in Edmonton. The ballots feature the questions to be presented to voters in the province's Oct. 19, 2026 referendum. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

blocks.text: Albertans are divided over immigration but attitudes are “softening,” while nearly half still don’t know which way they’ll vote on nine non-separation questions in the Oct. 19 referendum, a new poll commissioned by CBC News suggests.

“There's a huge contrast between opinion toward question 10 (the separation question) and opinion toward the other nine,” said Calgary-based pollster Janet Brown, whose Janet Brown Opinion Research directed a random survey of 1,200 Albertans between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21.

“We really have seen a great deal of consistency over the last several months on … how people would vote for separation. You know, attitudes there are only changing slightly and very few people remain undecided about those questions.
“But the other nine, there's not a high level of familiarity with those questions … A lot is up in the air right now on the other nine questions.”
Five of those nine questions deal with immigration issues, the other four deal with changes to the Constitution.
On the immigration questions, the poll found 54 per cent of respondents agree that Alberta should take more control over immigration to the province, down three points from April.
“We're seeing that overall attitudes haven't changed very much, but those attitudes are softening,” Brown explained.
Those who “strongly agree” with the statement dropped from 40 per cent to 33 per cent, with those who “somewhat agree” increasing by four percentage points since the last poll.
“The intensity has changed, but the overall ‘agree,’ ‘disagree’ numbers haven't changed very much,” she said.

The original nine questions announced by Premier Danielle Smith in February focus on immigration policy and constitutional changes. In May, the question relating to separation was added to the ballot and has since occupied much of the discourse around the referendum.
According to the survey, 49 per cent of respondents did not yet know how they will be voting on the nine questions apart from the one on separation.
“With less than a month remaining, people aren't feeling very connected to these nine questions yet,” Brown said.

items: Albertans are voting on Oct. 19. Here’s the simple version of what you need to know

blocks.text: Immigration attitudes becoming less ‘intense’
“There is a consensus — a bare consensus — that we should take more control over immigration, but not a consensus on what that should look like,” Brown said.
The poll, carried out by Trend Research, did not put the immigration and constitutional referendum questions to respondents directly, but rather addressed larger themes.
When asked if the province should limit temporary residents’ free access to health care and education, about 45 per cent of respondents agreed.
But compared to a similar question posed in April this year, those who strongly disagreed increased by four percentage points.

Lisa Young, a professor of political science at the University of Calgary, said that as Albertans discuss the ideas on the ballot, such as the proposed policies to restrict temporary residents’ access to public services, support for those ideas seems to be decreasing.

“I think that what we've seen over the last number of weeks as people have come back from summer vacation, they've seen signs saying 'no to the nine,' for example, and they've started wondering what are the nine [questions] and engaging a little bit more around that," said Young.
The poll also asked people if, “on the whole, Alberta benefits from immigration to the province from other countries.” Sixty-three per cent of respondents said they strongly or somewhat agreed.
“That's a very strong number,” Brown said. “That's almost two-thirds of Albertans. So on balance as a province, we do feel that immigrants have a positive contribution.”

That figure is down 18 percentage points from Sept. 2021, when the same question was posed for a poll conducted for the Business Council of Alberta. But, Brown said, the context in which the question was posed is entirely different.
“It was the ‘Alberta is Calling’ era. It was the era when we were fretting about not having enough people coming to the province, having a labour shortage,” she explained.
“Fast forward to today, now that we're in a trade war, now that we're feeling like housing prices are going up, I think that accounts for the difference of opinion.”
In the past five years, Alberta’s population has grown by roughly 600,000 people. Much of that growth has been from international and interprovincial migration.

items: Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: People not feeling ‘connected’ to the 9, yet

While 49 per cent of respondents say they don’t know how they will vote on the non-separation questions, 75 per cent say they will definitely cast a ballot for all nine questions, with 11 per cent suggesting they may possibly skip some questions.
Forty-four per cent of those polled said they feel either not at all familiar or not very familiar with the nine questions.

“When we look at some of these responses together, what we're seeing is that people have the intention of figuring out these questions and answering them when they go to vote, but they haven't yet done that,” Young explained.
“And it'll be interesting to see how many of them follow through once they do start trying to wade through the specifics of the questions and trying to make sense of the context for them.”
Polling data indicate that NDP voters seem to be a lot more familiar with the nine questions than UCP supporters, Brown said.

Sixty-nine per cent of respondents who identify as NDP supporters say they’re very or somewhat familiar with the nine questions, while 45 per cent of those expressing support for the UCP feel the same.

“I think that speaks to the fact that there's been a very strong ‘no to the nine’ campaign,” Brown said. “And I don't think there's been an equally strong campaign coming out of the UCP to vote yes for the nine.”

“So it seems right now that those people who are in the NDP camp — those people would vote NDP if we had an election today — they are more tuned in right now to those other nine questions, paying more attention to them than UCP supporters are.”

Only 11 per cent of UCP supporters said they will vote ‘yes’ to all nine questions, despite the province promoting this position. 61 per cent of UCP voters said they do not know yet how they will vote.
In contrast, 52 per cent of NDP supporters said they would vote ‘no’ to all nine, showing greater support for their position.

“For people who don't follow politics closely, who aren't as interested, there may be a desire to go out and vote on this one kind of existential [separation] question that I think most Albertans have got their head around one way or another at this point, but then not feel prepared to vote on the others,” Young said.
“It's going to be really interesting in the days or weeks after the [vote] to see what the differences in turnout are between question 10 and the other nine.”
Albertans head to the polls to vote on 10 questions Oct. 19.

The CBC News random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted using a hybrid method between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, 2026, by Edmonton-based Trend Research under the direction of Janet Brown Opinion Research. The sample is representative of regional, age and gender factors. The margin of error is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

The survey used a hybrid methodology that involved contacting survey respondents by telephone and giving them the option of completing the survey at that time, at another more convenient time, or receiving an email link and completing the survey online. Trend Research contacted people using a random list of numbers, consisting of 30 per cent landlines and 70 per cent cellphone numbers.

Telephone numbers were dialed up to five times at five different times of day before another telephone number was added to the sample. The response rate among valid numbers (i.e., residential and personal) was 11.3 per cent.

articles.title: Switzerland: Voters reject stricter view of neutrality
articles.summary: Early projections show Swiss voters rejecting a stricter application of the country's vaunted neutrality. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since 1848.

image.caption: The referendum calls for writing a strictly defined version of neutrality into the Swiss constitutionImage: FABRICE COFFRINI/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: Voters in Switzerland look set to reject a proposal for stricter neutrality in a referendum held on Sunday, according to projections by state broadcaster SRF.
According to SRF figures, 29% voted for tighter rules on neutrality while 71% voted against adopting stricter measures.

Although Swiss ‌neutrality has ⁠been recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, exactly how the government implements it is not clearly specified.

The initiative was brought forward by the Pro Schweiz association, a right-wing organization with links to the right-wing populist Swiss People's Party. They argue that the Swiss government has moved too close to the European Union and NATO since Russia's war in Ukraine.
What the Pro Schweiz Association wanted to achieve
The group said its aims were for:

items: Swiss neutrality to be applied "permanently and without exception"
Switzerland to maintain an army capable of defense
Switzerland not to get involved in conflicts between third parties
Switzerland not to join a defense alliance unless attacked
The UN to approve any sanctions before Switzerland joins them

blocks.text: Swiss sentiment on neutrality

According to a poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) earlier this month, the move toward a stricter interpretation of Swiss neutrality does not have the traction needed to pass a referendum. Some 63% of respondents said they intend to vote against the initiative, while 34% plan on backing it.
Nearly all major political parties rejected the initiative, with the exception of the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP).

"Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue," SVP vice president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate. "To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality."
Swiss foreign minister: Neutrality needs 'degree of flexibility'
Opponents of the initiative argued that in the modern world a country cannot hide behind neutrality and treat perpetrators and victims equally.
"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis insisted during a recent televised debate.
In-person voting will begin at 10:00 am (0800 GMT) and polling stations close at noon. The result should become clear around an hour later.
Another referendum on food security has also taken place with that initiative calling for the Swiss population to have access to enough high-quality and affordable food at all times.
According to SRF figures 28% of voters supported the initiative and 72% rejected it.
The food initiative seeks to have Switzerland produce significantly more of its own food.

articles.title: Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
articles.summary: French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic…

image.caption: The pope urged humility and respect for life while addressing the crowd in LourdesImage: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

blocks.text: Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.

The shrine is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site, located near the Spanish border, in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.

blocks.caption: Pope celebrated Sunday Mass at Lourdes (pictured) in front of some 150,000 people, following a mass in Paris attended by 800,000 believersImage: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.

"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."
Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone

The head of the Catholic Church was due to meet with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse later on Sunday — part of Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.
A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.
As pope visits France, sex abuse survivor hopes for healing
While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.

"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."
But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.
"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."
Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops

Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."

He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."
"You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican.

articles.title: Sibol nails maiden Asian Games esports medal with Pokemon Unite bronze
articles.summary: The Sibol Pokemon Unite team of Lance David, Ducke Harnold Leoncio, Lawrence Anthony Gatmaitan, Kim Rey Salazar, Robert Jon Mempin, and Michael Vaughn Ocio earn the Philippines' first-ever esports…

blocks.text: SQUAD. The Sibol Pokemon Unite team of Lance David, Robert Mempin, Ducke Leoncio, Kim Rey Salazar, Vaughn Ocio, Lawrence Gatmaitan together with head coach Albert Camp and PESO president Brian Lim.
PSC-POC Media Pool

The Sibol Pokemon Unite team of Lance David, Ducke Harnold Leoncio, Lawrence Anthony Gatmaitan, Kim Rey Salazar, Robert Jon Mempin, and Michael Vaughn Ocio earn the Philippines' first-ever esports medal in the Asian Games
MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines scored a breakthrough esports medal at the Asian Games as Sibol clinched a Pokemon Unite bronze at the Aichi Sky Expo in Japan on Sunday, September 27.

The team of Lance David, Ducke Harnold Leoncio, Lawrence Anthony Gatmaitan, Kim Rey Salazar, Robert Jon Mempin, and Michael Vaughn Ocio still secured a bronze despite a 2-0 loss to Indonesia in the semifinals.
Sibol built a commanding lead in the first game but ran out of steam, surrendering the opener and failing to recover as it fell to a sweep in the best-of-three affair.

Nevertheless, it was still a commendable result as the Philippines won its first-ever esports medal in the Asian Games, which included esports as a demonstration competition in 2018 then adopted it as a medal event in 2023.

“I’m still in awe because this is the first time and I’m really happy for the boys because this is something they’ll carry with them for the rest of their lives, that they were able to bring home a medal to the Philippines,” said Sibol head coach Albert Camp.
Sibol topped Group A with 4 points then scored a 2-0 win over Hong Kong in the quarterfinals to assure itself of a podium finish.

Another Sibol squad is guaranteed a medal as the Honor of Kings crew of Golden Hart Dajao, Justine Ritchie Tan, Charles Roman Esguerra, Dragon Hart Dajao, Jhon Mike Tungol, and Chammy Paul Nazarrea advanced to the semifinals following a 2-0 victory over South Korea.
Sibol battles China on Monday, September 28, for a spot in the gold-medal match. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope, during Lourdes visit
articles.summary: Pope Leo spoke to bishops before leading a service attended by thousands of worshippers in France.

blocks.text: Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, telling them to "maintain the greatest vigilance", ahead of a meeting with abuse survivors.

The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.
A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.
The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes, before he was scheduled to meet survivors of abuse privately later.
Before giving Mass the Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context.
"It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."
The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.
The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.
Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.
On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.

articles.title: QC school gets detention basin under covered court to curb flooding
articles.summary: A detention basin has been installed beneath a covered court at Masambong Elementary School in Quezon City to help reduce flooding during heavy rains.

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 7:04pm

A newly installed detention basin sits beneath the covered basketball court of Masambong Elementary School in Quezon City to help mitigate localized flooding during heavy rains, as shown in this image. Photo by Luisito Santos via dzBB
A detention basin has been installed beneath a covered court at Masambong Elementary School in Quezon City to help reduce flooding during heavy rains.

In a Super Radyo dzBB report by Luisito Santos on Sunday, the newly constructed drainage system was described as having a total capacity of 200 cubic meters, equivalent to 1,000 200-liter water drums.
Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte said the detention basin was installed to help prevent flooding at the school, which is regularly submerged during heavy downpours.
The Quezon City government previously launched a gravity-operated underground water detention basin beneath a barangay covered court.

Reports later showed that despite continuous heavy rains brought by the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) in August, several areas in the city experienced reduced flooding following the installation of detention basins.
A GMA News explainer said a detention basin serves as a temporary storage facility for rainwater, helping prevent large volumes of water from quickly flowing into low-lying communities.
Structural Engineer Juan Paolo Bersamina said detention basins are considered an effective flood mitigation solution for highly urbanized areas.

However, he noted that connecting disconnected or misaligned drainage lines from different locations to a single detention basin presents a significant engineering challenge. — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
articles.summary:
Supplies cut off from Ukrainian city where bodies are being left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones

The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly…

blocks.text: The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter of fact: food for the 2,000 or so civilians still remaining in the city and its surrounding villages had finally run out.

“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message, from a woman in the besieged city, who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.
Before the war, she weighed 110kg (17 stone); now she weighs just 67, she wrote.

“At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”
Oleshky, across Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.

Accounts of the dire conditions in the city emerged as the Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.
In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.
“Russia is deliberately making life there impossible,” Sybiha said in an address during the general assembly. “They are starving them to death.”
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.
Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000.
But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.

Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has also caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops – who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.

In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.

“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”
On 1 September a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.
Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.

According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, issues began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.

“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.
“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning.

blocks.caption: War-damaged buildings in Oleshky. Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine Brigade

blocks.text: “People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson City. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”

Hasanenko described another reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.
“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.

Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.
“The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields,” said Hasanenko.

“It’s an old city,” adds Hasanenko. “It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”
In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”
“A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.

“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”

articles.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
articles.summary:
Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer

Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up…

blocks.text: Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.

blocks.caption: A community volunteer reminds drivers to slow down to protect baboons in Cape Town, May 2022. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.

Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.

“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”

blocks.caption: A young boy at a protest outside the Urban Wildlife Centre near Simon’s Town on 13 September. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters

blocks.text: Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”

The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.
In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.

blocks.caption: A baboon tries to open a car door. The animals often enter cars and buildings and take food.  Photograph: Gallo Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.

However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.
Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.
Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.

blocks.caption: A chacma baboon looking through a windscreen on the Cape of Good Hope. Photograph: Ryogo i Kubo/imageBroker/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.

“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.
