articles.title: Germany news: Are Germans giving up their beloved meat and sausages?
articles.summary: Germans used to be all about sausages and meat. While those do remain popular, things seem to be slowly changing. There also are new insights into the economic side of East Germany's espionage DW has…

image.caption: A recent study found 93% of households in Germany buy meat productsImage: Maurizio Gambarini/picture allianc/dpa

blocks.text: September 27, 2026
How Cold War espionage helped to boost East Germany's economy

blocks.caption: Karl Marx's economic policies were somewhat helped by the Stasi's foreign espionageImage: Michael Nitzschke/picture alliance

blocks.text: Would you think that espionage could significantly boost a country's economy? In the case of communist East Germany, that seems to have been the case — and to a significant degree.
According to Reuters news agency, a study by the Rockwool Foundation suggests that espionage boosted East Germany's GDP by a whopping 7.4% in the 1970s and 80s.
How, you ask? Well, the notorious Stasi stole scientific and technical information from companies in the West, handed it to companies in the East and helped them increase productivity and growth.

"Stasi espionage strengthened East Germany's ​position within the socialist ‌bloc," said Albrecht Glitz, co-author of the study. "It did not, however, significantly improve success in ​Western markets."

The authors stressed that the East Germany case offers crucial insights for today, as countries again seek to protect strategic technologies, tighten export controls and screen foreign investment in sensitive industries.

articles.title: Ortega: SC petitions won't hinder prosecution preparations for Sara Duterte trial
articles.summary: The petitions seeking to overturn the impeachment court"s ruling on the vote threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte"s conviction will not hinder the prosecution"s preparations for the impeachment…

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 6:31pm

The petitions seeking to overturn the impeachment court’s ruling on the vote threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s conviction will not hinder the prosecution’s preparations for the impeachment trial, House Deputy Speaker and La Union Rep. Paolo Ortega V said Sunday.

“Every move by the [House] committee and every development in the impeachment proceedings always draws questions from the defense. These will not hinder the prosecution’s preparations. This has already been anticipated,” Ortega told Super Radyo dzBB in Filipino.
“With or without the Supreme Court’s decision, the trial will continue,” he added.

This came after former Executive Secretary Vic Rodriguez asked the Supreme Court to declare null and void the Senate impeachment court’s September 23 ruling on the voting threshold in Duterte’s impeachment trial.

He also asked the high court to issue a temporary restraining order against the ruling, which changed the basis for calculating the two-thirds vote needed for conviction from all 24 senators to senators who are legally and factually capable of participating in the proceedings.
Rodriguez argued that the Constitution sets the voting threshold at two-thirds of all the members of the Senate, which would be 16 votes if all 24 senators are counted.
Meanwhile, lawyer Ernesto Francisco Jr. asked the Supreme Court to issue a Status Quo Ante Order (SQAO) reversing the changes that took effect following the impeachment court’s ruling.

“It is most respectfully prayed that upon the filing of this Petition, a Status Quo Ante Order be issued directing the parties to maintain the last actual, peaceable and uncontested state of affairs that existed before the present controversy,” the petition’s prayer read.
“It is further prayed of the Honorable Court that the proceedings conducted on 23 September 2026 that led to the issuance of the Ruling be declared null and void,” it added.

On Wednesday, the Senate impeachment court voted to base the two-thirds vote needed to convict Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of “legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings.”

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion filed by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought to overturn the July 6 ruling after several senators became unavailable to participate in the impeachment trial.

Under the new rule, senators who are detained, medically or physically incapacitated, legally restrained from performing their functions, being sought by authorities with their whereabouts unknown, or otherwise beyond the Senate’s coercive processes may be excluded from the voting base.

Among those who have been largely absent from the proceedings are Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are detained over separate plunder charges; Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court; and Loren Legarda, who has been on prolonged medical leave abroad.— Mariel Celine Serquiña/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: South African police probe mining feud, business rivalry after shootings kill 27
articles.summary: South African police on Sunday were hunting the perpetrators of two separate shootings that killed 27 people within hours of each other, highlighting the country's gun violence problem.

image.caption: An emergency vehicle is seen at the site of a deadly shooting at a tavern in Wedela township, southwest of Johannesburg on Sunday. (Oupa Nkosi/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Updated
South African police on Sunday were hunting the perpetrators of two separate shootings that killed 27 people within hours of each other, highlighting the country's gun violence problem.
'This cannot go on like this,' President Cyril Ramaphosa said of the incidents
"This cannot go on like this," South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said of the incidents, which came only days after another shooting killed 11 people at a house party near Durban.

Authorities were still working to establish the motives for the shootings near Johannesburg and Cape Town, but initial investigations suggested one could be a turf war between illegal miners and the other a business rivalry.
"This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going to continue pulling out all stops," Ramaphosa told local media channels.
Violent crime is rife in South Africa, despite efforts to curb one of the world's highest per-capita murder rates.

In Wedela township, about 80 kilometres from Johannesburg, 17 people were killed and 15 injured at a tavern when suspects armed with AK-47 rifles opened fire at around 9:30 p.m. local time on Saturday, police said.
Ramaphosa said police had images of the suspects in that incident and were working to track them down.
Shooting could be retaliation

Residents were reluctant to speak about the incident, but one said that illegal miners, known locally as zama zamas from an isiZulu expression for "taking a chance," live in the area, where powerful gangs control the illicit gold mining trade.
The province's police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one line of inquiry was that the shooting was a "turf war in terms of illegal mining."
Saturday's shooting could be retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago, he added.
Soldiers and police pathologists had arrived in the township, where there were two burnt vehicles and the tavern where the shooting took place had a sign saying "No weapons allowed."
Threat to democracy
At the scene of the shooting in Lwandle on the outskirts of Cape Town, onlookers gathered behind police lines but did not want to speak to journalists, saying they feared for their safety.

items: Mass shooting at house party in South Africa leaves 11 dead, 3 wounded: police

blocks.text: In that incident, gunmen opened fire in a venue selling grilled meat at around 2:00 a.m. local time on Sunday, killing 10 people and injuring 11.
An eyewitness video from the venue shows people dancing and singing in a crowded outdoor area when a burst of shots rings out and screams are heard.
A police official said, "a business jealousy might have been the issue," as there were reports that people had been buying alcohol in cheaper places and going to the venue to drink.
No arrests have been made yet and detectives are working to find the gunmen, police said in statements.

items: South Africa's anti-migrant protesters march nationwide after thousands flee violence

blocks.text: Crime is expected to be a major issue for voters in municipal elections in November, when the African National Congress is facing further erosion of voter support. Fear and anger over high rates of femicide have risen after the discovery of women's bodies near Johannesburg since July.
Ramaphosa said earlier this year that organized crime had become the biggest threat to South Africa's democracy, and he deployed the army to help police in some areas.

"South Africa has a serious illegal firearms problem, and firearms are frequently used by organized criminal groups as well as in gang-related and other violent crimes," crime expert Yusuf Abramjee told Reuters.
"Authorities need to look at the wider networks behind the violence," he added.

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Rappler was built for stories like Mary Jane Veloso’s
articles.summary: Our work will only make a difference if we don’t treat stories as one-offs that we abandon once a new viral obsession grips the country

blocks.text: We have variations of this reminder to the team: “Follow through.” “Don’t drop the ball.” “Own the story.” “This story is ours.”
They all mean: Our work will only make a difference if we don’t treat stories as one-offs that we abandon once a new viral obsession grips the country.
And at Rappler, by stories we also mean the campaigns and engagement we do with partner organizations and local communities.
They can also mean the cause of an individual that has become larger than herself.
Such was the case with Mary Jane Veloso, the poor single mother from Nueva Ecija who, on Thursday, September 24, was pardoned by President Bongbong Marcos.

That was 11 years after Rappler, through our civic engagement arm MovePH, threw its full support behind the Change.org petition started by the Promotion of Church People’s Response and the network of Church Task Force to Save the Life of Mary Jane Veloso.

Mary Jane, tricked into smuggling drugs into Indonesia in 2010, was set for execution in the Wirogunan prison in April 2015. With a few days left for Philippine officials to convince Indonesian counterparts to stay the execution, MovePH “published the [PCR] call and put click buttons under all related Rappler articles.” As a result, “a global conversation was sparked. It pushed the petition to the top 10 of the most signed petitions globally over that weekend.”

The execution was deferred. Mary Jane stayed behind bars in Indonesia for a decade more, repatriated to Manila in 2025 — but straight to the correctional for women. With the presidential pardon, she walks free.

In those years of waiting, Rappler did its part not to forget Mary Jane in prison, her family beyond the rice fields of Cabanatuan, and her volunteer lawyers who had made her case the fight of their lives. I share below the milestone contents we have done in the last decade.
We would do this again. And I hope you can support our work to make that possible.

articles.title: U.K. police evacuate homes near U.S. air base and detain men on suspected explosives offensives
articles.summary: British police said on Sunday they had arrested several men on suspicion of explosives offences and Army bomb disposal experts were examining a number of vehicles in a "major incident" near an air…

image.caption: Emergency vehicles are parked at Fairford Youth Football club, near RAF Fairford, which hosts US Air Force personnel, in Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain, September 27, 2026. Police declared a major incident at UK's Fairford air base after several men were arrested on suspicion of offences under t

blocks.text: World

British police said on Sunday they had arrested several men on suspicion of explosives offences and Army bomb disposal experts were examining a number of vehicles in a "major incident" near an air base used by the U.S. in southwest England.
Police say several men have been detained on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act
Police said nearby residents had been evacuated from their homes.

The British government gave authorization to the U.S. to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned in July that any base used in strikes would be a legitimate target.

A Reuters eyewitness said armed police had blocked access to the main gate of the base, while equipment had been positioned in front of access points and residents of a nearby village were evacuated to a leisure centre.

items: Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report

blocks.text: Around 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were stationed in the village of Fairford near the base.

"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident. It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act," Gloucestershire police said in a statement, referring to a village near the air base.
"The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles."
Police said they believed the incident was now contained.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures.

"The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow U.K.-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families," the spokesperson said.
"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families."
Britain said in July its armed forces were ​ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned the U.K. not to allow U.S. bombers to ‌fly from Fairford.

British ministers have also briefed providers of critical infrastructure on the threat posed by Russia, with the government increasingly concerned about possible sabotage operations and cyberattacks. Russia denies mounting hybrid attacks on Western nations.

articles.title: PhilHealth: 123 facilities offer heart surgery under Z Benefits
articles.summary: Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) has 123 hospitals and other healthcare facilities that provide heart surgery under its Z Benefit program as of June 30, 2026, President and Chief…

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 5:14pm

Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) has 123 hospitals and other healthcare facilities that provide heart surgery under its Z Benefit program as of June 30, 2026, President and Chief Executive Officer Dr. Beverly Ho said Sunday.
Ho made this disclosure during the World Heart Day celebration in Manila, where she presented the health benefits offered by PhilHealth.
“This is an important network, but we recognize that we need more, more providers, particularly in areas where access to specialized cardiac care remains limited,” she said.
Ho said PhilHealth looks forward to continuing its partnership with the Philippine Heart Association and the cardiac care community.
The Z Benefit packages cover healthcare services and rates for “Case Type Z,” or serious illnesses that may require long hospital stays and could lead to poor outcomes without early treatment.
The packages include benefits for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, total correction of tetralogy of Fallot and surgery for ventricular septal defect in children, among others.

“PhilHealth is continuing to expand our cardiovascular benefits in response to the evolving healthcare needs, and among the areas in the pipeline is the expansion of coverage for emergency CABG surgery, recognizing that in cardiovascular emergencies, timely intervention can be life-saving and life-changing,” Ho said.
CABG surgery is an operation used to improve blood flow to the heart when the coronary arteries are blocked or narrowed.
“We are also looking towards expanding coverage for congenital heart disorders, particularly to further support children and families who require specialized cardiac care,” she added.

World Heart Day is observed every September 29 as the World Health Organization, its member states and other stakeholders renew their commitment to reducing preventable and premature deaths from cardiovascular diseases.
WHO has also referred to September 29 as World Heart Day in its previous observances. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Could a single Maritime power grid make electricity more reliable?
articles.summary: When Canada's premiers met in Prince Edward Island back in July, leaders from the Maritime provinces had power on their minds — just not the political kind.

image.caption: An independent energy system operator, or ISO, would be at arm's length from governments and power utilities with the idea that it would work on behalf of electricity customers, not private for-profit private businesses. (CBC)

blocks.text: PEI
When Canada's premiers met in Prince Edward Island back in July, leaders from the Maritime provinces had power on their minds — just not the political kind.
Some experts are pushing for an Independent System Operator (ISO) to unite electricity across the provinces

During those meetings, the premiers of P.E.I., Nova Scotia and New Brunswick signed a non-binding agreement known as a memorandum of understanding, or MOU, pledging to co-operate on a regional road map for electricity transmission by next spring.
A key component of that MOU was for the three provinces to explore the possibility of a Maritime-wide independent system operator, or ISO.

items: ‘It will save money,’ says N.S. premier of regional electricity operator
Maritime provinces to consider regional electricity operator

blocks.text: The idea — a regionally integrated power grid — is one the Halifax-based Ecology Action Centre has been pushing for years.

"When we're making decisions about … how do we make sure that the grid is stable out to 2050, those kind of planning initiatives should incorporate the kind of resources we have across the Maritime region," Thomas Arnason McNeil, the centre's senior energy co-ordinator, told This is P.E.I. host Mitch Cormier.

"I think it is encouraging that we're starting to have the conversations now before we walk too far down the road. I do have faith that it is something that can happen quickly, in large part because it needs to happen quickly."
The MOU notes that demand for power is rising — the federal government is planning for energy use to double by 2050 — and the Maritime provinces are aiming for efficiency through resource sharing.

An independent energy system operator would work at arm's length from governments and power utilities. The idea is that it would work on behalf of electricity customers, not private for-profit private businesses like Nova Scotia Power, N.B. Power or P.E.I.'s Maritime Electric.

It would also make decisions about how best to generate that energy in a way that makes sense for the entire grid — whether it's building new transmission lines or generating power from wind, solar or battery storage.

items: 'We haven't got much time': N.S. energy system operator takes on challenging renewables target
N.S. grid operator to open new, broad search for energy technology, including batteries

blocks.text: Nova Scotia launched its own ISO last year, carving out some responsibilities from the private utility and giving them to a new non-profit entity. The Independent Energy System Operator is gradually taking over the procurement of new energy generating projects and decisions about power dispatch, among other jobs.

"You're going to look at the whole system and say, 'OK, brass tacks: where do we need to build generation, where do we need to build transmission lines, how do we make decisions that are in the best interest of ratepayers across the region?'" Arnason McNeil said.

"[With] a systems operator that operates at arm's length from a private utility, at arm's length from government, you're able to make decisions about electricity that are not perceived as having a conflict of interest."
Planning 5 minutes — and 5 years — ahead
When it comes to examples of how an independent system operator could run, Arnason McNeil said, there's no need to look very far — just south of the border from the Maritimes, in fact.

ISO New England is an independent entity that's responsible for the power grid and wholesale electricity market for most of the region's six states — a service area with a population of 15 million customers.
Formed in 1997, it orchestrates how energy flows between sellers and customers on a minute-by-minute basis, but also over the long term.

"Any time anyone in New England is using power, there is a group of operators in our control room in Massachusetts making sure that the supply and demand across the region is balanced," said Matt Kakley, ISO New England's manager of media relations and strategic communications.

"But then we also, in the day to day, are looking 10, 20 years into the future and trying to project what we anticipate we'll need so that we can ensure that we have that supply and balance, not just in the next five minutes, but in the next five years."

The non-profit is funded by a tariff on wholesale energy transactions, Kakley said, so it doesn't make any money from electricity rates in the markets it's responsible for. He added that the competition in that wholesale market also helps keep power rates lower for customers.

It's the ISO's job to synthesize all the electrical generation and use among all six New England states. It's tasked with creating decades-long plans for power supply and demand, as well as for transmission infrastructure.

"If you suddenly have a portion of the region that is experiencing a lot of population growth, you want to make sure that that portion of the system is able to accommodate that new electricity demand," Kakley said.
"[We're] making sure that everybody is operating from a shared understanding of where we are and where we're headed."
Ottawa kicks in funding to get the ball rolling on new power cables between P.E.I. and N.B.
Whether the Maritime governments can make an ISO happen remains to be seen, and Arnason McNeil knows creating a region-wide energy grid will take time.
But he's encouraged by the fact that the conversations have started.

"Frankly, we are so far behind places like New England at this stage when it comes to regional co-operation on electricity and reliability that I do think that we need to think really big and really ambitiously, and I think we do see that reflected in the memorandum of understanding," he said.

"But man, we've got to have these conversations right now because we're going to be caught flat-footed if we're trying to do things like phase out coal and build offshore wind and build onshore wind and solar and batteries."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Stephen Brun is the copy editor for digital news at CBC Prince Edward Island. A graduate of UPEI and Holland College, he has been a writer and editor for a number of newspapers and websites across Canada for nearly two decades. You can reach him at stephen.brun@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Northern Ireland: Pro-UK march to go through Catholic area
articles.summary: Northern Ireland: Pro-UK march to go through Catholic area

image.caption: The Orange Order march will go through the largely Catholic streetImage: Paul Mcerlane/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Northern Ireland's Protestant, pro-British Orange Order was set to parade through a mainly Catholic and nationalist area on Sunday.

It's the first time the march has been allowed to go through the area since 1997. Overnight, a court ruling allowed it to take place after a series of last-minute legal challenges that reached Belfast's High Court.
Thirty-five members of the Orange Order are to march silently through Garvaghy Road in the town of Portadown, without any bands or other Order supporters participating.
About 2,000 people gathered on the street Sunday morning in a counterprotest to prevent the march.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for "calm on all sides." In a BBC interview, he said "big gains" had been made in Northern Ireland "and we don't want to see things go backwards."
Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, a member of the Irish republican Sinn Fein party, spoke against the decision to allow the march to take place.

blocks.caption: Pro-Irish protesters are expected to protest against the marchImage: Cathal McNaughton/REUTERS

blocks.text: "Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever," she said, also voicing her support for the local residents to protest against the march, which she labeled "unwanted" and "sectarian."

Carla Lockhart, an MP from the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said local residents have nothing to fear from "thirty five men walking down a road silently and with no bands and in an orderly fashion."
History of conflict
Garvaghy Road was one of the epicenters of the conflict between the Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and the Protestant, pro-British unionists in the late 1990s.
Back then, clashes between residents and the marchers repeatedly triggered disorder, also known as the Drumcree dispute.

blocks.caption: Some 2,000 people joined a  counterprotest against the Orange Order marchImage: Cathal McNaughton/REUTERS

blocks.text: As part of the Good Friday Agreement, a deal signed in 1998 that largely ended three decades of conflict between the two sides known as the Troubles, an entity was established to regulate contentious processions named The Parades Commission.

The Commission repeatedly rejected the Orange Order's requests to march through the area, with a High Court ruling quashing the rejection this year due to a procedural error. The Order then issued a fresh application, which was approved.
Northern Ireland still troubled

articles.title: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the Kings of K-pop are back
articles.summary: Big Bang played London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, marking a long-awaited return for the group that helped build the blueprint for modern K-pop.

blocks.text: Image source, Timothy Norris/Getty Images
Taeyang, G-Dragon and Daesung of BigBang perform during the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival
A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean.
An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back.

Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour.
Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert; they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history.
As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Inside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium

blocks.text: Inside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia.
Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia.

The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal.
Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking.

Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio , comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community.

By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging.
The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful.

blocks.caption: Image caption, G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung on stage with dancers

blocks.text: Image source, YG Entertainment
G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung on stage with dancers
In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards.
When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours.
They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible.
Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List.
"When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool.
"Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds.
"Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be."

blocks.caption: Image caption, G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung celebrating their 20th anniversary during the XX: Cosmos World Tour

blocks.text: G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung celebrating their 20th anniversary during the XX: Cosmos World Tour
Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies.

But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre.
For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live.
"They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore.
"They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me."
The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fans arrived kitted out with Big Bang merchandise

blocks.text: Fans arrived kitted out with Big Bang merchandise
And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong.
In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks.
But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise.
"Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology."
The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow.
Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years.
Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, coordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fans exchanging handmade gifts outside the stadium

blocks.text: Fans exchanging handmade gifts outside the stadium
Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success.
South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus.
Then came the scandals.

In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group.
Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal.
It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars.
South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fans with their merchandise, holding up free banners ahead of the show

blocks.text: Fans with their merchandise, holding up free banners ahead of the show
Although the band didn't openly acknowledge the departure of two of their former members from the stage, their absence was obvious to long-time fans in the audience.
Though it did not matter to fans like Annie, who flew from New York to see the show with friends. She said Big Bang's perseverance through hardship made their music mean even more.
"Big Bang was my starter," she says. "I love how they move through the obstacles - it gives me hope. After years of hiatus, it's amazing they're coming back. They are the OGs."
The crowd erupted as the opening chant of Bang Bang Bang echoed before the band even walked out, while their iconic 2008 ballad Haru Haru produced a massive stadium-wide singalong.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fans meeting up ahead of the concert

blocks.text: Fans meeting up ahead of the concert
The K-pop industry Big Bang helped build has changed almost beyond recognition.
Yet their return has drawn a striking mix of original second-generation fans and younger Gen Z listeners who were barely born when the group debuted.
While many veteran followers grew up alongside the band, a whole new generation discovered them through digital archives or cross-media appearances.
Gemma and her daughter Casey travelled from Edinburgh wearing handmade custom jackets.
"I found out about them through T.O.P in Squid Game and then fell down a rabbit hole," Gemma says. "I've converted so many of my friends to K-pop now. It's all about the energy."
For Korean diaspora fans, the show carried an even deeper cultural resonance.
"I got into Big Bang when their Alive EP (in 2012) was released because I felt they were quite ground-breaking," says Kevin.

"Before, I felt there was a lot of mimicking by Korean artists on what was happening in the West, but here they took full ownership of their unique identity. It's very rare in K-pop that you have a band around for 20 years, and they definitely played a part in making K-pop mainstream."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nicole and her son Arthur attended the concert to celebrate his 8th birthday

blocks.text: Nicole and her son Arthur attended the concert to celebrate his 8th birthday
Much of this multi-generational pull is driven by archival concert footage, TV appearances, and classic music videos circulating across social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube.
"Nostalgia can be built upon something people didn't even experience personally at the time," notes Um.

"It comes through shared digital memory. YG Entertainment was early in leveraging digital platforms like YouTube, which built a lasting global fan foundation that has accumulated across two generations."
While the band refrained from directly addressing their past on stage, the emotional weight of their history peaked during the finale Still Life.
As T.O.P's unmistakable baritone echoed through the stadium via recorded vocals, a visible wave of emotion swept across the crowd.
Addressing the venue during the encore, G-Dragon appeared clearly moved, admitting they never expected their music to leave such an enduring global mark 14 years after their London debut.
As fireworks lit up the night sky, the three members linked hands and bowed deeply - a triumphant moment for the group widely credited with helping reshape modern K-pop.

articles.title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
articles.summary: The two attacks hours apart come as the country struggles to stop high levels of gang-related armed violence.

blocks.text: Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.
Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured.
In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks.
In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.
Police said thirteen men and four women were killed, adding that the motive was not clear.
In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.
No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.
The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.

articles.title: At least 27 dead in two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
articles.summary:
Seventeen people killed at township bar near Johannesburg and 10 killed in separate incident at store near Cape Town, officers say

Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest…

blocks.text: Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, police have said.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, south-west of Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at a store in Lwandle, near Cape Town, at about 1am on Sunday. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.
The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.
No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.

articles.title: India news: Kolkata's SRFTI students allege violent attack
articles.summary: Students at Kolkata's Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute say they were attacked with knives after confronting an outside group over a meeting they allege was affiliated with the right-wing…

image.caption: Violence erupted at Kolkata's SRFTI after students object to outside group's eventImage: Shamayita Chakraborty/DW

blocks.text: September 27, 2026
SRFTI students attacked after objecting to outsiders' event on campus
Shamayita Chakraborty

blocks.caption: Students at Kolkata's SRFTI say they were attacked after objecting to a meeting they allege was affiliated with the RSSImage: Shamayita Chakraborty/DW

blocks.text: Students of the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) in Kolkata said on Sunday they were violently attacked after objecting to a meeting held on campus by an allegedly rightwing group, a student representative told DW.

A scuffle broke out between the students and members of the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat (ABGP) after the student union confronted the group saying it had not been informed about the meeting and questioned the participants before the confrontation turned violent.
The students allege that members of the group attacked them with knives.

Poorvi Bondre, an editing student from Maharashtra and a member of the SRFTI student union, told DW that the event was affiliated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and was being used to promote its agenda on campus.
She said students had opposed the meeting because it was not a film screening but what she described as direct RSS promotion.
The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization and the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"This was an RSS event. We were completely unaware of this event. When we asked them what this was about, the fight started," Bondre said. "They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives."
Videos of the incident have circulated on social media, showing students with what appear to be knife wounds. However, DW could not independently verify their authenticity.
The campus remains tense, with students inside and members of the ABGP gathered outside, according to the student representative.

articles.title: Iran sticks to Hormuz plan after Trump rejects it
articles.summary: Iranian officials that while they were aware of Trump's comments on rejecting the new proposal, they had not received a formal message rejecting the plan that would open the Strait of Hormuz.

image.caption: The Strait of Hormuz was a crucial waterway for much of the world's oil and gas before the start of the warImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Iran on Sunday insisted on its conditions for reopeningthe Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump's public rejection of the proposal that had birthed some hope for reopening the key waterway.

"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights," he said.
Iran proposed a seven-day plan aimed at reopening the strategic waterway at the UN General Assembly in New York, which it said could put an end to fighting within days.
Iran offers plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days
Tehran said it had transmitted the proposal to Washington via Qatari mediators.

Iran's plan, Araghchi said, called for cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including Lebanon, and fulfilling the conditions of the ceasefire deal that fell apart months ago. That agreement called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
Trump rejects plan, but no communication to Iran
Trump publicly rejected Iran's proposal on Saturday while speaking to reporters at the White House.
"I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal," he said. "They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly."
Responding to Trump's comments, Araghchi said Iranians "saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators."
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them," the foreign minister added.

blocks.caption: Under Iran's proposal, Washington would have to meet certain conditions before the strait was reopenedImage: Hamed Malekpour/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The strait stalemate

Iranian ports are currently under a US blockade as Washington attempts to pressure Tehran into lifting its closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The key waterway remains largely shut to international shipping despite Trump's claims that the US controls it.
Early Sunday, the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) — set up by Iran to manage the Strait of Hormuz — warned ships of consequences if they use "illegal routes" in the region.
"This risks financial and life losses for the vessel, owner, master and crew, and seriously restricts its future Strait of Hormuz passage," it said in a post on X.
The authority said if ships breach its rules, all vessels belonging to the company could face restrictions in the future.
Around a fifth of global oil demand passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war began. The waterway is also a crucial route for liquefied natural gas and fertilizer.

articles.title: No public mentions of Taiwan at official Xi and Trump meeting
articles.summary: At a high-profile summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Washington, there was much talk of trade and artificial intelligence. One of the most contentious issues, Taiwan, was only…

image.caption: Image: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump picked his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping up directly from the airport and in his welcoming remarks he praised the strong friendship between their two nations, as well as recalling how China and the US fought together as allies during World War II.

"Look at the greatness that we had together fighting in World War II," he said. "Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country," he said at the White House, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that fought alongside China against the Japanese between 1941 and 1942.

However, these pilots did not actually volunteer to fight with the People's Republic of China, whose leader was visiting Washington and which was not founded until 1949. The Americans were risking their lives for the former Republic of China, whose government relocated to Taiwan after communist victory in the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

"China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen," Trump said at a state dinner for Xi on Thursday evening. Sun Yat-sen was the founder of the Republic of China in 1912 and the Kuomintang, or KMT, which remains a major political party in Taiwan today.

blocks.caption: US Flying Tigers were used to defend China against Japan during World War IIImage: United Archives/TopFoto/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Taiwan a major problem between US and China

Ever since the end of World War II, Taiwan has been a point of contention between Beijing and Washington. For decades, the US government ignored the communist regime in the People's Republic of China. But since 1972, Washington has acknowledged the "one China principle," according to which there is only one China, whose legal government is in Beijing and Taiwan belongs to it. Diplomatic relations between the US and China were only established in 1979.

The Taiwan Relations Act came into effect in 1979 too. The US law legalized arms exports to Taiwan. It also allowed the US government to take military action to prevent changes to the status quo in the Taiwan Strait.

A potential war between China and Taiwan would not only jeopardize stability in the Asia-Pacific region but also plunge the global economy into a prolonged recession, as supply chains would be severely disrupted.

During their high-profile meeting, Xi did not openly urge the US to respect the "one China" principle as he has done in the past, and Trump did not mention Taiwan in public either. In May, he put on hold a $14-billion arms deal that the US had concluded with the Taiwanese government late last year. The arms sales deal remains under review.

"Given the US' production capacity and its own military needs, it will take some time before approved arms can be delivered," said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist and professor at the National University of Singapore. "It remains unclear what else the US can currently offer Taiwan."

Ahead of crucial midterm elections in November, Trump urgently needs some positive headlines. He and his Republican party rely on farmers for support so they need China to import US agricultural goods. In 2023, before their current trade war, China imported $43 billion worth of soy, beef, wood and other goods from the US. However Beijing has drastically reduced its imports since.
Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit
Taiwan mentioned behind closed doors

China used the meeting "to make clear to Trump its opposition to any US military support for Taiwan," said William Yang, an analyst with the International Crisis Group. "Xi wants to convey this message personally and behind closed doors, thereby influencing Trump's decision on arms sales to Taiwan."

China's Xinhua news agency said that Xi had addressed the issue behind closed doors. It reported that Xi had expressed hope that the US would take strong action against Taiwanese independence and said that China's position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was clear. He reportedly added that "building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability is neither an expedient measure nor something that can be achieved overnight."

It will not have pleased Taiwanese politicians that the US president openly considered treating Taiwan as a bargaining chip in its negotiations with China, German sinologist Eberhard Sandschneider of the consultancy Berlin Global Advisers suggested during a political chatshow on German public television. "People living on the island of Taiwan do not take this lightly. This is an existential issue for Taiwan."
He added that he did not think China would take military action against Taiwan. That would be a move just as illogical as the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US attack on Iran, he argued.

Nobody is playing poker in China, Sandschneider continued. "Clear strategic interests are pursued there. National sovereignty and winning back Taiwan are key concerns. At the same time, it is well known that any military attack on Taiwan would not only lead to a military disaster but also to an economic collapse. The resulting setback for the global economy would call into question the Communist Party's legitimacy," the expert said.
De Zheng contributed to this article, which has been translated from German.
Trump-Xi summit: Results or just symbolism?

articles.title: ‘An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’ and Bicol’s unwavering fight for human rights
articles.summary: Weaving Bicol folk dance and music, the film 'An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’ shows the enduring hope of the families of the desaparecidos

blocks.text: ALBAY, Philippines – Drawing inspiration from the lives of Bicol farmers, An Sayaw nin mga Salampati (Dance of the Pigeons) transforms the grief and longing of the families of desaparecidos (victims of enforced disappearances) into a sharp look at the region’s long-standing fight against systemic human rights violations.

Through the haunting cadences of “Sarung Banggi” (One Evening), playful beats of “Salampating Guminaro” (The Little Pigeon That Has Grown Tame), the melancholic rhythm of “Kudot-kudotan” (The Pinching Game), and other Bicol folk music and dances, the film not only puts the spotlight on regional traditions, but also the people’s collective courage and resistance.

“Beyond being an agricultural nation, the Philippines suffers among the highest recorded cases of disappearances and extrajudicial killings targeting farmer-activists fighting for their ancestral land rights — a reality we aim to shed light on in this film,” said multi-awarded Bicolano filmmaker Arjanmar Rebeta.

Since the 1970s, at least 2,300 desaparecidos have remained missing in the Philippines. Among the latest recorded cases in Bicol are human rights defenders James Jazmines and Felix Salaveria Jr., who were both abducted by alleged state forces in Tabaco City, Albay.

Jazmines was taken on August 23, 2024, and Salaveria suffered the same fate five days later on August 28. Two years on, their families continue to search tirelessly and demand the safe resurfacing of both activists.

“In the fictional town of Sinibaan, women dress scarecrows in the last-worn clothes of the disappeared to stand across the fields as a symbol of their families’ longing for their return. The women left behind by their desaparecido husbands dance the pantomina,” shared Rebeta.
Pantomina is a traditional Bicolano courtship dance, typically performed by newlyweds during weddings to mimic the movements of doves or pigeons.
For Rebeta, the characters performing the dance serve as “a stark reminder for the government and a courtship for justice — a movement that will continue as an act of remembrance and resistance.”
In the film, Ramona Yusay portrays Maura, a folk dance instructor whose husband, Lando (played by Jhong Hilario), has been forcibly disappeared.

Maura and the women of Sinibaan — including Gunda, played by Marietta “Pokwang” Subon — danced pantomina to “express their grief into the streets and fields, turning the dance into a challenge against a system that silences their voices and leaves their loved ones unaccounted for.”

The cast is also joined by local Bicolano artists and the region’s top creative talents in music, dance, and production, including performers Mildred Estella and Kyle Adrian Paga, alongside renowned composer and arranger Ruben Federizon.

As a full-scale musical film, the production faced significant resource hurdles, especially for Giya Studios. Seeing the challenge, the local community stepped up — everyone from thrift shop vendors and farmers to even pigeon owners donated goods and services to drive the project forward.

“During our six-day first shooting leg in Cabusao and Libmanan, Camarines Sur, the community truly adopted us and helped us in so many ways — from small gestures to large contributions,” said Khaye Medina, managing director of Giya Studios.
“They helped us save on costs and sustain this advocacy project, doing everything from building production sets to joining us as talents.”

blocks.caption: SOLIDARITY. Jhong Hilario, local talents, and volunteers help complete the first six-day shooting leg in Cabusao and Libmanan, Camarines Sur.

blocks.text: Medina shared that the local community members who joined as talents did not just help on set; they even organized a “Zumba for a Cause” event to raise funds for the film’s upcoming second shooting leg.

With most of the production crew working as volunteers, Medina and Rebeta emphasized that their top priority for the upcoming second leg is providing proper meals, accommodations, and transportation allowances for the team.
As of September 17, the film’s online crowdfunding campaign has raised P130,000 in cash donations, alongside production support and meal sponsorships provided by local communities.

“Of course, we provide honoraria to our talents, but we never expected them to take the initiative to give back and help us raise funds for production,” said Medina. “That is the real beauty of making this film — it is not just about the community; it is supported and embraced by them.”

blocks.caption: FILMMAKERS. Filming across rural villages, production volunteers bring to life the 1990s landscape of the fictional town of Sinibaan.

blocks.text: The production team is preparing for its next shooting schedule and continues to seek partnerships, major sponsorships, collaborations, and other forms of support.
Those interested in helping can message ‘An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’s (Dance of the Pigeons)’ official Facebook page or contribute through its crowdfunding campaign.

articles.title: What Trump's 'most favoured nation' drug pricing policy might mean for Canadians
articles.summary: To avoid triggering massive U.S. price cuts, pharmaceutical companies now incentivized to protect their larger U.S. profits by raising prices elsewhere, drug policy experts say.

blocks.text: Trump’s push to cut pharma costs could drive up drug prices in Canada

U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement that all 50 states will join his proposed drug-price lowering policy is leading Canadian pharmaceutical experts and international researchers to warn how prices could rise around the world.

On Sept. 18, Trump announced in the Oval Office that all state Medicaid programs for Americans with low incomes will benefit from lower prescription drug prices under agreements with pharmaceutical manufacturers to match the lowest prices paid by other developed nations.
"We went from paying the highest drug prices in the world to paying the lowest drug prices in the world," Trump said about the intention of the new policy.

The Trump administration has also cut deals with 26 large pharmaceutical companies. The goal is to keep U.S. drug prices more comparable with the 19 countries that the Trump administration proposes as reference countries, which span Europe, Canada, Australia, Japan and South Korea.

It’s a big shift; the U.S. has had the world’s highest drug prices. With brand-name drugs, on average, significantly cheaper in Canada, will that make this country’s drug prices a target under the new policy?

Such questions became sharper this week when Public Citizen, a U.S. consumer advocacy group, posted copies of Pfizer and Eli Lilly's agreements it sued to obtain. Though key sections are redacted, the group said the agreements "reveal concerning terms that will help facilitate pharma companies charging more for drugs abroad or discontinuing supplying drugs in other countries so that they can continue to charge U.S. customers high prices."
Multinational pharmaceutical companies also have incentives to raise prices or restrict supply.
What do we know about what drug companies agreed to?
Trump's agreements with drug makers to match low prices in other countries are known as most favoured nation, or MFN, prices.

While new to the U.S., MFN is already common across Canada and is widely used in Europe and elsewhere to control prescription drug spending, said Dr. Thomas Hwang, an assistant professor at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston.
While the name most favoured nation may sound like favouring one nation over another, it is not about special treatment, pharmaceutical policy experts say.
Trump takes aim at major pharmaceutical companies, demands lower drug prices
"It basically says that the United States wishes to get the price that's being offered to similarly sized countries and similarly wealthy countries," Hwang said.

Similar countries, including Canada, are bundled, based on net pharmaceutical pricing deals, said Mina Tadrous, an associate professor at the University of Toronto's pharmacy faculty who evaluates drug policy.
Why should Canadians care?
Tadrous said the Trump administration's MFN does not mean Canadian drug prices will automatically go up.

But to make up for — or avoid — lost revenue in the U.S. due to the new policy, pharmaceutical companies might seek higher Canadian prices, reduce the discounts they offer, or delay launching certain medicines in this country, Tadrous said.

Innovative Medicines Canada, which represents the pharmaceutical industry, says most-favoured nation (MFN) pricing in the U.S. threatens to disrupt access to existing medicines, delay introduction of new medicines and undermine confidence in Canada's pharmaceutical market.

items: Sanofi launching $925M vaccine manufacturing facility in North York
The hurdles facing Canada's planned pandemic-busting lab

blocks.text: "For Canadians waiting for a new cancer therapy, a rare disease treatment, or first-in-class medicine, these aren’t abstract policy debates. The changes could have serious consequences for them and their families," Innovative Medicines Canada said in an emailed statement.
Nav Persaud, a family physician with St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto, said he already sees patients struggle.
"People are paying a lot for food and for rent, and they don't have money left over at the end of the month to pay for medicines and medicines end up getting sacrificed," Persaud said.
"I see patients who do not take recommended medicines because of the cost. That happens every day."
What's the basis for concern?
Last week, Hwang and his co-authors published a modelling study of the Trump administration's proposed MFN pricing in the medical journal The Lancet.

Hwang said in an interview that the study was motivated by wanting an independent and rigorous assessment of what the savings could look like in the U.S. and "secondly and equally as importantly," the potential impacts of the policy outside the country.

Hwang and his team wrote that MFN pricing for brand-name medicines could decrease net Medicare spending, but the policy change "could have unintended effects on prices and access to medicines in referenced countries."
Generic Ozempic is coming to Canada. This company wants to make it
What’s more, the redacted agreements posted by Public Citizen show carve outs for Eli Lilly's popular weight-loss drugs, like the GLP-1 medication Zepbound.
"That carveout is new from what the administration has told us in the months leading up to this as well what even the companies have disclosed," Hwang said.
"But as of this past weekend, we now understand that the GLP-1 drugs are not going to be subject to most-favoured nation pricing."
Another deal suggests Pfizer agreed to share revenue with the U.S. government if it raises drug prices outside the U.S.
Hwang said raising foreign prices aligns with Washington's broader goals.

"In the executive order that President Trump released last year, it's not sufficient for the administration for prices to be lower in the U.S. There's also a deep desire at the highest levels of the executive to raise prices outside the U.S, too."
Under the United Kingdom's pharmaceutical trade agreement with the U.S., for instance, the U.K. committed to increasing spending on medicines as a percentage of GDP, Hwang noted.
What's unknown?
Key financial terms and the negotiated prices for drugs are heavily redacted in the records released by Public Citizen.
That makes it difficult for anyone to independently assess value to taxpayers or companies.

"The huge asterisks around all of this is like are we [Canada] actually the lowest prices? How good are the deals we're getting? And until we know that, we don't know what the impacts are going to be on Canadians."
Confidential discounts and rebates, both in the U.S. and in other countries, weren't consistently or reliably available, Hwang added.

articles.title: Getting my Canadian permanent residency should have felt like a win. But I've lost a lot along the way
articles.summary: When Areena Shrestha arrived in Canada as an international student, she didn't fully understand how uncertain and emotionally exhausting the journey to permanent residency could be.

image.caption: When Areena Shrestha arrived in Canada as an international student, she didn't fully understand how uncertain and emotionally exhausting the journey to permanent residency could be. (Submitted by Areena Shrestha)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person
When Areena Shrestha arrived in Canada as an international student, she didn't fully understand how uncertain and emotionally exhausting the journey to permanent residency could be.
Many of my friends who also applied for PR have left
· for CBC First Person
· Posted: Sep 27, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 6 hours ago
This First Person is the experience of Areena Shrestha, who lives in Vancouver. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

I was 18 when I moved to Canada as a Nepalese international student, carrying two suitcases and a simple dream: to study, build a career and eventually call this country home. However, I didn't fully understand when I first arrived how uncertain and emotionally exhausting the journey to permanent residency could be.

While I studied psychology and international relations at the University of British Columbia, I interned at the Canadian Cancer Society and worked as a research assistant in a lab. I said yes to opportunities, built connections and slowly started to feel like I belonged here.

By the time I graduated four years later, my path felt clear. I wanted to work in the non-profit sector and give back to the same kind of communities that had supported me. So I began building a career in social services, supporting vulnerable communities as a program assistant, crisis responder and youth worker.

Today, I work as a case manager at a rent bank, helping people facing housing insecurity access financial support to avoid eviction. My job focuses on helping others find stability during times of a crisis.
Yet while I help others find stability, my own future in Canada has often felt uncertain.

For years, my future in Canada depended on my immigration status and the ticking clock of my work permit. I applied for permanent residency in December 2023. I would check my application status late at night, calculate points for Canada's comprehensive ranking system, and refresh the draw page for permanent residents over and over again. I thought about moving to a rural area just to increase points, hoping something would change.

items: Canadian citizenship certificate applications now facing nearly 3-year delays

blocks.text: As time passed, that uncertainty started to take a toll, especially six months before my permit was due to expire.

My closest friends — the same people I had grown up with and went to UBC with — began to leave. One by one, they packed up their lives and returned to countries they hadn't planned on going back to. They told me it wasn't worth sacrificing their mental health for a system that felt so unpredictable. Before one can even apply for permanent residency, you have to get an invitation to apply (ITA).
One of my friends even received an ITA for permanent residency — something we had all been working toward. But their application was rejected over a small mistake: uploading the wrong document.
Just like that, years of building a life here came to an end as they had to leave Canada within a 60-day period. Watching that happen made everything feel even more sad.

As my own work permit expiration date got closer, the anxiety became harder to ignore. I would wake up in the middle of the night with panic attacks, overwhelmed by the thought of losing everything I had built. Every phone call with my parents ended in tears — not just from stress, but from a growing sense of hopelessness.

I felt I had done everything "right." I had paid international tuition fees, built a career in the non-profit sector and was contributing to my community. And still, it felt like it might not be enough. I was not enough for Canada.

items: Trump says Canada is 'destroying itself' with immigration. Ministers say that's bogus

blocks.text: Going back to Nepal didn't feel like an option. My dad's job took him to work in many different countries which meant my parents no longer lived in Nepal. I realized how disconnected I had become since I grew up speaking Nepali, but couldn't read or write it.
Canada was the only place that felt like home. Yet I wasn't sure if I would be allowed to stay.
Out of desperation, I started relearning French — not out of passion, but because it felt like one of the only ways to increase my chances of getting an ITA.
Then everything changed.

After two years and eight months, I received my permanent residency approval through the health-care and social services occupations draw, which is a specific, express entry draw for individuals who are currently working in those fields. On March 22, 2026, my PR card finally arrived.
I expected to feel overwhelming joy. Instead, what I first felt was something quieter: Relief.
Relief that I could finally breathe without checking immigration updates. Relief that my life here was no longer temporary.
But the feeling is complicated.
Because while I stayed, many of the people who were part of my journey did not.

items: 2.1 million temporary residents will have expired or expiring permits this year. But will they leave Canada?

blocks.text: The friends who once made Canada feel like home are now scattered across different countries. The support system I built over the years is no longer here in the same way. And now I find myself starting over again, like when I was 18 and new to Canada: building new friendships, considering moving to a new city, trying to reshape what "home" looks like.
When I think back to the 18-year-old version of me who had just arrived in Canada, I realize she believed that if she worked hard enough, everything would fall into place.
In many ways, it did.

But what I didn't expect was how much waiting, uncertainty and quiet fear would come with it. I am grateful to be here. But I also carry the weight of everything it took to stay. And sometimes, that feeling doesn't disappear overnight.

When I voiced my concerns on TikTok, my videos went viral with more than 900,000 views. I realized that my story is not unique. Across Canada, immigrants like myself are navigating the same uncertainty while continuing to contribute to the country's workforce and communities.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Areena Shrestha is a Vancouver-based case manager and content creator passionate about community, culture and storytelling. She is doing a master's of arts in applied social psychology. She uses her experiences as a young immigrant in Vancouver to explore identity, belonging and life in Canada.

articles.title: Behold the pawpaw, the tropical ‘alien banana’ that grows right here in Canada
articles.summary: The pawpaw fruit tastes of banana, mango and pineapple and was once abundant across parts of North America, but it can still be found growing wild and in some orchards.

image.caption: The pawpaw fruit was once abundant across parts of North America, but it can still be found growing wild and in some orchards. (Colin Butler/CBC News)

blocks.text: The Current
The pawpaw fruit tastes of banana, mango and pineapple and was once abundant across parts of North America, but it can still be found growing wild and in some orchards.
Pawpaws taste like a banana, mango and pineapple all rolled into one
LISTEN | Why this chef calls pawpaws 'a treasured little gift':
The Current9:51What does pawpaw taste like and where can you find one?
You might be surprised to learn that the tropical pawpaw fruit grows right here in Canada. And if you can get your hands on one, chef Tawnya Brant says you’re in for a treat.

“What do you think tropical tastes like? If that was a flavour, if that was the smell on its own, that's probably exactly what a pawpaw would be,” said Brant, owner of Yawékon Foods and host of the APTN’s One Dish One Spoon.

Brant, a Mohawk chef from Six Nations of the Grand River, says the fruit tastes like a banana, mango and pineapple all rolled into one, with a custardy texture that gets almost caramel-like as it ripens.
“It's like a little alien banana … a little shorter and chubbier, I guess, more like an oval type of shape — and they have these huge seeds inside,” she told The Current’s Matt Galloway.

Pawpaws have grown in North America for millennia, and were once abundant from Florida to Missouri to southern Ontario. They were widely cultivated by Indigenous people before colonization, but were pushed back as forests were cleared for farmland. Some trees still grow in the wild and in some orchards in pockets of southern Ontario, B.C. and Quebec, yielding fruit in the fall.

Part of the reason pawpaws aren’t widely known is that they have a very short shelf life, browning quickly after they’re picked. They also bruise very easily, making it difficult to harvest and sell in large numbers commercially.
The Ontario fruit that sounds 'too mythical, too bizarre to be true'

Brant first tried the fruit about a decade ago when a friend brought some to her late mother’s garden. Before that, she’d heard of the fruit, and that the Haudenosaunee had helped to bring the trees up the eastern seaboard over the centuries, “just because we liked them so much.”
“I was told kids would go on like little rafts and go down creeks and … collect them that way,” she said.
“It was definitely a once-in-a-year [treat], something to enjoy, and really something to appreciate because we didn't really have a way of preserving them.”
The trick to growing pawpaws? Llama manure

Thomas Mathias started cultivating pawpaws on his farm about 15 years ago. He says he planted the first trees “just as a lark” to see what would happen, but it took a lot of “tinkering and research” to yield a crop.
“[It took] 11 years of experimenting before we got fruit,” said Mathias, who runs Mathias Farm in Ontario's Niagara region.
“One of the tricks to getting fruit to pollinate was to either put raw meat underneath the tree, or spread raw manure. I went with raw manure,” he said.
That manure is an untreated mix of horse and llama, sourced from a friend’s farm, which attracts blue bottle flies to pollinate the flowers.
Mathias runs the farm with his sister, Beth Secord. She described the trees as handsome and tropical looking, with huge leaves and flowers that look like “an upside-down burgundy tulip.”
She remembers the first time she tried the fruit: “I thought, ‘Wow, this is fantastic. Sweet, juicy, fresh, healthy. What's not to like?’”
Secord says the 11 trees yield about 250 to 300 pounds of fruit a year (roughly 115 kilograms to 135 kilograms). They sell the fruit at $20 per pound, though smaller quantities are available.

Now that they’re a few years into selling the fruit, they’ve noticed an uptick in interest. Secord says some people take a small sample and then come back for more. Word of mouth has also played a role.
“That one person is happy and they're telling 20 friends — and then the phone's ringing,” she said.
“One guy said I've been looking for pawpaws for five years and I finally found you. So he'll be back for sure.”
Secord says she’s thrilled more people are getting to try the fruit. She hopes one day it could make a comeback to the point of people having a pawpaw tree in their own backyard.
Ever heard of pawpaws? This Quebec town has a festival devoted to the special fruit
‘A a treasured little gift’
Brant says the best bet to finding pawpaws is probably a farmers’ market, though there are also pawpaw festivals in some parts of Canada, usually in early October.

If you can get your hands on some, she says they can be used in salad dressings, sauces and coulis, even a pawpaw cheesecake. But she warned that the fruit has quite a rich flavour and should be used in smaller quantities.
They’re also great just eaten fresh, but people should remember not to eat the skin or seeds, which are toxic.

items: The Ontario fruit that sounds 'too mythical, too bizarre to be true'

blocks.text: Brant currently has about 16 pawpaw trees growing, but they’re still too small to bear fruit. She hopes that when they’re bigger, it’ll allow her to introduce more people to this “alien fruit.”
“It's a treasured little gift that we only get once a year. If I can share that with groups, it's amazing.”
Audio produced by Ines Colabrese. With files from CBC London.

articles.title: DSWD provides financial aid to Mary Jane Veloso
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) Field Office 3 provided financial aid to former Overseas Filipino Worker Mary Jane Veloso and her family in their home in General Mamerto…

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 3:54pm

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) Field Office 3 provided financial aid to former Overseas Filipino Worker Mary Jane Veloso and her family in their home in General Mamerto Natividad, Nueva Ecija after she was granted absolute pardon.

On Saturday, Veloso returned to her hometown and was warmly welcomed by her friends and family in Barangay Burol, which she had not seen for 16 years. The municipality also gave her a cake and a tarpaulin to mark her personal milestone.
Mary Jane spent dinner with her loved ones at the home that was the fruit of her years of working as an OFW. To celebrate her freedom, she had her favorite dish: pinakbet and grilled tilapia.
Bataan 2nd District Representative Albert Raymond "Abet" Garcia said Tuesday night that the Office of the President (OP) was "seriously considering" the granting of absolute pardon to Veloso.
He reported matters during deliberations on the proposed OP budget, which he is sponsoring in the House of Representatives.
Garcia said the pardon was being considered "on humanitarian grounds in support of the government's commitment to protecting Filipino migrant workers."
Veloso maintained that she was innocent and that she was unknowingly used as a drug mule.

The District Court of Justice of Sieman in Yogjakarta, Indonesia sentenced her to death on October 11, 2010, but it was commuted in 2015 following an appeal from the late President Benigno Simeon "Noynoy" Aquino III.

In December 2024, Indonesian authorities agreed to transfer Veloso to Philippine custody. She was detained at the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City, initially serving reclusion perpetua, which carries a prison term of 20 years and one day to 40 years. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News
