articles.title: China sends two giant pandas off to Atlanta zoo after Xi-Trump summit
articles.summary: Ping Ping and Fu Shuang took off to Atlanta on a FedEx plane, with steamed corn buns, carrots and bamboo to snack on during the flight. Their trip is one of the few concrete things to come out the…

image.caption: The pandas will make a 15-hour flight journey to reach AtlantaImage: Xu Bingjie/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Two giant pandas departed China's southwestern city of Chengdu for new home in Atlanta, as part of an agreement between Washington and Beijing.
Chinese President Xi Jinping announced that the pandas would be relocated to the capital of the US state of Georgia during his three-day summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington.
Xi said the panda loan program was an example of "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."

The loan was one of the few concrete things to come out of the summit.China has long used pandas as a key part of its global diplomatic outreach, turning such agreements into a well tested tool of soft power. On the flip side, Beijing has also let agreements lapse and pulled pandas back from countries when tensions arise.
Trump-Xi summit: Results or just symbolism?
Meet the pandas

Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, two adult pandas, will be on loan to Zoo Atlanta for 10 years, as part of the agreement. Both pandas were born in 2020 and have lived at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
A farewell ceremony was held before their departure.

blocks.caption: Fans of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang gathered in Chengdu to wish them a good tripImage: Xu Bingjie/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ping Ping, who is male, Fu Shuang, female, departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport on a chartered flight around 3:00 a.m. on Sunday (1900 GMT on Saturday).

The FedEx-operated Boeing 777 was equipped with steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots to keep the animals nourished during their journey, Chinese media reported. They are also being accompanied by experienced US zoo keepers who had traveled to China ahead of time.

In preparation of their arrival, Zoo Atlanta renovated its panda facilities and ensured a long and stable supply of locally grown bamboo. The zoo has decades of experience with pandas, hosting the animals between 1999 and 2024.

articles.title: Subpoena for Sonny Trillanes has yet to be issued -- court spox
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has yet to issue a subpoena to former senator Antonio Trillanes IV to testify in connection with Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 27, 2026 3:31pm

The Senate impeachment court has yet to issue a subpoena to former senator Antonio Trillanes IV to testify in connection with Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte, Senate Impeachment Court spokesperson Reginald Tongol said Sunday.
Tongol made the statement as the Senate impeachment court tackles Article 2, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth, with three other personalities yet to be subpoenaed.
They are Kathy Florence Baldonado and Marco Pineda of the Davao City Register of Deeds, and Ronnel Buenaventura, executive director of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Secretariat.
The House prosecution team has asked the impeachment court to issue a subpoena for Trillanes to appear next week.

Trillanes’ testimony would cover matters concerning Duterte’s alleged “unexplained wealth and alleged receipt or acquisition of funds from persons or sources identified in the evidence presented before the impeachment court.”
Trillanes in April alleged that Duterte and members of her immediate family received P181 million from an alleged drug lord.
He made the statement during the House Justice Committee’s impeachment hearing before the panel voted to find probable cause to impeach the Vice President.
Tongol said the defense team may file a motion opposing the issuance of subpoenas for witnesses who would testify regarding Duterte’s AMLC records.
“We do not expect that from the defense, but if they have grounds for it, it’s up to them. It is their prerogative to file any motion regarding any of the witnesses being subpoenaed," Tongol said.
"They can either oppose the issuance of the subpoena or seek to quash the subpoena," he added.

Tongol said the testimony of Rendell Sopeña, division chief of the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS), is expected to conclude on Monday, Sept. 28, to be followed by cross-examination.

“Tomorrow (Monday), we expect that after the testimony of Rendell Sopeña, the PhilGEPS division chief, the cross-examination, redirect examination and re-cross-examination will begin, followed by interjections from the senator-judges,” Tongol said.
Tongol said the prosecution panel may decide to move Mayor Duterte’s testimony to another day if Monday’s schedule does not allow enough time.
"Of course, we don’t want to disrupt the flow of the witness’s testimony, so it may be moved to another day,” he said.
Tongol added that a witness from the Philippine National Police Firearms and Explosives Unit will testify on Monday regarding the Vice President’s ownership of firearms.

Sopeña is testifying as a prosecution witness on Duterte’s alleged corporate ownership and shareholdings in connection with Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment, which accuses her of accumulating unexplained wealth.
As division chief, Sopeña said he is the overall custodian of the PhilGEPS system database, validates requested data and issues certifications based on such requests.
The impeachment trial will run from 10 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. on Sept. 28-30 and for the whole day on Oct. 1-2, 5-9 and 12-15.— MCG, GMA News

articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Sunday questioned the Department of Public Works and Highways over a supposed project in Taguig City whose coordinates were located in the Visayas based on geotagged photos.

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 3:02pm

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Sunday questioned the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) over a supposed project in Taguig City whose coordinates were located in the Visayas based on geotagged photos.

“Sec. Vince Dizon, please explain how this finding of your own team should not be flagged as a ghost project in Taguig. (Since when has Taguig been located in Leyte?)” he said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).
The senator cited that the geotagged photos of the projects attached to the billing reports “reflected coordinates located approximately 600 kilometers away in Leyte Province.”
Lacson also claimed that the said project’s contractor is linked to the Discaya couple, who are big figures in the flood control scandal.
“To further highlight the red flag, Discaya’s St Timothy ang contractor. What do you say about this, Sec?” he said in a separate X post.
The senator’s social media post came after DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said that his office has yet to find a ghost or non-existent infrastructure project in Taguig City.
Meanwhile, DPWH Undersecretary Ricardo Bernabe III also claimed that their agency has so far listed 107 projects in Taguig, all of which have accomplishments.
In another X post, Lacson said that Dizon was suffering from a “clouded” memory following the DPWH chief’s claims about Taguig infrastructures.

"Poor DPWH Site Inspection Engineers. Their boss, Sec. Vince Dizon directly contradicted their own site inspection reports in Taguig, specifically submitted by personnel from the department's Bureau of Quality and Safety and Bureau of Maintenance," Lacson said in a post.
GMA News Online has reached out to Dizon for comment but he has yet to issue a statement as of posting time. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Asian Games organizer says sorry for logistical headaches
articles.summary: The unexpected surge of late entries has strained accommodation and transport networks in the Asian Games, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms, small beds, and…

blocks.text: STAY. A man walks near Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which will serve as a floating temporary athletes' village for 4,000 to 5,000 participants during the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games, after it docked at the port of Nagoya, Japan, September 15, 2026.
Edgar SuREUTERS

The unexpected surge of late entries has strained accommodation and transport networks in the Asian Games, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms, small beds, and travel delays

NAGOYA, Japan – The chief organizer of the Asian Games apologized on Saturday, September 26, for the logistical headaches plaguing the event, saying a late influx of athletes and officials had made it difficult to extend smooth service.

The number of participants at the continental showpiece ballooned to 17,000 following a flurry of late entries — around 2,000 more than the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games Organising Committee had initially projected.
The unexpected surge strained accommodation and transport networks, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms, small beds, and travel delays.
“There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport, for various reasons,” AINAGOC Secretary General Satoshi Murate told a press conference.
“Whatever the cause, AINAGOC is responsible for providing the service, and I frankly apologzse for the mistakes.

“Our staff work every day to identify the causes of each mistake and make sure they don’t happen again. I think you can see that accommodation and transport have improved greatly compared with the early days.”
Murate added that maintaining consistent service standards had proved challenging following the “significant” increase in delegation sizes.
“Our top priority is making sure the athletes can compete at their best. We are fully committed to making the necessary improvements to ensure that they can do so,” he said.

“We are already working on a number of improvements, and in the second half of the Games, we want to make sure those efforts produce results and that we can manage things more smoothly and effectively.”
Mongolian women’s basketball coach Javier Garcia Alvarez criticized the transport system after a training session had to be scrapped when the team bus failed to arrive.
“I played in many FIBA Asia basketball cups and even Asian Games in Incheon some years ago. I never had this kind of issue that the bus is not coming for practice,” he told Reuters.
“It was kind of disappointing because we were planning some practice, some shooting for the girls and the mind was prepared for that, and then at the end we had to cancel.”
Filipino squash player Yvonne Alyssa Dalida had to endure a lengthy wait before checking into her room aboard a chartered cruise ship, though she found a silver lining in the unconventional setup.
“I think Japan or AINAGOC could have prepared better for this event, but I find it cool as well because it’s very unique.”
“I’ve never been on a cruise, so I think that’s also the upside of them using this.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Tech Thoughts] How bad actors weaponize copyright to silence journalism online
articles.summary: Bad actors use legitimate takedown mechanisms to remove journalistic content they don't want online

blocks.text: Bad actors use legitimate takedown mechanisms to remove journalistic content they don't want online

items: The author learns about how bad actors exploit copyright and social media moderation to silence investigative journalism.
These bad actors use tactics such as cloning content, backdating it, and making false reports to social media companies to remove legitimate journalistic work.
To combat this issue, journalists can seek help from organizations like Access Now and advocate for accountability from social media platforms regarding their takedown processes.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

As a journalist whose primary world is being online, I didn’t really think much about how social media impacted the reach of stories. My concerns were mostly about writing stories, leaving much of the amplification of my work to others in Rappler.

It wasn’t until I attended an online webinar this week that I learned more about how bad actors use copyright and weaponize social media moderation and website takedown mechanisms to silence journalists and weaken — or negate — the reach of investigative journalism.
The webinar, hosted by the Global Investigative Journalist Network (GIJN), had experts speaking out about instances journalists from around the world had experienced being silenced.
This isn’t a physical access issue, like what would happen if a president barred a reporter or a group of reporters within a press pool from being able to be in the same room with the president.

Instead, the webinar shared experiences and case studies showing how rampant and far-reaching the effects of bad actors are when they undertake the process of copyright-striking legitimate pages to get them taken down or to otherwise negate the ability of an investigative journalism piece to be shared or read.

There are a number of ways in which this takes shape, but in broad strokes, it’s basically stealing and backdating content or faking evidence to make it appear as if the bad actors are the originators of the content seeking to be taken down.

There is apparently a thriving industry of “reputation management groups,” whether legitimate businesses or just smaller unofficial outfits willing to do dirty work for money, that advertise specific services. like content removal, webpage removal, mass reporting, astroturfing, or similar tasks.

To silence journalists, these bad actors make false reports to social media companies and fake evidence against legitimate groups or posts to get the social media companies’ automated systems to do the work of taking down a page for them.
For instance, Bangladeshi-based networks were operating to take down content in Central Asia and Africa.

To get takedowns done on social media, they would clone videos or steal the text of reports — say from an African investigative report. The bad actors would then, in the case of videos, add Bengali voiceovers on top of videos to make it seem from their region.

For videos or text pieces, they would then falsify further by backdating the content on social media or on a legitimate-seeming website so that they could say the content came from them and request the takedown of posts from the automated systems handling moderation on social media platforms like Facebook or X.

In some other instances, bad actors abuse the memorialization feature of Facebook — the feature that creates a static memorial page for dead Facebook users — to disable the posting capabiltiies of specific journalists.

The memorialization trick is more involved, as it requires falsifying death certificates and submitting the fake death certificate and possibly other documents to Facebook so the page can be memorialized.
In other parts of the world, where investigative journalists or teams work together and have a website for their investigations, copyright abuse is the trick used to get legitimate sites taken down.
Similar to social media takedowns, copyright abuse see bad actors cloning content and making a false website that backdates the content.

They then make bogus copyright requests so legitimate sites can be taken down and their search results scrubbed from search engines through the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act, even if the sites aren’t based in the United States.
While journalists are fighting the good fight of doing research and investigating anomalies, there are ways in which things could change to make this industry die out.

For victims of such actions, they can reach out to Access Now, a global nonprofit organization that helps get people back online by defending digital rights, or seek help from their local digital rights helpline, if a country has one.

Journalists may also want to investigate these malign actors, while digital advocacy groups can hold platforms — especially social media platforms frightened by intellectual property claims — accountable for offloading takedown requests to machines rather than humans. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Chinese Embassy slams US for backing PH in Ayungin
articles.summary: The Chinese Embassy on Sunday hit back at the US Embassy after the latter sided with the Philippines over Beijing's reported interference in Manila's recent rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to…

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 2:56pm

The Chinese Embassy on Sunday hit back at the US Embassy after the latter sided with the Philippines over Beijing's reported interference in Manila's recent rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin Shoal.

“We strongly condemn the US Embassy in the Philippines’ disregard for right and wrong and its insistence on supporting the Philippines’ provocative and unlawful actions at Ren’ai Reef in China’s Nansha Qundao,” the Chinese Embassy said in a statement.

China issued the statement hours after US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton described the maneuvers by the China Coast Guard (CCG) and the People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) as “dangerous” and “irresponsible.”
The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) earlier said three PLAN warships and five CCG vessels, including two Houbei-class missile boats, interfered with the mission.
The AFP said the Philippine RoRe mission was temporarily suspended due to the possibility of escalation that could endanger personnel and vessels.
However, the Chinese Embassy maintained that the Philippines had “breached its commitments” while disregarding China's warnings.

“The Philippines’ provocative actions and its subsequent hype and publicity during a traditional Chinese festival seriously violated the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) and severely undermined peace and stability in the South China Sea region,” it said.
The US Embassy, for its part, called on China to stop its provocations.

“We stand by our Philippine Allies and laud their professionalism and restraint. We call on the China Coast Guard and PLAN to cease the use of escalatory tactics that threaten the freedom of navigation and a free and open Indo-Pacific,” said Lipton.
China, however, told the US “to stop fanning the flames and refrain from actions that undermine regional peace and stability.”
In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal in The Hague ruled on a case brought by the Philippines challenging China's maritime claims in the South China Sea.

Among its findings, the tribunal said there was no legal basis for China to claim historic rights to resources within the sea areas falling within its nine-dash line. China has rejected the ruling and does not recognize it.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Gunmen kill 27 people in two mass shootings in South Africa
articles.summary: South African police have launched a search for suspects after 17 people were found dead at a tavern southwest of Johannesburg. A separate tavern shooting near Cape Town left 10 dead.

blocks.text: At least 27 people have been killed in separate mass shooting incidents in South Africa's Gauteng and Western Cape provinces overnight.
In the first incident, gunmen armed with assault rifles killed 17 people and wounded 15 others at a bar in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg, police said on Sunday.
Manhunt underway for 8 suspects
Gauteng police said they have launched a manhunt for eight unidentified armed men following deadly shooting.
"They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles," the South African ​Police Service (SAPS) ‌said.
Emergency ‌services ‌declared all ​17 victims, 13 men and four women, dead at the scene. Authorities said the shooting occurred Saturday at around 9:30 p.m. local time (1930 UTC).
A motive for the shooting ⁠was ​not ​known, the SAPS said, adding that "suspects ​were reportedly ⁠armed with AK-47 rifles ⁠and ​pistols."
10 killed in Lwandle tavern shooting, Cape Town
In a separate shooting in the Western Cape, police said gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more at an entertainment venue in Lwandle township at 1:46 a.m. (2346 Saturday GMT).
Authorities said five of the victims died at the scene while another five succumbed to their injuries after being taken to hospital.
Police said that no arrests have been made and that a "multi-disciplinary team" led by serious and violent crime detectives had been established to track down those responsible.
More police resources have been sent to the area as the search for the perpetrators continues.
The latest incidents came just days after at least 11 people were gunned down at a home in KwaZulu-Natal Province.
That shooting occurred in KwaMakhutha, a township some 30 kilometers (19 miles) south of Durban, the eastern province's largest city.
South Africa has been grappling with violent crime and has one of the world's highest murder rates, with around 60 people dying violently in the country each day.
This article will be updated as more details become available.

articles.title: Why farmers are pairing crops with solar panels
articles.summary: From cooler soil to paid grazing land, farmers in the US are finding that solar panels can do more than generate power.

image.caption: An agrivoltaic pilot project shades a pear orchard in Llupia, France, part of a push to protect crops from droughts, frost and other extreme weatherImage: Michel Clementz/MAXPPP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Traditionally, solar panel farms are quiet — save for the faint hum of the inverter. But on about one in 10 of American solar farms, there's a new sound reverberating through fields: baaaa.
Letting sheep roam under solar panels is just one of many forms of a burgeoning strategy called agrivoltaics, where crops grow or livestock graze in tandem with renewable energy infrastructure.

It's not only of potential benefit for the animals, which get additional shade. The panels can also protect crops from the elements as well as divert water to them, creating cooler, damper conditions that even boost yields.
And even the solar panels themselves tend to respond well to this co-existence — as the cooler they are, the more electricity they produce per watt of sunlight.

"Having concrete or something underneath the solar panels — you're going to have lower efficiency than having something like plants that are transpiring and cooling off on the land surface," Carl Bernacchi, professor of plant biology and crop sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, told DW.

While the potential is enormous, especially as climate change puts more and more heat stress on agriculture, the practice is still in its infancy. In Europe, if agrivoltaics were implemented on just 1% of available agricultural land, the continent could exceed its solar energy targets for 2030.
But uptake has been slow: agrivoltaics represents just 18.4 gigawatts of energy worldwide as of mid-2025, less than 1% of the world's solar capacity.

blocks.caption: Sheep graze under solar panels in Guizhou province, southwest China, part of a growing practice of pairing livestock with solar energy productionImage: Tao Liang/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: What thrives under the panels

The idea for agrivoltaics dates back to 1981, when two German scientists published an article titled "Kartoffeln unter dem Kollektor" (or "Potatoes beneath the collector"). But the first pilot project didn't begin until 2004 in Japan, a land-constrained country, where there's particular concern over balancing solar deployment with the protection of farmland.

There are three main types of agrivoltaics: horizontal, where panels look directly up at the sky, vertical, where they're placed in large rows, perpendicular to the ground, and integrated, often installed atop greenhouses.
Research suggests shade-tolerant crops stand to benefit. That includes berries, grapes and tomatoes — where the panels' steel framing often doubles as trellises — as well as peaches and peppers.
The panels can also prevent water from fully evaporating, creating a more humid microclimate that benefits the soil — though humidity is a double-edged sword, sometimes introducing plant disease.

Sheep have also proven to be a particularly good match. Compared to cattle or goats, they're generally easier to manage around solar infrastructure, less likely to damage equipment, and small enough to fit comfortably beneath panels. The practice has other sustainability upsides too: sheep manure fertilizes the soil, and sites require less herbicide.

"If we look at the sheep industry, this has been a real paradigm shift for them, where instead of having to pay to lease land to graze their animals — now they're actually getting paid to graze," said Austin Kinzer, an agrivoltaics specialist at the American Farmland Trust conservation movement . "So it completely puts the economics on its head and is a huge opportunity for the sheep industry, which is really struggling in the US pretty much since World War II."

blocks.caption: Solar panels raised on steel supports shade a French orchard, one of several agrivoltaic setups now in use across EuropeImage: Michel Clementz/MAXPPP/picture alliance

blocks.text: A double climate win
Agrivoltaics sit at a rare intersection of climate mitigation (cutting emissions) and adaptation (adjusting to a warming planet).
"It is both, which is pretty unique as far as climate solutions go," Kinzer said.

The practice offers one answer to where solar panels could go, helping to produce cheaper and more efficient energy, while also benefiting crops that might struggle due to rising temperatures or volatile weather.

And research suggests that climate change will only make regions grow drier, "broadening areas where agrivoltaics can mitigate crop yield penalties (even boosting yield) and improve overall profitability," writeresearchers in a journal article for Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
A dual-income stream can also offer farmers some insurance should temperature or weather knock out a season's plantings.
"Being able to have that alternate form of income, it's massive for folks who are depending on weather to make their living that is becoming increasingly more extreme and varied," Kinzer said.
Tamil Nadu farmers learn to thrive despite water scarcity
Not every farm benefits
So why has adoption been so slow?
"In theory, it's a win-win scenario," Bernacchi said. "But of course, with any technologies, there are always caveats and issues."

One reason is that agrivoltaics don't work everywhere. In America's arid West, where heat stress and less available water can threaten crops, yields stayed the same or even rose under panels. In the humid Midwest, on the other hand, panel shading limited photosynthesis and led to reduced yields in maize and soybeans.
For cash crops, where there's a very small margin for profit, even a minor reduction in yield is a no-go for many farmers.

Then there's the expense. For solar producers, every added inch to mount panels higher means more labor and steel costs. And farmers might need to find new equipment or change methods to adapt to a new system.

"Farmers want to learn from other farmers," said Kinzer, who works with farmers across the US to see how agrivoltaics are being adopted. "They want to hear from folks who are doing it. And so there's a little bit of a chicken-and-the-egg problem for farmers: In most cases, they can't just go across the street or into the next county over and see a project like this and talk to the farmers doing it."
Bridging the divide between farmers and solar

Solar power's land footprint has made it controversial in certain communities — some farming associations have protested converting farmland into acres of solar panels, arguing their members cease to be farmers and become energy producers instead.
It's a tension agrivoltaics helps to address.

One survey found that more than 80% of Americans would be more likely to support solar development in their community, if it allowed for the co-production of energy and agriculture — about 10% more than those that support solar development in general.

"There's this cultural conflict between the farmers who want to farm and the solar companies that want to produce electricity," Bernacchi said. "And agrivoltaics really does bill itself as sort of a middle ground. You can still farm and still get the electricity from the same land."
Agrivoltaic combines solar power and agriculture

articles.title: US Embassy condemns Chinese interference of PH RoRe mission to Ayungin Shoal
articles.summary: The United States rallied behind the Philippines and condemned China for interfering with the Philippine rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin Shoal earlier this week.

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 11:44am
The United States rallied behind the Philippines and condemned China for interfering with the Philippine rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin Shoal earlier this week.
In a statement on Sunday, US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton described the maneuvers by the China Coast Guard and the People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) as “dangerous” and “irresponsible.”

“The United States strongly condemns the use of dangerous blocking and other irresponsible maneuvers by the China Coast Guard and the People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) that threatened a collision with a Philippine vessel and prevented a lawful and routine resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal on September 24,” Lipton said.

“We stand by our Philippine Allies and laud their professionalism and restraint. We call on the China Coast Guard and PLAN to cease the use of escalatory tactics that threaten the freedom of navigation and a free and open Indo-Pacific,” he added.

On Thursday, the National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea (NTF-WPS) reported that the task force said China Coast Guard (CCG) and People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) hindered the delivery of essential supplies to the Filipino crew aboard BRP Sierra Madre.
Meanwhile, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said three PLAN warships and five CCG vessels, including two (2) Houbei-class missile boats, interfered with the mission.

“While still approximately 60 nautical miles from Ayungin Shoal, M/V Lapu-Lapu and three (3) Philippine Navy and Philippine Coast Guard support vessels were hindered by the PLAN and CCG vessels,” the AFP said.
According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the planned rotation and resupply (RoRe) mission to Ayungin Shoal was discontinued at 11:08 p.m. for the safety of its personnel.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
Beijing has refused to recognize the decision. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Powerful storm batters northeast US, hundreds of flights canceled
articles.summary: Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed as a nor'easter brought flooding, power cuts and travel disruption to cities like New York, Boston and Philadelphia.

image.caption: Authorities warned of flooding in coastal areas as high tide coincides with the stormImage: Vincent Alban/REUTERS

blocks.text: Heavy rain and strong winds pounded the northeastern United States on Saturday, forcing authorities to cancel hundreds of flights and leaving thousands without electricity.
New York, Boston and Philadelphia were in the firing line of the 'Nor'easter,' named after the northeasterly winds.
What is a nor'easter storm?
Nor'easters are large cyclones in the western North Atlantic Ocean, which typically form off the east coast of the US.
They can occur throughout the year but are more frequent between fall and early spring.
Nor'easters are almost always accompanied by heavy rainfall or snow, as well as strong winds.
What have authorities said about the nor'easter?
Residents in low-lying and coastal areas were warned of potential flooding and road closures, as the storm coincides with high tide.
"This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend," the National Weather Service said in its latest forecast.
"Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses," it said.

Some 95,000 people in the states of New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Pennsylvania were facing a power outage as of 3 p.m. on Saturday (1900 GMT), as per poweroutage.com.
Local leaders urge caution
New York Governor Kathy Kochul said the storm was particularly impacting the coastal areas of New York City and Long Island.
"Conditions are extremely dangerous. Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life," she said in a press briefing.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani warned residents of the strong winds, saying "Don't travel if you don't have to."
Flights, events canceled
Hundreds of flights were cancelled due to the storm, with 253 at Boston's Logan airport alone, according to tracker FlightAware.

blocks.caption: The unusually powerful autumn storm intensified, forcing the cancelation of hundreds of flightsImage: Matthew Hatcher/AFP

blocks.text: Airlines including JetBlue, United and American have issued travel alerts, allowing passengers to change their flights without a fee.
As of 6:13 p.m. local time (2213 GMT), FlightAware said 439 flights involving US airports had been canceled and 2,459 flights were delayed.
Major cultural events have also been called off.
The Global Citizen and All Things Go Festivals in New York, and the Oceans Calling Festival in Maryland were canceled.

"Safety has to come first. This is the first time in 14 years we've had to cancel," said organizers of the Global Citizen event in Central Park, which was meant to feature Lenny Kravitz, Lauryn Hill, Alicia Keys and country stars Lainey Wilson and Shaboozey.
British Pop star Ed Sheeran's Weekend concerts near Boston were also canceled due to the storm.
About five inches (13 centimeters) of rain was forecast in areas of Massachusetts, including Boston. That's equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain.

blocks.caption: 'Nor'easter' are named so for its northeasterly windsImage: Joseph Prezioso/AFP

articles.title: Iran says it will wait for official US response after Trump rejects Strait of Hormuz proposal
articles.summary: The US president earlier said that Tehran only made the proposal to open the strait within seven days because "they're losing so badly".

blocks.text: Iran has said it will wait for an official response from US negotiators after President Donald Trump rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within seven days.
In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but accused the president of previously making contradictory statements.
Earlier, Trump told reporters at the White House that Tehran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that they wanted to make a deal to open the strait immediately because "they're losing so badly".
On Friday at the UN, Araghchi told reporters that an agreement could be reached if "necessary conditions are met" between the two countries.
Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran that was signed in June.
Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.
The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it.
Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi said.
Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.

Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.
Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by the US ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker.
Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage".
"President Trump's right to reject it," he said.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic pressure from the US was taking a toll on Tehran.
Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.
The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran as "Operation Economic Outcast", and is using sanctions to pressure Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.
These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

articles.title: Spain: Thousands protest in Madrid against housing crisis
articles.summary: Tens of thousands rallied in the Spanish capital after an 87-year-old woman was dramatically evicted from her home this week. Protesters called for measures to curb rising costs and reduce evictions.

image.caption: The rally was a response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman Image: Susana Vera/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of people protested in central Madrid on Saturday to denounce Spain's housing crisis.
The demonstrators called for better protection for tenants, anti-fraud rules and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.
The march through the center of the Spanish capital was called after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted from her apartment where she had lived for seven decades.

blocks.caption: Protesters carried signs reading 'we are all Maricarmen'Image: C. Carvajal/JNA/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent ahead of a general election next year.

Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth has put pressure on the already limited housing supply in the cities. The Bank of Spain estimated a shortage of 550,000 homes across the country last year.
Toxic tourism — Mallorca's housing crisis
Protesters camp out in Puerta del Sol

Government authorities estimated that around 25,000 people had shown up to protest against Spain's growing housing crisis. The Madrid Tenants' Union, which organized the protest, said over 300,000 had taken part.

Once the rally wrapped up, some activists set up a protest camp in the city center's Puerta del Sol square with plans to stay put. Some even pitched up tents to stay the night, or until the police forcibly removed them.
Police officers looked on at about a dozen tents, surrounded by thousands of protesters, news agency AFP reported from the scene.

blocks.caption: Spain previously built homes with public funds that were later sold into private ownershipImage: Tomas Calle/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Rallying around Abascal
The protest was triggered by Maricarmen Abascal's dramatic eviction on Wednesday from the house she had lived in for decades.
Abascal was greeted by supporters as she was removed from her home on a stretcher and loaded onto an ambulance.

"We're here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes," said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse. "And we can't keep maintaining this. Housing is a right, and we don't have it," she said.

According to Spanish media, Abascal's father first rented the home in the upscale Retiro neighborhood in 1956. After her parents died, she continued to live in the flat, which had a rent cap at the time.
Spain: Tourism boom worsens housing crisis
In 2018, the building changed ownership, and Urbagestion, an investment fund, bought the unit, raising the rent from €500 ($570) to €2,650 ($3,018).
Abascal had been offered an opportunity to buy the apartment before this but could not afford it.

The fund later lowered her rent to €1,650, but Abascal could not afford that either. Courts had blocked her eviction three times previously and extensive media coverage turned her into a symbol of the crisis.

"This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we've been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now," said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher.
"It's unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can't afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted," she added.

articles.title: ‘Cash grab’: One Nation demands up to $630,000 from Victorian election candidates
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Many applicants left feeling ‘used, lied to, misled and gaslit’, complaint letter seen by Guardian Australia says

  • Listen to the Guardian podcast

blocks.text: One Nation could collect as much as $633,000 from people who have put their hand up to run in the Victorian state election, with potential candidates questioning whether the party is staging a “cash grab”.

Guardian Australia has spoken to multiple former councillors, mayors and deputy mayors who expressed an interest in running for the party. They claim they went through what one called a “pay-to-play” application process, after which they were rejected.
Those who applied to be considered were required to pay $150 as a “non refundable application fee”, invoices seen by the Guardian show.

One Nation told the Guardian that 1,209 people put in an expression of interest to run in the November state election, and approximately 220 proceeded to the final stage, resulting in an estimated $33,000 flowing into party coffers if all final stage candidates paid this amount.
Applicants were also expected to be party members, with this translating to an additional $72,000 based on the minimum membership fee of $60 a year.

In addition, candidates were advised in interviews that they would be required to pay $5,500 of their own money to run if preselected, even though the vast majority of lower house electorates are not deemed winnable.
While it is not uncommon for the major parties to require candidates to pay an application fee, they do not levy campaign fees on candidates like those being charged by One Nation.

The candidate fee will bring $528,000 into the party’s coffers, based on running 88 lower house candidates and eight for the upper house. In total, the amount paid by candidates could be as much as $633,000.
Aidan McLindon, a political consultant who worked with One Nation in Victoria last year, said many potential candidates had been left frustrated by what appeared to be a “money-spinning exercise”.
One Nation was “disproportionately focusing on profits over policy”. McLindon said in an interview for episode three of The Populist, out on Monday.
Based on the party’s polling numbers, One Nation is also in line to receive as much as $10m through Victoria’s public electoral funding scheme.

Applicants who spoke to the Guardian have questioned whether the application process was genuine, saying the party had conducted 15-minute video interviews with each candidate before a decision was made. Potential candidates were all required to sign non-disclosure agreements about the process on application.

There is also concern that the upper house candidates were “captain’s picks” selected by the party’s state leader, Warren Pickering, with One Nation overlooking candidates with significant local government and professional experience.
A complaint letter sent to the party by one former Victorian mayor says the process has left many candidates feeling “that we were used, lied to, misled and gaslit”.

“The issue is that the process increasingly looks as though it was used as cover to conceal decisions that had already been substantially made, while creating the public appearance of an open, merit-based candidate search,” the letter seen by the Guardian states.

“Applicants should not have been encouraged to invest their time, energy, reputations and personal information in an elaborate exercise merely to provide legitimacy, numbers or political cover for what now appears to have been a biased and self-serving leadership process.”
after newsletter promotion
Another local government member who had applied questioned whether the process was a “cash grab”.
“They are asking everyday folk, hard-working mums and dads, for $5,500 which is a lot of money,” one said.
“I just think it is a cash grab for the federal election. My feeling is they are just using all of the states to fundraise for the federal election where they want to take power.”
Another said they believed that under the party’s constitution, all funds would be transferred to One Nation’s Brisbane headquarters.
“They will get $800,000 in the kitty for doing absolutely nothing,” one said.
A spokesperson for One Nation said the party uses “a nominal cost recovery model to do police and other checks on candidate nominees”.
“All candidate fees have been paid into the Victorian state campaign account in accordance with the Victorian Electoral Commission rules.
“Application fees and campaign contributions are a standard requirement implemented by all major parties within Australia.”
The Guardian has previously reported that candidates at the 2025 federal election were left out of pocket by the party’s candidate funding agreements.

articles.title: Christa Pike to be first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years - but her defence say she's a victim too
articles.summary: Lawyers for Pike, who killed a fellow student in 1995, say she should get clemency and would not be sentenced to death if the crime happened today.

blocks.text: Christa Pike to be first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years - but her defence say she's a victim too

blocks.caption: Image caption, Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date

blocks.text: Image source, Tennesse Department of Corrections
Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date
ByStephanie Hegarty
BBC World Service Correspondent

Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.
Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.
"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.
Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.
Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder
But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external

Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.
In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider.

"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence.
"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parents

blocks.text: Image source, Christa Pike
Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parents

In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.

But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.
In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.

Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her.
"Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.

Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."

Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say

blocks.text: Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say
'She should pay for it'
Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.

A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict.
The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.
Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.

Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.
The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.

On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.
Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution.
"She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.
Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."

blocks.caption: Image caption, May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006

blocks.text: Image source, J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via Reuters
May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006
"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added.
"There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."
The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.
The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want.
"We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."

Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption.

"When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says.
"These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."

Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime.
"People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says.
"Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

blocks.text: Albanese says announcement of Medicare breach ‘purely in national interest’

Anthony Albanese says he was not aware of other cases of AI agents wrongfully accessing classified information before he revealed OpenAI’s unauthorised infiltration of the Medicare Statistics Reporting portal in New York on Thursday, Australian Associated Press reports.
“At the time we made our announcement … we weren’t aware of other occurrences,” the prime minister told reporters at Sydney airport on Saturday.
“We were acting purely in our national interest.”
The PM landed back in Australia on Saturday after a week in the US where he addressed the United Nations General Assembly on the international need to rein in AI.
He said news that autonomous agents allegedly infiltrated American university and commerce department sites, as well as the US Securities and Exchange Commission, further proved that need.
“We now know it wasn’t just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation,” Albanese said.

double quotation markWhat this does is confirm that approach of making sure that it needs to be an appropriate national response, as well as an international response to make sure that humans are in charge of this new and emerging technology.
Albanese said it was up to OpenAI to state why multiple breaches occurred.
Good morning

Welcome to our Sunday live blog. Flight delays and cancellations caused frustration and heartache for some footy fans racing to make it to Saturday’s AFL grand final before the first bounce. And the PM says the timing of his announcement of OpenAI’s Medicare hack was made “purely in the national interest”. More on both those stories shortly.
Also, the Liberal deputy leader, Jane Hume, will be speaking on the ABC’s Insiders this morning. More on that coming up.

articles.title: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
articles.summary: China's economy and tech have developed at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing country
"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".
Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.
And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.
China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up.

"The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home.
"People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."

She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".

Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full. "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.

blocks.caption: Image caption, About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently

blocks.text: About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently

In Sinapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging.
It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.

These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times".
"Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore.
"But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it."
He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.

Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.
China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says

blocks.text: Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says
Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air.

"The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.
This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers.

One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."
Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."

Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures

blocks.text: Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures

Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.

Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."

And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.
Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.

They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.

Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects

blocks.text: Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects

Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward.

Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition.
The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home.
"When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution."
About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles".
Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation.
But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity.
"If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

articles.title: Are claims of a white genocide in South Africa real?

But South Africa's new ambassador to the US, Roelf Meyer, says that the notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.

articles.title: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
articles.summary: Christy Spivey tells the BBC she only has more questions now police think Tasia Fortune's body was put in the tree after her death.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details

The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene.
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree.
"I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC.

The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".
Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging.
Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black.
"I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way.
"Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?"
Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes. But the latest developments have created more confusion.

Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought.
"When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people."
When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down".
Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs.
Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction.
"Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said.
"If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does."
She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes.
Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted.

articles.title: Helicopter crashes outside Montreal, killing all 4 occupants
articles.summary: Police are investigating after a helicopter crashed in a field near the Rang des Écossais in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville on Saturday afternoon.

blocks.text: Montreal
Police are investigating after a helicopter crashed in a field near the Rang des Écossais in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville on Saturday afternoon.
Major crimes unit investigating crash
Helicopter crash in Quebec kills all 4 on board
Police are investigating after a helicopter crashed in a field near the Rang des Écossais off Highway 10 in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville on Saturday afternoon.
Sûreté du Québec spokesperson Brigitte Dorsainville said it happened at around 2:30 p.m. ET and the helicopter was on fire when first responders arrived.
Dorsainville said all four occupants on board were declared dead at the scene.
Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville is located roughly 55 kilometres southeast of Montreal.
Police said Saturday evening that the helicopter likely encountered difficulties shortly after takeoff and crashed not far from its departure point, according to early information.
The SQ did not specify where the helicopter took off from.
According to Radio-Canada, the pilot was named Suzanne Jutras. She regularly offered helicopter tours.
She was experienced, said one of her friends, a fellow pilot. He spoke to Radio-Canada off camera.
The identities of the passenger have yet to be released. Police said they believe the helicopter was a "private aircraft."
The fire has since been brought under control and the SQ's major crimes unit has taken over the file.
Transport Canada to appoint minister's observer
The Transportation Safety Board of Canada confirmed it has deployed a team of investigators to the crash site in a statement to CBC News.
Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon took to social media to express his condolences.
"My thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragedy," he wrote, adding that safety of civil aviation operations is a top priority for Transport Canada.
MacKinnon said the federal government is monitoring the situation and will provide necessary support. He also announced that Transport Canada will appoint a "minister's observer."

The observer's role is to monitor the response alongside the TSB and provide the minister with updates on the investigation. The observer can also help identify regulatory issues or safety deficiencies.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Annabelle Olivier is a digital journalist at CBC Montreal. She previously worked at Global News as an online producer. You can reach her at anne.isabelle.olivier@cbc.ca.
With files from CBC's Alexandre Silberman

articles.title: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
articles.summary: Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.

image.caption: Tech giant Google has several data centers in Europe Image: Patrick Scheiber/IMAGO

blocks.text: Like coal-fired power plants and wind turbines, few people actually want a data center in their backyard. But they do want to use their services. As a global debate rages about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence, there are also many local discussions about where exactly the data centers needed to train and run AI should be built.

This is currently a major issue in Europe, where many governments and companies have decided that they would prefer to store data in Europe rather than in the United States, which is the global leader in computing. But more digital sovereignty in Europe will mean more consumption of the continent's resources.

According to the German Ministry for Economic Affairs, for every kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed, an average of between 0.4 and 4.4 liters (0.8 and 9.3 pints) of water is used to cool data centers, with the water either evaporating or being diverted back to tanks in a warmed state.
What happens when data centers lose power?
Massive water consumption

The summer that just ended was the hottest on record in Europe — in some areas, water use was restricted for residents, agriculture and even nuclear power plants. The summers are expected to get warmer, so many are wondering about the potential water consumption of data centers in the future.

They are also worried about the high electricity consumption of the centers. Fingrid, Finland's national grid operator, recently forecast that electricity consumption would rise by almost 40% if all projects with signed connection agreements were implemented in full.

This week, the European Commission announced a new scheme for data centers to increase transparency on their energy and water use. Those with a capacity of more than 500 kW will receive an efficiency grade that will also take into account their contribution to the grid, such as the reuse of waste heat. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills," said Teresa Ribera, the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.

blocks.caption: Several data centers are currently under construction in EuropeImage: Maksim Zabarovskii/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Data centers in urban hubs and rural areas

Europe's most powerful data centers have primarily been built near the major cities of Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin (FLAP-D) because of high connectivity, proximity to users and businesses, and well-established ecosystems with specialized engineers and secure supply chains.

However, according to a report by the investment group CBRE, the situation is changing as these markets face power and grid infrastructure constraints. New data centers are being built in the Dutch city of Groningen, Barcelona in Spain or the Belgian capital Brussels, as well as in more rural areas.

And as this happens, there are more and more protests taking place, both on and offline. Earlier this month, hundreds turned up for a protest in front of tech giant Google's offices in the Austrian city of Linz, demonstrating against its already advanced plans to build a data center in the small town of Kronstorf.

blocks.caption: Hundreds protested against a Google data center saying that AI needed democracy Image: APA-Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Earlier this month, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney successfully led a campaign to overturn planning permission for a proposed data center in the village of Killala, arguing that it would breach national climate policy.

In central France, meanwhile, several elected officials in the village of Etrechet have resigned over Google's plans to build a massive data center, which, at full capacity, would require between 880 megawatts and 1.1 gigawatts of electricity or the equivalent of the total output of a nuclear power plant. Etrechet mayor Florence Laurent told the French daily Le Monde that she was resigning out of a "sense of powerlessness, since the village has no decision-making power" regarding the project.

Some operators of data centers argue that the facilities can be built in such a way that they save energy. A large data center currently being built in Marseille will reportedly use a cooling system that requires 30% less power and consumes no water.
Other data centers, in Scandinavia, for example, use waste heat from the servers and route it into district heating networks via heat exchangers and pumps.

This spring, the German energy company E.ON published the results of a survey that found nearly three-quarters of people would be more likely to welcome data centers near residential areas if they fed their waste heat into the heating network.
Data centers face backlash from US communities

Data center operators also argue that the facilities can serve the public by connecting the batteries that usually provide backup power to local grids so that there is uninterrupted service in the event of power outages or at times of peak demand.
For proponents of building more data centers in Europe, the facilities not only contribute to the continent's digital sovereignty but also help to strengthen energy independence.
Monir Ghaedi contributed to this article, which was translated from German.

blocks.caption: Irish writer Sally Rooney spearheaded a successful campaign against the building of a data center in IrelandImage: Ullstein/dpa/picture alliance

articles.title: Nor'easter storm brings coastal flooding, as New York and New Jersey declare emergency
articles.summary: Tens of millions of people from Maine to Virginia are in the path of the powerful storm.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded

Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm this weekend, which has already brought coastal flooding, power outages, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.
