Peaking on Saturday, the so-called nor'easter will "bring dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds, and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.
States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, the latter of which is already facing a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine.
Ed Sheeran's much-awaited Boston concert was among events called off.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood
The nor'easter is already causing widespread power outages. Nearly 150,000 households have so far lost electricity, according to poweroutageus.
The Federal Aviation Administration recommended flyers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 1,100 flights have been delayed and another 400 grounded, according to FlightAware.
Saturday's full moon is projected to worsen coastal inundations. Streets and homes were flooded on Saturday in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan.
"I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert, and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Flooding in New Jersey

blocks.text: Flooding in New Jersey

blocks.caption: Image caption, Flights have been cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport

blocks.text: Flights have been cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport
NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."
In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power outages.
"Don't travel if you don't have to," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."
In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs from Sunday afternoon game to next Friday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Waves pound the coast in Massachusetts

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Waves pound the coast in Massachusetts
A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled.
Nor is the Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, going ahead.
Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston-area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.

articles.title: Greek authorities seek answers after six killed in Athens apartment block explosion
articles.summary:
Emergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in a matter of seconds’

Greek authorities say they are trying to discover what caused a…

blocks.text: Greek authorities say they are trying to discover what caused a two-storey apartment block in the heart of ancient Athens to collapse “in a matter of seconds”, killing six people.
Emergency teams found the victims, including four American tourists, on Saturday, more than 24 hours after an explosion prompted the early morning tragedy in the historic Plaka district.

The fire service said the bodies of three women and three men had been found, but stopped short of identifying them. A Briton and his Greek wife, aged 77 and 78, who lived in a flat on the building’s upper floor, were among those killed, the Guardian was told.

“The bodies have been taken to the morgue where postmortems will be conducted,” the city’s vice-mayor Paris Charlaftis said in a telephone interview from the blast scene. “Our focus now is on the explosion’s cause. What could have happened to bring the building down in a matter of seconds?”

Rescuers had deployed thermal cameras and geophones, used to detect deep subsonic frequencies, in the hope of finding survivors. Earth-moving machines and specially trained search dogs were brought in to move and comb mounds of rubble through the night.

Before the bodies were pulled from the ruins on Saturday, police put the missing at six, saying four were Americans staying in a short-term rental on the building’s first floor. Two brothers and their wives, all four were due to fly to the US on Friday, just hours after the explosion.

blocks.caption: Police have put the missing at six. Photograph: Costas Baltas/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: “When they failed to turn up for the flight they had checked into only a day earlier, that gave us a further lead,” a source said. “It became clearer that they must have been there when the blast occurred.”

The Briton, a talented artist, who lived with his wife on the second floor, was described as being partially disabled by Charlaftis. “He had kinetic issues, and it was thought likely they, too, were in the building [at the time of the blast].”

Nestled around the foot of the fifth-century BC Acropolis, Plaka is especially popular with tourists. The picturesque district draws thousands of visitors daily, with many staying overnight in the hotels and short-term rentals in neoclassical houses and small apartment blocks along its alleyways and narrow streets.
The mayor of Athens, Haris Doukas, who rushed to 15 Lysikratous where the mid-20th century building had once stood, was quick to describe the incident as an “unprecedented disaster”.

At least three people were known to have been injured when the 7.30am explosion occurred, shattering the windows of nearby buildings and scattering debris far and wide. A motorist driving down Lysikratous described how his car was lifted into the air by the sheer force of a blast that some in the neighbourhood likened to an earthquake, others to a bomb. Emergency workers could be seen hastily removing two women on stretchers from a building next door who had been wounded by flying debris.

Speculation is rife that a gas leak triggered the collapse but officials said there were many “cogent theories” at play. Fears of the leak emanating from the first-floor short-term rental was among them.
after newsletter promotion
As part of efforts to address a burgeoning housing crisis, Greece’s centre-right government has sought to ban short-term rentals in Plaka – clamping down on permits and tightening regulations.
On Saturday, as speculation mounted over the cause of the blast, criticism grew over the ability to “properly control” establishments that were often unregulated.

“This awful incident will fuel further debate over who inspects short-term rentals that no one who lives in Plaka wants anyway,” said Giorgos Zafeiriou, an architect who heads the local residents’ committee. “Hotels have chambers that regulate them but who inspects and controls Airbnb and serviced apartments that often may not be up to par?”
Civil protection crews and emergency disaster management teams have been ordered to remain on site until the cause of the explosion is found, officials said.
“It was a huge explosion, so getting to the bottom of it must now be the priority,” added Zafeiriou. “Six people have lost their lives.”

articles.title: China, US agree to set up channel for AI safety incidents
articles.summary: Following the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the two superpowers pledged to set up a "communication channel" for AI incidents and boost coordination on…

image.caption: The two leaders are expected to meet twice more before the end of the yearImage: Jim Watson/AFP

blocks.text: Beijing and Washington promised to expand dialogue on AI safety and between the countries' militaries while also cutting tariffs on about $30 billion (€26.3 billion) of "non-sensitive goods."
The pledges follow the three-day summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in the US.
US President Trump described the summit in an online post as "one of Friendship, Strength, and Success" for both nations.
Trump-Xi summit: Results or just symbolism?
China's President Xi was more constrained, saying the two sides agree on "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."
Beijing and Washington to improve military communication

On Saturday, with Xi back in Beijing, China said the two sides agreed to a mutual tariff reduction on roughly $30 billion of "non-essential" goods. This applies to exports such as agricultural products or holiday decorations.
The Chinese statement also confirmed that the two side will be setting up a "communication channel" for AI incidents.

"Artificial intelligence technologies are continuously developing, all parties can strengthen exchanges, discuss in-depth and seek consensus in light of the latest situation," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.
A new round of AI-focused dialogue is due to be held in November.
The two nations will also accelerate their work on military crisis communications, Beijing said, without providing details.
Xi to travel to the US again in December

The US had previously announced that Beijing and Washington agreed to extend their "trade truce" agreed by Trump and Xi in Busan last October. The agreement, which saw China suspending its controls on rare earths and the US cutting back on some of its tariffs, was due to expire on November 10. According to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the deal will remain in effect until January.
Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit

The White House also said the two sides addressed American concerns about rare earths supply "with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels." China also agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the US in 2027 and 2028, according to the Trump administration.

While Donald Trump confirmed the Iran war was also on the agenda during the US talks, no major breakthroughs were reported on the issue. However, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said both sides agreed that Iran should not have nuclear weapons, and no country should impose transit tolls on international waterways, in reference to the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump and Xi are due to meet twice more by the end of the year, with Trump expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ​summit in China in November and Xi expected back in the US for a G20 summit in December, which is due to be hosted in Trump's National Doral Miami golf club.

articles.title: US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering
articles.summary:
Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’

While the US secretary of state,

blocks.text: While the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific.

blocks.caption: Ecuador’s president, Daniel Noboa, right, presents the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, with Ecuador’s highest ranking National Order of Merit, the Grand Cross, at Carondelet palace in Quito, on 9 September. Photograph: Dolores Ochoa/AP

blocks.text: On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador.

“The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added.

blocks.caption: A US patrol vessel intercepting the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador. Photograph: US Southern Command/X

blocks.text: “They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities.

But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US.

blocks.caption: Ten crew members from the five skiffs belonging to the vessel Don Rufo, after they were located and taken aboard the BAE Atahualpa, following air-maritime search and reconnaissance operations conducted by the Ecuadorian navy. Photograph: Ecuadorian Navy

blocks.text: US Southern Command posted an edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny.

It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the latest on 16 September – to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk.

blocks.caption: A still from a video released by US forces intercepting a floating refuelling station supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in the eastern Pacific. Photograph: US Southern Command @Southcom

blocks.text: Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”.

Donald Trump has compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday.
Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase.

blocks.caption: Marines and sailors with Maritime Raid Force, LCF-24, boarding the Ecuadorian fishing vessel Conquista 2 in the Pacific on 2 September. Photograph: US Marine Corps Forces, South

blocks.text: “Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place.
Noboa has responded with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces.

blocks.caption: Relatives of the four minors apprehended by soldiers and found dead near a military base dance during a rally to demand justice a year after their apprehension in Guayaquil, Ecuador on 8 December 2025. Photograph: Marcos Pin/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has eroded human rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered.

Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorising joint operations and granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troops taking part in raids last Thursday.

“Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador for the New Yorker magazine.

blocks.caption: People look at the remains of a burned-out fishing boat in the port of Manta, Ecuador, on 6 June 2026. The Ecuadorian national police said at least 20 fishing boats had been damaged.   Photograph: Ariel Ochoa/EPA
The Ecuadorean army shows drug trafficker Adolfo Macías, alias Fito, being guarded after his recapture in Manta, which is in the Manabi province. Photograph: Ecuadorean Army/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created called Shield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is a serious contender in October’s election.
So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.
Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region.

blocks.caption: Fishermen work along the shore as local fishermen are increasingly being pursued by Ecuadorean gangs to move drugs and for their skills navigating the Pacific waters along Ecuador’s coast, in Manta, on 4 June. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters

blocks.text: Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four people were killed in the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity.

During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the US would “still blow up ships if need be”.

Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes as extrajudicial killings, and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”.
Despite Trump’s claims, available data show they have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the country.

Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks.

blocks.caption: Relatives wait for 32 crew members to be released under precautionary measures in Manta, Ecuador, on 8 September 2026. The 24 crew members of the Maria Candelaria and eight from the Conquista II face judicial proceedings on suspicion of illicit association and fuel trafficking after their vessels…

blocks.text: In Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishers have been subjected to “violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations.
None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted for lack of evidence.

“Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías.
A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”.
Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this year remain unclaimed.

The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vessel Fiorella disappeared with eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag.

Human rights organisations and journalists identified two more cases with similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Post reported that the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment.
A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”.

blocks.caption: Maria Mero and her mother, Maria Cueva, speak during an interview after Mero’s husband Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado and brother Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva disappeared from the boat Fiorella after a strike in June 2026. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters
Maria Cueva holding a picture of her son Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva. Photograph: Karen Toro/Reuters

blocks.text: Both the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian.
The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success.

“They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.

articles.title: German town bans 'stumbling stone' memorials to Nazi victims
articles.summary: Germany's education minister has branded the ban on the small brass memorial plaques a "scandal".

blocks.text: There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victims of the Nazis.
Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien told newspaper Bild that the ban was a "scandal".
Since the 1990s, many towns in countries across Europe, including in Germany and Austria, have embedded small brass plaques in the streets in memory of Jews and other victims of Nazi atrocities.
The plaques, called Stolpersteine in German, are often placed outside the houses where the victims used to live or work. They are frequently funded by donations.
But now councillors from the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party and the conservative CDU in Heidenau have voted to ban stumbling stones - or "Stolpersteine" in German - in their town.
The AfD in Saxony has been classified as extreme-right by German intelligence, a designation the party rejects.
The motion in the town council said that many citizens felt that this form of commemoration of Nazi victims was inappropriate.
Memorials should in future be placed at the city's Nordfriedhof cemetery to make it "impossible to step directly onto the memorial elements", the motion stated.
However, Karin Prien, a member of the CDU, criticised the decision.

"Anyone who banishes Stolpersteine and memorial sites commemorating Jewish life from public spaces to the cemetery is prioritising death over life and rendering Jewish people invisible once again," she told Bild.
She said her own CDU party in Saxony also bore responsibility for the decision.
Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and president of the Jewish Community in Munich, said that removing memorials from the cityscape was "completely the wrong approach".
She told the Funke Media Group that she was "appalled that a democratic party would stoop to supporting such a transparent manoeuvre by the extremists of the AfD".

Knobloch said that she was not a supporter of the stumbling stones, but added that "decentralised remembrance – which is not banished from public space but, on the contrary, permeates and shapes it" was crucial to a genuine culture of remembrance.
In her own city of Munich, there are no Stolpersteine on municipal land. Instead, the city allows memorial plaques on public buildings.
As the name suggests, Stolpersteine are intended as memorials people stumble upon, making them reflect on the history of their location.
Gunter Demnig, the artist who initiated the Stolperstein project, said that given the recent electoral successes of the AfD "it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen".
The AfD recently secured major victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party strongly rejects.
Its anti-immigration, "Germany first" and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.

articles.title: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
articles.summary: Drone explosions, airspace violations, arson attacks: Poland, Romania, and Moldova are now regularly targeted in Russian attacks against Ukraine. More governments are calling these attacks deliberate…

image.caption: Aftermath of a drone attack near the Ukrainian-Moldovan border Image: OdeskaODA/Telegram

blocks.text: Just a few months ago, Russia's war was an distant reality for many people in Europe outside of Ukraine. If Russian drones occasionally entered the airspace of countries like Poland or Romania, even official statements seemed strangely dismissive and abstract. Even after a Russian drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati in late May this year, many EU and NATO representatives hesitated to accuse Russia of intentional action. At most, there was discussion of hybrid warfare.

The situation has changed radically since the summer. Drone overflights have become almost daily in certain parts of central and southeastern Europe, and there have even been crashes and explosions, particularly in countries bordering Ukraine. Alerts are becoming more frequent, with authorities increasingly having to close airspace or suspend operations at airports, as unauthorized flights are detected. Russia has been bombing border crossings, infrastructure and trains in Ukraine, but very close to other borders. Acts of sabotage are also increasingly common.
For the Baltic states, Poland, Moldova and Romania in particular, the war has long ceased to be "hybrid." More and more, politicians in these countries are saying that Russia is acting deliberately.
Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats
Drones violate Moldovan and Romanian airspace

This became evident this week in an unprecedented manner. Moldova recorded four drones entering Moldovan airspace, two of which exploded in Moldovan territory. Wreckage of another was also found. The country's northern airspace was closed temporarily. Two drones also violated Romanian airspace; with one crashing near the northern town of Solca. A nearby border crossing with Ukraine a few dozen kilometers away was closed as a result. NATO aircraft were scrambled near the Danube Delta.

blocks.caption: The wreckage of a drone found in Moldova Image: Polizei der Republik Moldau

blocks.text: The scrambling of NATO aircraft has become more common in response to Russian air attacks in Ukraine.

In Poland, NATO fighter jets were scrambled twice in response to Russian attacks near the border with Ukraine. Two Polish border crossings were evacuated after a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station near the village of Wola Krobowska, 40 kilomters (ca. 25 miles) south of the Polish capital Warsaw, on Wednesday night. The station is used to route internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine.
On the same day, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds according to the Polish military.
Polish Prime Minister Tusk says Europe needs to prepare
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke very bluntly in Krakow on Thursday and said that Russia was refining its "disgusting forms of pressure" and Poland must be prepared for them.

Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to exhaust Ukraine by destroying its industrial and energy infrastructure, but he also wants to exhaust Europe," Tusk said. He added that there was a suspicion that the fire at the Starlink ground station had been deliberate.
Earlier this month, Tusk had already warned the Polish parliament that there might be Russian drone and even missile attacks against those who supported Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Donald Tusk has warned that Poland has to prepare for possible drone attacks Image: Lukasz Glowala/REUTERS

blocks.text: Moldovan President Maia Sandu also reacted very strongly on Thursday, saying that Russia's war was a danger to all of Europe and reasserting Moldova's support for Ukraine.

In Romania, reactions were less clear. Defense Minister Radu Miruta said that not more than a "diplomatic protest" was needed, though he acknowledged that the drone that had crashed in Solca had new technical features, which suggested it could be a newer type of Russian jet-powered drone.

In New York on Wednesday, in his address to the United Nations General Assembly, Romanian President Nicusor Dan had said: "We are in the fifth year of the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression waged on a large scale against Ukraine by a permanent member of the Security Council." He had added that as the "EU member state with the longest border with Ukraine, Romania has directly felt the effects of this war through repeated violations of our airspace."

And he too reasserted support for Ukraine: "We have said it before, and we say it again: Romania will stand with Ukraine and its people, who are acting in legitimate self-defense, for as long as it takes."

blocks.caption: Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Romania would stand by Ukraine Image: Heather Khalifa/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Attacks on western Europe from the Mediterranean?

Meanwhile, there is growing speculation that Russia could expand its war to Western Europe. On Thursday, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo published information about a CIA report warning that Russia could be preparing drone attacks on Italy, France and Spain. The attacks could be launched from international waters in the Mediterranean and from vessels that were part of Russia's shadow fleet.

There has been no official confirmation so far. French President Emmanuel Macron said that that the CIA had not informed France of this information, but he did say that the possibility Russia could launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."

blocks.caption: French President Emmanuel Macron said the CIA had not warned France of possible drone attacks from international waters Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP

blocks.text: At a press conference in Denmark on Thursday, politicians and military officials warned that Russia was expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months. The situation is currently the most serious since the end of the Cold War," said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Watch: Bangkok declared flood disaster zone
articles.summary: Heavy rain over the last two days has overwhelmed Bangkok's water systems, with more rain forecast on Sunday.

blocks.text: The whole of Bangkok has been declared a flood disaster zone as authorities try to pump days of floodwater into the sea.
Heavy rain over the last two days has overwhelmed Bangkok's water systems, with more rain forecast on Sunday.
People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors.
BBC South East Asia Correspondent Jonathan Head reports from Bangkok

articles.title: Trump rejects Iran proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump says he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and put an end to hostilities.

image.caption: Trump's rejection of the deal comes as US midterm elections loom in November Image: Aaron Schwartz/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and bring about an end to hostilities.
"I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal," Trump told reporters at the White House in Washington, DC.
Iran had proposed an initiative aimed at reopening the strategic waterway at the UN General Assembly in New York, which it said could put an end to fighting within seven days.
Tehran said the proposal had been transmitted to Washington via Qatari mediators.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," said Trump, claiming: "We're winning tremendously."
Earlier, a US official had told the Associated Press that discussions with Iran, conducted through mediators, were "positive and constructive."

But the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was skeptical that Tehran would meet his demands. He reportedly told staff that a renewed bombing ‌campaign ​is likely following the November US midterm elections.

"They want to make a deal and I think that's fine, I like making a deal too," said Trump. "What they want to do is ​immediately open the Hormuz Strait ... because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait."
More to follow ...

articles.title: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
articles.summary: The indpendent report also says Kirk's aides insisted he speak outdoors, overriding concerns from campus officials.

blocks.text: An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.

The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.
It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.
The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.
Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.

University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report, external - published by UVU - says.
"But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds.
Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.
They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team.
A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said.

The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures.
However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.
Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action.
The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones.

"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."
When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.
The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events.
UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".

It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures now common practice at high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.

Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.
His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

articles.title: Canadian citizen detained at U.S. border crossing, questioned about voting for hours

image.caption: Paige Adamson says she was detained until nearly 3 a.m. PT and was 'basically treated like a criminal' when she attempted to cross the Canada-U.S. border at the Point Roberts border crossing on Sept. 15. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Paige Adamson was on her way home from a birthday dinner in Tsawwassen, B.C., on Sept. 15 when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing and questioned about voting for hours. Lawyers are raising concerns around vulnerabilities Canadians face while living in the U.S., especially over being registered to vote.
'Tip of the iceberg': One lawyer warns more Canadians could be detained over illegal voting concerns
Paige Adamson was on her way home from a birthday dinner in Tsawwassen, B.C., on Sept. 15 when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing.
It was a regular stop that Adamson — a Canadian citizen who has lived in Point Roberts, Wash., as a U.S. permanent resident for 14 years — had grown used to.
But this time, they had a new question for her.
"The very first thing she asked was, 'Have you ever voted in a federal U.S. election?'" said Adamson.
Adamson, 61, said she told the border agent she had never voted in a federal election.
"They immediately said, 'Park over here and come into the office.'"

What happened next, Adamson said, was a nearly six-hour-long process — where she went through secondary inspection just after 9 p.m., was interrogated until after 2 a.m. and signed documents before being admitted into the U.S.
One of the documents CBC News reviewed said Adamson "must surrender for removal from the United States, if so ordered."

Lawyers who spoke with CBC News said U.S. voter registration systems can sometimes catch non-citizens up in errors, and one of them says he has seen an uptick in non-citizens being questioned in the last week.
Grounds for removal

According to documents provided by Adamson, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) alleges she falsely claimed she was a U.S. citizen "for the purposes of registering to vote in Whatcom County, Washington state."
The department also alleges Adamson voted in Washington state's 2018 general election.
DHS cites those allegations as grounds for removing Adamson from the U.S.

But Adamson maintained during questioning, a transcript reviewed by CBC News showed, that she has never voted in a federal election and doesn't remember ever voting in a state election — though she acknowledged receiving a ballot and may have been registered.
Adamson is now scheduled to appear for a hearing in Seattle, and is grappling with potentially being removed from the state she has lived in since 2012.
"My anxiety is over the top," she said.
A broader trend
In the past week and a half, immigration lawyer Len Saunders said he has received calls from three people — including Adamson — about being detained at the border and questioned about voting.
One, he said, was a Blaine, Wash., resident who crosses the border daily to work as a nurse in B.C.
Saunders said three near-identical situations like this in such a short period is unprecedented in his career that stretches back more than 25 years.
The Blaine-based lawyer told CBC News there could be hundreds of Canadians facing similar issues, and expects more cases as Canadians cross the border during the holidays.
"This is just the tip of the iceberg," he said.
B.C. immigration lawyer Chris Anders said border enforcement is "way, way stricter and tougher" than at any point in the last two decades.
He said the databases used by border officials are constantly expanding, meaning something that did not cause problems for someone previously could suddenly pop up during a new entry.
Voter registration issues
Washington state automatically registers some eligible voters when they get or renew a driver's licence or state ID, but the state says the system is tied to proof of U.S. citizenship.

But internal Washington Department of Licensing emails, obtained by the non-profit Federation for American Immigration Reform through a Freedom of Information request, show instances where non-citizens were registered to vote.
"A lot of Canadians say, 'Well, I thought I was entitled to [vote] because I went in, got my driver's licence and they registered me to vote,'" said Saunders.

items: Change in Canada's citizenship law hitting U.S. archives
Winnipeg-born man deported back to Canada after 9 months in ICE detention

blocks.text: Saunders said that in those situations, he has told clients to immediately deregister and submit a declaration saying they "unknowingly registered or unknowingly voted," and that used to be a consistent solution.
"Now, it seems to be a completely different scenario during this current administration."
The detainment

In an email to CBC News, a spokesperson for the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said when a permanent resident arrives at a port of entry, officers screen their documentation against federal and state databases.

The CBP says if those records indicate "potential unlawful voter registration, illegal voting, or a previous false claim to U.S. citizenship," the individual is subject to "rigorous examination and detailed questioning."
Depending on the case, an individual may face "prolonged" immigration inspections, receive a notice to appear and formal removal proceedings, the spokesperson said.
Are U.S. border agents allowed to search my phone? Your border questions answered
Adamson said she wasn't offered water until around the five-hour mark of her detainment, and no one asked whether she needed to use the bathroom.
"I was basically treated like a criminal," she said.
She said the large Canadian population in Point Roberts — an exclave of the U.S. located just south of Delta, B.C. — has left her concerned that some of her neighbours could face similar problems.
"This beautiful little place, it's kind of being invaded," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Russian students: Propaganda in school prepares them to die
articles.summary: The Russian government wants children to learn about patriotism from an early age. DW spoke to students in Siberia about their views on propaganda at school on the war in Ukraine and their future.

image.caption: Patriotism has become a core part of the national curriculum since 2022Image: Konstanin Kokoshkin/Pivcario/picture alliance

blocks.text: Earlier this year, several schools in Novosibirsk, a city of 1.6 million in southern Siberia, received a textbook on patriotism from the authorities. According to students, with whom DW spoke to on condition of anonymity, in the book the authors urge children to prepare themselves to die for their country. Furthermore, they equate homosexuality with pedophilia and Disney cartoons with pornography, and give instructions on how women should use their "charms." Europeans are described as "thieves, murderers and liars."

The textbook, which provides "materials for spiritual, moral, and patriotic upbringing" is supposed to be used as part of "patriotism lessons" that have been on the curriculum since 2022. Though it is not included on the national list of core curriculum books, the content reflects the Kremlin's intentions to spread propaganda in educational institutions.
'Love always involves sacrifice.'

One of the main topics of the book is the war in Ukraine and the idea that dying for one's country is a blessing is repeated several times: "Love always involves sacrifice," writes one of the authors. "The sacrifice of a defender of the homeland is their life."

Elsewhere in the book, the authors make constant claims that Russia is better than Western countries. They also say that children are "mentally crippled" because of "computer games, Hollywood action films, pornography and Disney cartoons."

They argue that European nations that used to be colonial empires legitimized "murder, lies and plunder" through the conquest and subjugation of new territories. Russia, on the other hand, "never exploited its numerous peoples," they say, but merely improved their living conditions. The book makes no mention of the culture of Indigenous peoples in what is Russia today, or of any religions other than Christianity and "Slavic paganism."

blocks.caption: This textbook is used in certain Russian schools to teach children about patriotism and other subjectsImage: M. Remaevich

blocks.text: 'More cannon fodder'

For Ilya, a 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk who has read the book and whose name has been changed, the idea of dying for his country is anathema. "It's proof that the country wants more cannon fodder," he told DW, adding that "dying for the country" actually meant dying for "the president's interests and ambitions."

He said that a few years ago, he had started watching the videos of Alexei Navalny, the Kremlin critic and opposition leader who died in jail in 2024 "more for fun than for any other reason." He said it was Navalny's 2021 investigation into Russian President Vladimir Putin's Black Sea palace that had first drawn his attention.

But it was when the authorities decided to block access to the US platforms YouTube and Discord that he began to oppose the government. He set up a VPN out of "contrariness" he said, looking for information about other opposition figures and reading the independent media. As he found out more about the cruelty and senselessness of the war, he criticized the government more strongly.

He confirmed that propaganda had become an integral part of the curriculum in the past four years. On top of the "Conversations about Important Things" that take place every Monday morning, there are now also subjects such as "Fundamentals of Homeland Security and Defense." He said that people who have taken part in the war in Ukraine are invited to lessons focusing on students' future and decisions regarding what career path to take.

Even outside of the classroom, students are encouraged to be "patriotic." Ilya said that a student had been reprimanded by the principal for wearing a sweater with a slogan written in English on it. "Young man, do you realize that your sweater has words on it in the language of unfriendly countries?" she reportedly asked him. "A call to the Federal Security Service will take care of that!"

Ilya also recalled that a school assembly held to mark May 9, which commemorates the Soviet Union's victory over Nazi Germany in 1945, the principal and her deputy had compared what is known in Russia as the "Great Patriotic War" to the current war in Ukraine. They had said that Russia would once again be steadfast and emerge victorious.

blocks.caption: Students are taught about being a soldier and told it is an honor to die for the country Image: Konstantin Kokoshkin/Picvario/Russian Look/Global Look Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'I love freedom'

Alexei (name changed), another 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk, told DW that many of his classmates avoided going to "patriotic events." He too said that the blocking of YouTube had made a difference to him. "I looked into why it was blocked," he said. "Because nothing happens by chance. And that's how my interest in politics began." That's when he realized that the authorities wanted to get rid of inconvenient citizens and suppress free speech. "I love freedom, so it was hard," he said.

Ilya thinks that most students don't take the propaganda seriously. "On the one hand, we laugh about it in class, at least my friends do," he said. "On the other, we don't care. Some simply don't listen. We're very good at being quiet and not talking much about it,"

Dima Zicer is an educator and the author of the Russian-language podcast "Love, Don't Discipline" who moved to Estonia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He told DW that "many students are happy to be part of a pro-Putin majority that doesn't think about things, according to the principle: 'We'll crush them all; we're stronger than everyone else. Everyone will be scared of us.'"

He said that there was no statistical data to back his argument, but he said that he had drawn his conclusions from his extensive experience working with Russian children, as well as his communication with parents. He said that these often only became aware of how serious the situation was when their children started saying things such as "We'll crush them" or "Putin is great," as well as talking about supposed Nazis and fascists in Ukraine.
Alexei and Ilya, who think differently and want the war in Ukraine to end, are worried about the unstable situation in Russia. They want to leave the country after graduating.
Protesting Putin: Russian opposition in exile
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: UN adds 61 companies to settlements blacklist over alleged Palestinian human rights violations
articles.summary:
Human rights council names and shames businesses with ties to illegal Israeli settlements in West Bank

The UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it…

blocks.text: The UN human rights office has added 61 more companies to a blacklist of firms that it says are involved in violating Palestinian human rights through business ties to Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The vast majority of the total 214 companies, which are based in 11 countries, are Israeli. Five of the 158 companies listed last year were removed in the latest update.

The blacklist, first published in 2020, was born of a vote by the UN’s human rights council, which has no ability to force companies to act. Its main goal is to name and shame businesses with ties to the settlements.
It is unclear how the inclusion on the list has affected the companies financially.

“This report is another reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities and are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses,” said Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, in a statement.

Israel said it “categorically rejects” the publication. “This database is meant to serve as a blacklist against businesses that have committed no wrongdoing,” the Israeli diplomatic mission in Geneva said in a statement. “We call on friends not to yield to this ugly attempt to blacklist Israeli firms.”
The UN office said it had advised the companies of their listing and given them a right of reply.
The latest report comes as Israeli settlements in Palestinian areas have faced new scrutiny.

Earlier this month, Britain banned trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, where it says “settler terrorists” are carrying out “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians. France and Canada announced they would take similar action.

articles.title: We followed five people in Gaza from dawn to dusk – this is what the headlines don’t tell us
articles.summary:
Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear

What does it take to make a morning…

blocks.text: What does it take to make a morning cup of tea in Gaza?

For Alaa Hessi, in her final month of pregnancy, this small ritual begins with a calculation of gas rations. Her family gets a ration of 6kg of gas every three months – enough to heat a pot for 18 precious minutes a day. That’s needed for cooking – so for tea, a fire must be built instead.

For 12-year-old Ramadan, the process begins with a hunt for anything flammable, in an environment where there is almost no wood left. He scouts through the sand dunes where he lives, snaps off a few twigs from a thorn bush, and feeds the flames with pieces of discarded plastic that wash up on the beach.

Before you boil the kettle, though, there is the matter of the water – with none running, the question is whether a water truck visits your area that day, and if not, how far you must walk to find it. Then there is transporting that water – how will Ramadan store it, given all of his family’s large water containers have been chewed through by rats? And how does a small boy carry the weight of it – enough liquid for a family to wash, brush teeth, cook with and drink through the next 30C summer day?

Finally, the water is boiling, but still there is the question of whether you even have tea or coffee or sugar to brew. Holding the paper bag of rationed sugar sparks a memory of what those goods have sometimes cost to acquire. Crouched over the teapot, Ramadan recalls last year’s famine, when aid points became death traps, and he and his brother risked everything to sprint for a bag of flour or sugar. He remembers the boys he saw shot beside him, because they moved too soon or too late.

blocks.caption: Ramadan on the beach at Al-Nuwairi, near Nuseirat, where he lives in a tent among the dunes. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Most of the headlines we encounter about Gaza are the extreme events: bombings, mass deaths, targeted assassinations. These demand attention.

There are some things, however, that rarely make the headlines, but have come to define life in Gaza. They are grinding, cruel realities that only really emerge when you inspect the minutia of a day – like a cup of tea. Over the course of this week, we documented the daily routines and mundane tasks of five ordinary Palestinians: a child, a pregnant woman, a teacher, a skateboarder and a grandmother. We followed them from sunrise to dusk, through the small, ordinary moments that rarely make international news – and through them, hoped to get a different, deeper understanding of what life is like now for Gaza’s people.

There is a lot you can understand from the anatomy of a day in Gaza. One thing that comes sharply into focus is the effect of dismantling or withholding those things – higher education, books, arts, museums, hobbies, musical instruments – that take human life beyond pure survival.
Israel continues to control everything that passes into Gaza, deciding how many calories it will allocate to its citizens, how much gas can be eked out to heat a minimum of hot meals.

Along with restricting the essentials required for life, the blockade bans a plethora of ordinary objects from entering Gaza, classing them as “dual use” items that could be used by Hamas. The blacklist and its criteria are opaque, arbitrary and ever-changing. At various times they have blocked the import of ventilator machines, medications for cancer, wedding dresses, sewing machines, toys, musical instruments, spices, dates and crutches.

blocks.caption: Rajab al-Reefi, leader of Gaza Skate Team, helps other team-members to repair some boards. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: From the story of Rajab al-Reefi’s day, we learn how the ban on skateboards has reverberated through his life. The 30-year-old has spent the past five years running Gaza Skate Team, a youth club that teaches children how to skateboard. During the war, their weekly gatherings became a lifeline and outlet for displaced children. Even after their skatepark was demolished, the team continued, posting videos of landing tricks on the rubble, kickflips executed on collapsed beams of concrete and tangled metal pylons.

But skateboards only have a lifespan of a couple of years: one by one, their layers snapped, wheel bearings wore out, parts salvaged from one broken board could no longer be fitted to another. With none left, the club went on a salvage mission, to dig some equipment from the rubble of a bombed building. Now, they have a handful of working boards again, and the girls are back to skating. But even these boards are on their last legs. When they wear out, there is nothing coming to replace them.

A skateboard is not essential to live – its absence will not make headlines like the systematic deprivation of food. But their absence illuminates the nature of the blockade in a fuller way: its random cruelties, the curtailing of opportunities for lightness, fun, self expression.

blocks.caption: Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem in front of the flat-bed truck that is now her home. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Still, against the odds, each person finds ways in their day to keep hold of the things that make them feel human. Prof Mahmoud Seydam wires a solar panel to power a laptop, uploading lectures over WhatsApp and taking oral presentations instead of written exams – battling to provide an education with no paper, no notebooks, no university campus. Alaa Hessi does her best to prepare a safe crib for her baby, in a tent pitched above the rubble where her three children were killed in a strike. Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem, living in the back of a truck, tells her grandchildren stories of their history. Ramadan watches the ocean and dreams of becoming a lifeguard.
You can read all five of their days here.

articles.title: One dead and five missing after explosion destroys building close to Acropolis in Athens
articles.summary: Local media report the property included a holiday rental, with US tourists and a UK national among the missing.

blocks.text: At least one person has died and five more are missing after an explosion destroyed a building in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis, with local media reporting the building housed a holiday rental.
Four American tourists, one British national and a Greek national are said to the people involved - though that has not been confirmed by authorities.
Pictures from the scene showed emergency service workers searching through the rubble, with a gas leak suspected as the cause of the blast.
The body of a woman was found on Saturday morning, with the search ongoing.
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
BBC News has contacted the UK Foreign Office.

articles.title: Trump reportedly rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Tehran awaits official response to plan, but US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms

Iran is ⁠awaiting an official US response to its proposal to reopen the strait of…

blocks.text: Iran is ⁠awaiting an official US response to its proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the Middle East war as Donald Trump was reported to have rejected the deal.

Iran raised the diplomatic initiative at the UN general assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted ⁠to the Americans via Qatari mediators and could ⁠reopen the strategic waterway and put an end ​to hostilities in the region within seven days.

But the US president is sceptical and has told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed US officials.
Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive”.

Iran has offered to reopen the strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear programme in seven days if the US lifted its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waived sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observed a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council on Friday, saying the country would also restart stalled talks with the US on Iran’s nuclear programme. “The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said.

Araghchi said the initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, and the strait would be open on the sixth day. “And on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects,” he said, referring to the nuclear programme.
“If there is seriousness on the US side to ⁠come to a deal and reopen the strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared,” Araqchi said.

The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the strait, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and taken a toll on the global economy.

Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons“.
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump during his address to the UN general assembly. Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

blocks.text: Since then the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.

Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.

Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict, which has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and drawn in regional and world powers.
Early on Saturday, Yemen’s ⁠Saudi-led ⁠coalition said ⁠it ​intercepted ‌two ‌drones ‌launched by the Iran-backed ‌Houthis towards ​the ⁠Saudi ​capital, Riyadh.

Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq have been blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. All the while, Iranian-backed Hezbollah has been engaged with Israeli forces in Lebanon.
With Reuters and AP

articles.title: Lula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian elections
articles.summary:
President’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggest

Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning…

blocks.text: Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning fixed-odds sports betting just over a week before the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt.
The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting.

The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until 5 October to withdraw their funds.

Lula’s government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common and dominant type of online sports betting – such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit punters.
“I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in São Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumour, or the tumour will kill us.”
Lula had also criticised the betting industry earlier this week at the United Nations general assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes”.
Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread support among Brazilians. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s main rival in the upcoming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure”.

Brazil’s president has sharply criticised online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. The public backlash against it grew during the Fifa World Cup when advertisements were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged.

Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8bn reais (£5.6bn) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies.

The country’s central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30bn reais on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare programme Bolsa Familia (family grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year.
Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year.

Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro’s father.

In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked more than 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organisations such as the First Capital Command from São Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector.

Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to both close a drain to the country’s economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms.
Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4bn (£3bn) per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world.
Before Friday’s move, Brazil’s main football clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned that their sponsorships would end immediately if the government banned betting.
They said the move could lead to the end of Brazilian football, a claim mocked by some social media users in the football-mad country.

articles.title: Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared
articles.summary: An emergency has been declared across the capital of Thailand as days of heavy rain leave the city inundated.

blocks.text: Disaster declared as heavy rain sparks Bangkok flooding
A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after 48 hours of heavy rain left roads in the Thai capital submerged.
People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors.

Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested.
The rain is expected to continue into Sunday, raising fears that more canals could burst their banks.
Image source, Getty Images
Canals across the Thai capital have burst their banks, leaving roads under water
Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now.
"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now."
She said water levels in the city appeared to be worse than in 2011, when Bangkok was impacted by nationwide flooding.
Hundreds were killed across Thailand then in an extreme weather event that lasted for three months. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding.
The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the area of low pressure causing the downpours of recent days is expected to move towards central Thailand.

blocks.caption: People holding umbrellas and walking down a narrow flooded street in Bangkok

blocks.text: All 50 of Bangkok's districts have been declared emergency zones.
Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's governor, said the east of the city had been hardest hit, AFP reported.

He continued: "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled."

articles.title: Brazil's Lula bans online gambling ahead of presidential election
articles.summary: Lula, who is currently in a tight presidential race against Flávio Bolsonaro, said the industry was a "cancer" that he must "remove".

blocks.text: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has announced a ban on online gambling, just days before an election in which he is seeking a fourth term as the country's leader.
Lula, who is running against the son of the incarcerated former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, signed a provisional order on Friday that "prohibits all sports betting and online casinos".
The online gambling industry in Brazil was legalised in 2018 and has since been blamed for widespread household income losses due to addiction.
Lula described the industry as a "cancer" in his announcement, adding "either we remove the tumour, or it kills us".
The move comes just over a week before the first round of voting in Brazil's presidential election. Recent polls have the 80-year-old leader almost neck-and-neck with Flávio Bolsonaro.
The new measures must receive congressional approval within 120 days to remain in force.
Lula acknowledged online betting was created under the former President Michel Temer's administration but that it "grew without regulation under Bolsonaro's management", in a statement on X .
He said that there were "no restrictions" particularly for preventing children and adolescents from accessing online betting.
"We won't allow betting companies to profit at the expense of Brazilian families' income and lives," the president added.
The president described how he had heard from families who had sold everything in their houses because of their gambling addictions.
Separate to the online betting order, Lula also signed a bill to penalise criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting.
Earlier this week, at the United Nations General Assembly, Lula accused the industry of "transforming addiction into profit".
But Flávio Bolsonaro called the gambling crackdown "populist, hypocritical and politically motivated" during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday, according to Reuters.
Most types of gambling, such as casinos and slot machines, are illegal in Brazil, but ever since online betting was legalised in 2018, it has exploded in popularity.
About 59.9% of Brazilian adults support banning internet betting, a survey by Atlas and Bloomberg published this week has found.

articles.title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
articles.summary: Voters are turning away from the centre in Germany as fears grow about the economy and migration.

blocks.text: A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis.
But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years.
It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities.
Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again.
A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more.
A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story.
A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time.
Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity.
And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered.
That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results.
In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap).
But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch.
It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue.
Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people.
Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU.

Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag.

"I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way."
Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy.
He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition.
And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success.
This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year.
But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue.
Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector.
It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy.
And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration.
While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD).

Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence.
Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania.
Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered.

articles.title: Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters
articles.summary:
Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada

The CEO of a

blocks.text: The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.
In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.

Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to say Lake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.
Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will.”
The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.
Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.

Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.

As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.

“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.

“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.
“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”
Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.
“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said a statement from the organization shared on social media.
