After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.

“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”
Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.
“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote on X.
Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.
The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.

Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

articles.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
articles.summary: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.

blocks.text: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
Image source, Project Pressure/Klaus Tymann
Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman Range
ByAbraham Utama
BBC Indonesia
The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.
The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.
They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.
But now, nearly all the snow is gone.
A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.
But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.

Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.

blocks.caption: Map and satellite image showing rapidly shrinking glaciers around Puncak Jaya in Indonesia's Papua region. Labels mark nearby peaks including Sumantri, Ngga Pulu and Carstensz East, with a callout noting that glaciers near the peaks are disappearing. An inset map locates Papua on the island of Ne…

blocks.text: "There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".

She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.
Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history.

Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.
But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936

blocks.text: The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936
Proof of a warming planet

The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.
El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.
The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.
A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.
The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems

blocks.text: Image source, Marie Šabacká
Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems
A spiritual anchor
At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.
The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow".

"Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."
According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.
Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts.

"How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe

blocks.text: The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe
For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.
The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.
Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.

Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded.
The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment.

"Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."

blocks.caption: Image caption, This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue

blocks.text: This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue
As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.
Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.
From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."
Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change.
"When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.
Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed.
"I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

articles.title: What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US?
articles.summary: Kratom, found during an investigation into the deaths of two college students, has been sold in the US for around a decade.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByBrandon Drenon and Madeline Halpert
Jeffrey Deaver, a 58-year-old retired timber cutter in the state of Washington, has taken kratom for four years to help with severe chronic hip and knee pain.
He discovered the herbal product when he couldn't find relief from doctors and while waiting for surgeries. Scared at first, he "started small", but then took more until his pain went away.
"It was like a miracle," Deaver said. "I could sleep. I could function.
"I just don't know what I'd do without it."
Kratom - an herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over-the-counter and consumed in pill or liquid form.

This week, investigators found packaged kratom in the possession of two deceased University of Mississippi students. Although their deaths were not attributed to kratom, officials are now issuing warnings about its consumption.

For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it's illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi.
Here's what we know about it:
What is kratom?
Kratom is a tree that is native to Southeast Asia in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.
It's been used for centuries for its stimulant properties, grounded and consumed similar to tea.
As its popularity spread around the globe, it entered the US market as a supplement around 2016.
"That's really where the problems began," said Dr Shane Speights, dean of the New York Institute of Technology College of Osteopathic Medicine at Arkansas State University.
In the US kratom is mostly sold in highly concentrated forms either via pill, powder or liquid, Speights said.
It's also widely available - found everywhere from convenience stores and petrol stations to vape shops.
Also, because of the supplement classification, kratom products are not federally regulated.

"There's no way to know exactly what you're getting," Speight said. "You could go and create something in your basement, market it as a supplement, and nobody's really going to check and see what's in it."
What is kratom used for?
Kratom is often marketed as a safe, natural herbal supplement that helps with pain management, anxiety and depression.
In lower doses, its stimulant properties create a "caffeine-kind of buzz", Speights explained.
Because of its opioid-like effects, it has also been used with the goal of curbing addictions to actual opioids like fentanyl.
Those properties stem from the way the plant's compounds - like 7-Hydroxymitragynine - activate various hormones, including dopamine.
What are the effects and how dangerous is it?
"It's almost like taking a narcotic," Speights said. "At higher doses, it can create more euphoria and give you more of a general high."
Hallucinations are possible, too.
The higher doses also pose greater risk for adverse side effects.
That includes central nervous system (CNS) depression - which is "where the deaths come in," Speights said.
CNS can result in cardiovascular collapse and loss of breathing.
Withdrawal symptoms and addiction are also risks, said Jana Wu, director of clinical integration at the addiction treatment centre Mountainside.
"It affects marriages, relationships," she said. "I've seen people lose jobs, spend thousands of dollars a month on it."
Because it's easy to develop a high tolerance to the herb, users may need to take an increasing amount to achieve the same effect over time.
"I've worked with people that were taking like up to 20 pills a day," Wu said.
Experts told the BBC that the biggest dangers come from the fact that kratom is not federally regulated.
"Is there a safe dose?" Speights said. "My answer is going to be no because - I'm going to go back to this - we don't know what's in it."
Is kratom legal?
Kratom is banned in 11 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts, North Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont and Wisconsin.
Massachusetts was the last state to make it illegal, issuing a temporary emergency order in August.
Ten years earlier, the US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) had moved to classify kratom as a Schedule 1, the most dangerous level for drugs, calling it "an imminent hazard to public safety".
But the effort failed a few months later, after the justice department said it received "numerous comments from members of the public challenging" the attempt.
That leaves states to take action, like Arizona, which recently sued a company selling kratom beverage products.
Groups opposed to kratom want states to do more, saying "gas-station drugs are poisoning our communities".
Pro-kratom groups like the American Kratom Association are pushing for bans against synthetics "posing as natural kratom".
Internationally, kratom is banned in the UK. In Europe, the laws vary by country.
In Malaysia, where the kratom tree is native, consumption and sale are banned under the Poisons Act of 1952.

articles.title: Alberta’s ‘rat patrol’ ramps up operations as vermin makes inroads in province
articles.summary:
‘Rat-free’ Canadian province recently took a verminous hit when a dead rodent turned up in town of Bowden

For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common…

blocks.text: For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common with Antarctica and the high Arctic: all locations are officially free of rats.

But on Thursday the Canadian province’s reputation as a firewall against rodent infestation took a hit when the town of Bowden announced the discovery of a dead rat and called on the province’s “rat patrol” to investigate.
“If you’ve noticed rat droppings or any signs of rats, please contact Rat Patrol Alberta so they can follow up,” the town said in a statement. “Please stay alert and report any sightings.”
Officials in Bowden did not say where in the town the rat was found.

But as global temperatures increase, rat numbers have surged in major cities. Over the past decade, rats increased by 390% in Washington DC, 300% in San Francisco and 162% in New York, according to researchers, who analysed public sightings and infestation reports. Toronto, Canada’s largest city, is facing a “perfect rat storm”, with numbers up 186% in the last 10 years.
Unlike other regions in the world that have been overrun by the wily and adaptable urban mammals, Alberta has actively fought rats from entering at all.
“Albertans have enjoyed living without the menace of rats since 1950 when the Rat Control Program was established,” the province says in its rat guide.

It cites both the province’s unique geography, with mountain ranges and boreal forest surrounding most of Alberta, and the fact that the Norway rat – “one of the most destructive creatures known to man”, the province claims – cannot survive in vast natural areas and cannot overwinter in cultivated fields. The very lack of the humans and their structures that rats need to survive has given the province a chance to ward off infestation.

In the 1950s, suspecting rats might try to enter from the east by way of neighbouring Saskatchewan, Alberta officials created a “rat control zone” – a strip of land measuring 373 miles by 18 miles (600km by 30km) – to monitor incursions that ranges from Cold Lake in the north to the Montana border in the south.
In addition, from June 1952 to July 1953, 140,000lb of 73% arsenic trioxide powder was used to treat 8,000 buildings on 2,700 farms to slow the spread of rats.

The province also amended the Agricultural Pests Act of Alberta in 1950, obliging “every person and municipality” to destroy rats they found; made posters reminiscent of a national war effort; and hosted a radio show, Call of the Land, to educate residents.
Today, there are dedicated telephone lines and an email address to report rats.
But while the rat patrol receives hundreds of calls each year, it says the vast majority are not rats but muskrats, voles and field mice.

Still, it concedes there are exceptions. “Alberta’s rat-free status means there is no resident population of rats and they are not allowed to establish themselves. It does not mean we never get rats.”

articles.title: DW shows solidarity with Georgians' commitment to democracy
articles.summary: Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.

image.caption: More than 70% of Georgians still support the country's accession to the European Union. Protesters are still fighting for a better futureImage: Sébastien Canaud/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I personally don't feel safe as a citizen in my country and as a person who has worked for independent media for a long time," Georgian media expert and advocate for press freedom Nino Robakidze told DW. Her activism with international civil society groups has made her a target in her home country.

Similarly, Georgian journalists are currently facing "physical threats, digital threats, psychological threats. And there is also financial and legal pressure around their media organizations," she reported.

Robakidze was one of the participants at DW's panel discussion "Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia," held on Thursday in Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie.

Host Jochen Rosenkranz, director of DW's Culture and Sports department, pointed out in his introduction that it had been difficult to find Georgians willing to participate in the panel. Many had refused, saying they feared the repercussions not only for themselves, but also for their friends and family.

"We're all afraid of the intimidation," Georgian-born musician, filmmaker, journalist and cultural organizer Marika Lapauri-Burk explained. She nevertheless agreed to take part in the discussion, alongside Nino Robakidze and journalist Juri Rescheto, head of DW's Riga bureau.

blocks.caption: Jochen Rosenkranz, Marika Lapauri-Burk, Nino Robakidze and Juri Rescheto at the DW discussion panel 'Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia'Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Lapauri-Burk added that the government had become increasingly creative in its arbitrary reasons to detain those with critical voices.
Local civil society groups and human rights organizations estimate that from 90 to over 100 political dissidents and protesters are currently imprisoned or in pre-trial detention.
Russian influence impacting democratization efforts
Once thought of as a leading democracy of the Caucasus region, Georgia is undergoing a rapid transition toward authoritarianism under the Georgian Dream (GD) party, in power now since 2012.

The party originally declared itself pro-European, but in recent years has sought more overtly to align with Russia. The party gained an increased majority in a contested October 2024 parliamentary election.

A month later, the GD announced the suspension of EU accession negotiations until 2028, despite a substantial majority of Georgians strongly favoring European integration. Halting the talks ignited demonstrations across the country as the government increasingly aligned its policies with Moscow.
Demonstrators try to storm Georgia's presidential palace

But the transformation could be felt years before the election: "The real pressure on independent media and professional journalists escalated after the Russia's unprovoked invasion in Ukraine," says Robakidze. An important anti-Western campaign followed the invasion, which "had a huge impact on Georgian media environment at large," she added.

The country was also rocked by anti-government protests in 2023-2024 as pro-EU protesters took to the streets. They were pushing back against new, Russian-style "foreign agents" legislation, which required all organizations that received foreign funding to register with the state and comply with extensive reporting requirements.

That came into force in June 2025, and a stricter version has introduced criminal liability and prison sentences of up to five years for individuals and groups who fail to register their activities as being "under foreign influence."

blocks.caption: Nino Robakidze speaking at the panel 'Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia'Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Culture directly affected by the law

Many independent cultural institutions, festivals, arts organizations and heritage projects are heavily reliant on funding from the European Union, European foundations and international cultural programs.
Critics say the law stigmatizes institutions for their vaguely defined "foreign influence."
The same laws that target activists and journalists threaten the grants, partnerships and institutions that have connected Georgian artists to Europe for decades.

The state agency responsible for enforcing the "foreign agents" law, known as the Anti-Corruption Bureau, uses the law to persecute prominent civil society groups, launching inspections and freezing their bank accounts.
Another law also operates in tandem with the controversial "foreign agent" legislation.

Georgia's anti-LGBTQ law, officially a legislative package entitled "On Family Values and the Protection of Minors," explicitly bans the "popularization" or "propaganda" of same-sex relationships and non-binary gender identities in public spaces, media, education and the arts.
Freedom of expression under threat
Cultural producers are forced to risk choosing between self-censorship, shutting down entirely or facing severe state retaliation.

"The situation is becoming increasingly difficult for critical thinkers — especially artists," explained Juri Rescheto, who notes that many critical thinkers can be found within artistic circles. They are affected "not only in their art but also in their private lives," he added.

Rescheto cited the example of a small gallery he visited in the city of Gori, where protesters' slogans were projected onto a wall as part of an exhibition. It all felt "harmless, really — or so we would say here in the West," the journalist said. Yet the gallery is now facing closure because the city refuses to renew their lease since the action, he added.

blocks.caption: A protest performance by the 'Vaso Abashidze State New Theater' in 2025Image: Jerome Gilles/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artists have generally been playing a powerful role in the protests: "There were many actions that were very artistically conceived," Lapauri-Burk noted.

"Ode to Joy" from Ludwig van Beethoven's 9th Symphony — the official anthem of the European Union — has often been played as a pro-European symbol of democratic resistance at anti-government protests in Tbilisi, Georgia, Rescheto added.
DW's new Georgian-language service
This year, Georgia is the focus of the Beethovenfest's Campus Project; a cultural exchange project developed in cooperation with DW.

"Music transcends borders and language barriers and brings people together," DW's director general Barbara Massing noted at the opening of the panel discussion, which also celebrated the recent launch of DW's new Georgian-language service on Instagram. Georgian has now become Deutsche Welle's 33rd language.

blocks.caption: DW's director general Barbara Massing at the James-Simon-Galerie in BerlinImage: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: "With the new Georgian-language service in cooperation with France Medias Monde and TVP World, we are strengthening the European commitment to free media and trustworthy information in a region that is specifically targeted by disinformation campaigns and faces unique political and social challenges," said Massing.

Robakidze welcomes such an initiation supporting Georgians who still hope for a democratic future. Severe fatigue, state crackdowns and a sense of despair among participants is seeing protest dwindling. Even so, "We still need to remain ready to take action," she said. To that end, "We need all the media support we can get."

articles.title: 'Lithuanian skies are NATO skies': DW speaks with Lithuanian premier Mindaugas Sinkevicius
articles.summary: In a DW interview, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius discussed threats to Lithuania from Russia and Belarus, NATO's need for stronger air defense and why military spending alone cannot ensure…

image.caption: Sinkevicius said that 'if Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well'Image: Denis Kishinevskiy/DW

blocks.text: Lithuania is on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, security has become one of the country's central political priorities.

The 42-year-old Mindaugas Sinkevicius recently took over as prime minister and also leads Lithuania's Social Democratic Party, a moderate center-left political force. In an exclusive interview with DW, he said he is concerned by the growing popularity of populist and far-right parties across Europe, particularly in Western Europe. But he also argued that the picture is more complicated, pointing to Social Democratic governments in several European countries and signs of renewed support for the center-left elsewhere.

For Lithuania, the war in Ukraine is closely connected to its own security. The country has experienced a series of incidents involving drones, instrumentalized migration and weather balloons entering its territory from Belarus. Sinkevicius said these developments have contributed to a broader sense of insecurity across Europe.
"As politicians, we have to tell society the truth," he said, identifying air defense as Lithuania's most urgent security priority.
"Lithuania's airspace is NATO's common airspace. Lithuanian skies are NATO skies," he said. "If Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well."
Drone incidents in Lithuania and beyond

Sinkevicius said Lithuania is seeking greater solidarity from its allies, pointing out that the threat goes beyond its national borders. A series of incidents involving drones have affected other European countries as well.
Sinkevicius stressed that NATO membership does not mean Lithuania can simply rely on its allies. Collective defense, he argued, works only when individual members are prepared to contribute.
How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare

"Of course, there is Article 5. Of course, there is collective defense," he said, referring to the NATO pact. "But at the same time, we need to do certain things ourselves, rather than relying solely on our partners, neighbors and alliances."

For Lithuania, this means strengthening its own deterrence capabilities while continuing to work through NATO and regional partnerships. He also pointed to the Nordic-Baltic Eight, or NB8, as an important framework for cooperation between the countries of Northern Europe and the Baltic states.
National security climbs national agenda
Sinkevicius rejected the idea that European countries should choose between traditional military equipment and newer technologies such as drones.
"Sometimes we see these issues being pitted against each other: drones versus tanks," he said. "I say we need both."

But for the Lithuanian prime minister, military equipment only goes so far. "Neither drones nor tanks will protect us if society does not feel safe, if people do not feel a connection with the state," he said.
Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation'
For Sinkevicius, that connection is linked to social policy as well as defense. He argued that a state must also support people who are unemployed, ill or otherwise vulnerable.

The argument reflects a broader challenge for Sinkevicius as leader of Lithuania's Social Democratic Party. Traditionally, Social Democrats have focused more on social policy, education and healthcare than on defense. Russia's war against Ukraine has changed the political environment, forcing center-left governments in Europe to place national security much higher on their agendas.
Sinkevicius said the challenge is to increase defense capabilities without abandoning the principles of social democracy.
'We will continue to support Ukraine'

Sinkevicius recently traveled to Kyiv and Lutsk, some 400 kilometers (250 miles) west of the capital, where he met with Ukrainian political leaders. Lithuania has committed to allocating at least 0.25% of its GDP annually to support Ukraine. According to figures cited by the Ukrainian side, Lithuania's support in recent years has amounted to around 0.3% of GDP.
The prime minister acknowledges that some degree of war fatigue exists in Europe. But he said European societies should consider the scale of what Ukrainians have experienced.
"I sometimes ask myself: if we Europeans feel tired, then what must Ukrainian society be feeling?" he said.
Sinkevicius also pointed to the key role of Western European countries, particularly Germany, in maintaining support for Ukraine.

"Support and assistance must continue," he said. "Because if the Western front, figuratively speaking, weakens and falters, then on the eastern front — where Russia is fighting Ukraine — the risk of failure increases."

articles.title: Bundesliga, other top European leagues call for major FIFA reforms
articles.summary: The Bundesliga and three other leading European football leagues have said major reforms to world-governing body FIFA are "essential." However, they stopped short of calling for the resignation of…

image.caption: FIFA has come in for much recent criticism over a private investment plan, which was quickly droppedImage: Christian Spicker/IMAGO

blocks.text: The letter released this Friday and signed by the heads of the Bundesliga, the Premier League, La Liga and Serie A called for major changes to how FIFA operates — and for a greater say in decision-making.

"Football's ​longstanding foundations have, in recent years, been threatened by a fundamental governance problem, whereby FIFA's president has actively promoted exploitative ​ideas rather than safeguarding against them," it said.
FFE private investment plan dropped

FIFA President Gianni Infantino has been facing a wave of criticism since late July, when his plan for private investment through a commercial vehicle, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), emerged. The idea was for FFE to organize FIFA's tournaments while maximizing profits.

Vigorous opposition from UEFA, European football's governing body, as well as CONCACAF (North and Central America plus the Caribbean) and the Asian Football Confederation led Infantino to quickly drop the plan.

However, the league bosses noted that this had not solved a deeper problem and appeared to dismiss a recent announcement by Infantino of an independent external review of FIFA governance as well as consultations on strengthening decision-making processes.
'Fundamental governance reform essential'

"It is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE — fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within FIFA, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference," Friday's letter from the leagues said.

The last line was in reference to the widespread discontent around FIFA's handling of the Folarin Balogun case, with the United States striker's one-match ban being suspended to allow him to play a World Cup last-16 match against Belgium in July. While the ban was imposed by FIFA's disciplinary committee, it came after US President Donald Trump had personally called Infantino asking for a "review" of the ban — something Trump publicly admitted.

blocks.caption: The suspension of Folarin Balogun's one-match World Cup ban following a call from Trump to Infantino caused controversyImage: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The leagues on Friday called for greater checks and balances to be implemented at FIFA, while at the same time demanding that they and others be given a say in decisions such as increases in the number of international matches.
Stakeholders 'not meaningfully involved in process'

The letter went on to say that "… when FIFA takes major unilateral decisions directly affecting us — for example, by expanding the International Match Calendar (IMC) and extending the periods in which domestic competitions must pause — the stakeholders most affected are not meaningfully involved in the decision-making process.
"A FIFA governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose."
The letter, while implying much criticism of Infantino, did not call for him to step down 3 it didn't even mention him by name.
Search for a challenger ongoing
The letter comes as UEFA has said it is looking for a suitable candidate to challenge Infantino in the next presidential election in March, in which Infantino has said he will run for reelection.

UEFA has also called for an independent external review of how the FFE plan was developed, and has filed legal applications through the US courts for the disclosure of documents related to the plan. This was with a view to a possible criminal complaint being lodged in Switzerland if it is established that Infantino undervalued FFE at $20 billion (€17.5 billion).
FIFA has described UEFA's legal moves as a "smear campaign" against it but has not yet commented on Friday's letter from the league bosses.
Infantino aims to discuss his proposals at a FIFA Council meeting in Zurich on October 15, a week after UEFA is to hold a meeting of all of its 55 member associations on October 8 in Berlin.
Any person aiming to challenge Infantino in the March 18, 2027 FIFA presidential election must register as a candidate by November 18.

articles.title: Pakistan locks down Islamabad as Imran Khan’s party vows to march on capital
articles.summary:
Tens of thousands of police deployed and roads barricaded as PTI party demands release of jailed former PM

Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide…
articles.byline: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad and Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi

blocks.text: Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide demonstration in Pakistan to demand the former prime minister’s release, even as the government deployed tens of thousands of police to Islamabad, barricaded highways and issued arrest warrants to try to stop the march.

The state has taken extreme measures to prevent Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party from proceeding with the march, due to take place over the weekend. It was announced after mounting concerns of the treatment of Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges.
On Friday, deliberation continued among PTI leaders over whether to begin the march on Sunday and move slowly towards Islamabad to “exhaust the government” or whether to delay until next week.

Analysts said the protest could present a major challenge to the military-backed government, which is widely regarded as weak, illegitimate and unpopular, while Khan remains a popular rallying figure. The ruling coalition is led by the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, but the army chief, Field Marshall Asim Munir, is widely seen as the country’s de facto leader.

This week, dozens of PTI leaders and ministers have been detained or given with arrest warrants, while Khan’s three sisters were arrested on Monday and remain in jail, charged with posing a “grave threat” to security.

Among those facing arrest is Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khan’s home province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, PTI’s stronghold where thousands of supporters are expected to join the march to the capital.

blocks.caption: Sohail Afridi at a press conference in Peshawar, where he insisted the march would proceed. Photograph: Arshad Arbab/EPA

blocks.text: Afridi said the PTI would carry out the march unless the government made significant concessions over Khan’s treatment and conditions in jail, including a fair hearing for Khan’s cases.
“The government is panicking – that’s why they have put Islamabad under siege, that’s why they are abducting our ministers,” he said.

“But Imran Khan is the most popular leader of the country and people will come out for him. I am certain they won’t be able to stop the public power of the masses when they come out on streets and take to Islamabad.”

Afridi acknowledged the scale of the security deployment had led many to fear there could be a violent confrontation to prevent Khan’s supporters entering the capital, as had been seen in previous demonstrations.
The government has already deployed tens of thousands of security officials to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and shut down the main highway connecting the provincial capital, Peshawar, to Islamabad.

“I know they can go to any extent to stop us by brute force, we have no doubt about it,” added Afridi. “But if we have a large number of people, they can’t open fire at us. Our plan is to bring so many people that they surrender.”

Faisal Karim Kundi, the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa – a central government appointee – defended the security measures being taken against PTI as “precautionary” and accused the party of trying to create “instability and violence”.
“The state can’t allow any violent group to march on Islamabad,” said Kundi.
Public frustration has mounted in Islamabad as the government’s measures to stop Khan’s party supporters having any way to enter the capital has led to the city resembling a high-security fortress.

blocks.caption: More than 1,000 shipping containers have been used to block access at key roads into the city. Photograph: Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

blocks.text: More than 1,000 shipping containers, many fortified with spikes, have blockaded roads and sandbags were placed on bridges, while a key highway into the capital was closed. Public gatherings have been banned in Islamabad and 22,000 police and other security personnel have been deployed across the capital.
The government’s shutdown has fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with many businesses unable to get supplies.

Shahid, 76, a retired businessman, said: “The entire city is suffering. The government has shut down the whole city and we, as citizens, are helpless. I have never seen such a situation. Joblessness, inflation and insecurity has made our lives hell but does the government care? No.”

Despite the considerable efforts by the government and the military to crush Khan’s party and remove the former prime minister from the public consciousness – with media organisations instructed to not even refer to him by name – Khan is still viewed by many as the political alternative to the current regime.
The PTI alleges Khan is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied adequate medical treatment and any contact with his family or his lawyers for months.

blocks.caption: Aleema Khanum (centre), one of Imran Khan’s sisters, at a protest near Adiala jail, where Khan is being held. She was arrested earlier this week. Photograph: SALAHUDDIN/Reuters

blocks.text: Khan denies all the charges against him and alleges he is being imprisoned due to the political threat he poses to the ruling government and the country’s powerful military. All but one of the court rulings against Khan have been overturned.

Analysts say the government and its military backers fear the PTI protest could escalate into a movement that could topple their administration, similar to protests seen in nearby Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

“They have an eye on what has happened in south Asia over the last five years, where country after country has seen huge protests snowballing suddenly out of nowhere and sweeping away a government,” said Niaz Murtaza, a Pakistani political columnist.

“Given the breadth of grievances in Pakistan at the moment – the performance of the government has been so poor on the economy and security while the repression is so high – that they are very nervous that the whole situation could combust very quickly.”

articles.title: Pomp over progress as Trump rolls out red carpet for China’s president Xi Jinping
articles.summary: While the US president hailed the visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved, which was a win for Xi

blocks.text: If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.

Instead, it was dubbed a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress, and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to the Atlanta Zoo.

Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi when he landed on Wednesday, and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit which involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad, the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting which Trump described as “great” and which revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaways is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.

blocks.caption: Expectations going into the summit were low. Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.

To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.

With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.

That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.

On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in over a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.

“This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear,” said William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group. The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues.”

China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
“Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis a vis China,” said Gewirtz.

Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.

blocks.caption: For China, the lack of big news from the state visit is a win in itself. Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPA

blocks.text: On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the X-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump that he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.

For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale which Beijing would like to see disappear completely.

On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is”, adding: “That is China’s position also.”

For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” said Thomas. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title: Hurricane Polo barrels towards Baja California region of Mexico
articles.summary:
Area’s second-most intense hurricane on record being fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific waters

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system…

blocks.text: Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.

Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.

In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.

Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

articles.title: At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
articles.summary:
Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade

Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with…

blocks.text: Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.

At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain.

Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.

“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.

“We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”

With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, referring to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.
Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.

His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.

blocks.caption: Trump and Xi speak next to Marine One at the White House. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters

blocks.text: Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president.
“President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said.

Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”

He said the current visit would include discussion over security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.
Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”

Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.”
The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.

Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on.
Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.

blocks.caption: China’s first lady Peng Liyuan, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and US first lady Melania Trump walk to a state dinner. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures.

“Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,” he said. “On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.”
Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader.
“President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said.
Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded “common understanding on many issues”, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together.
“China ⁠and the United States must act as responsible major countries,” he said.
Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.

blocks.caption: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman talks to Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg during the state dinner. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

blocks.text: In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.

A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said.

Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.
Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continued to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running.
Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting
